title: Packers CB Brandon Cisse Updates Health, Rookie Progress
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers cornerback Brandon Cisse is a bit like those old Timex watch commercials that he’s far too young to remember.
He’s taken a licking and kept on ticking.
Cisse missed the final 8 minutes of Sunday night’s win over the Dallas Cowboys due to a stinger but will be in the starting lineup, as usual, for Sunday’s game against the rival Detroit Lions.
“It’s just numb,” Cisse said on Thursday when asked to describe the sensation. “You’ve got to wait for the arm feeling to come back (and) you can’t really feel your fingers. It’s just kind of like your shoulder and everything goes numb for a second.”
After being limited participation for a second consecutive day with neck and shoulder injuries, Cisse proclaimed himself “all good.”
“I’m rehabbing and doing good,” he said.
Cisse has started all six games but dropped out of three of them with cramps or injuries. He’s been on the injury report for neck, shoulder and hip injuries. He even was limited for a couple days before the Atlanta game after having a wisdom tooth removed. He’d obviously rather have played every snap in every game this season, but his ability to answer the call has been impressive.
He knows his importance to the team as a starting cornerback for a defense that ranks first in interceptions, third in opponent passer rating, second in passing yards allowed per attempt and sixth in passing yards allowed per game.
“Just trying to be out there as much as possible,” Cisse said. “I know the impact that I bring to the table when I’m out there and the kind of player that I can become. That comes with experience. You want to see as much as you can and be out there as much as possible and help change games and help my teammates.
“Anytime I get a chance to be out there and play through something, I’m going to be out there.”
That’s obviously of great importance for the game against the high-powered Lions. Quarterback Jared Goff is second in the league in passer rating and hasn’t thrown an interception. Amon-Ra St. Brown is one of the league’s best receivers. Jameson Williams is a big-play threat. Isaac TeSlaa is a quality No. 3 receiver.
“Obviously a big challenge,” Cisse said. “They’ve got a very good core of guys. Obviously, they’ve done a really good job with their receiver room there. They’ve got four guys who can really play and, obviously, the tight end’s a really big challenge, as well. And the running back is one of the best in the league, if not the best in the league.
“And, obviously, the quarterback’s an elite quarterback. Got to make sure you’ve got your eyes in the right place and make sure we’re all ready to go.”
A similar scouting report could have been provided before last week’s game against Dallas. The Packers dominated against the Cowboys’ powerhouse group led by quarterback Dak Prescott and receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Dallas didn’t go over 200 passing yards until the fourth quarter and didn’t reach double-digits points until late in the game.
Is there confidence to be gained from a strong performance against a strong offense?
“Every week’s a new week,” he said. “It’s all about proving yourself, so every week, I try to go out there and be the best version of myself and let go of the last game and build off of it, take the good and the bad, and get the bad things corrected this week and try to go have a dominant outing this weekend.”
According to Pro Football Focus, 87 cornerbacks have played at least 100 coverage snaps entering Week 7. Cisse is tied for 32nd with a 60 percent completion rate allowed and ranks 21st with 14.2 snaps per reception allowed. He grabbed his first career interception last week against Dallas.
He’s allowed more than two catches in only two games. One was the blowout loss to Atlanta, when Drake London had a huge game against the secondary. The second was against Dallas, when he allowed 4-of-9 passing for only 46 yards.
Asked if he’s happy with his progress, Cisse shared the same sentiment from multiple interviews during training camp.
“No, not yet,” he said. “Got to keep getting better each week, keep building and see where it goes.”
Cisse is one of 13 rookie cornerbacks to have played at least 50 coverage snaps. He is second in snaps per reception and snaps per target.
“It’s definitely a hard adjustment at times, but that’s what they brought me here to do and that’s the kind of player that I know I can become,” he said. “I’m excited to keep accepting the challenge and continue to grow.”

title: Packers-Lions Thursday Injury Report: Three Huge Updates for Green Bay
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love progressed to full participation at practice on Thursday. Barring an unforeseen setback, he is locked in for Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions.
There were two additions to the injury report, and they are big ones. Starting linebacker and team captain Zaire Franklin (shin) and starting edge defender and leading pass rusher Lukas Van Ness (illness) were limited participation.
Franklin is second on the team with 41 tackles. He had games of 10, nine and eight before only three last week against Dallas, though he did have a big quarterback hit early in the game. Van Ness leads the team with 3.5 sacks and nine quarterback hits. As the team’s best pass rusher, the defense will need him to make life uncomfortable for Lions quarterback Jared Goff.
The Packers, who are coming off a Sunday night game, have 12 players on their injury report. The Lions, who are coming off their bye, have only three.
However, only one Green Bay player didn’t practice, receiver Bo Melton (back). Fellow receivers Christian Watson (ankle), Matthew Golden (shoulder) and Savion Williams (ankle) were limited participation. There’s no reason for concern, though. Watson and Golden will play, coach Matt LaFleur said before practice, and Williams made his season debut last week following an ankle injury that kept him out for five games.
Defensive tackle Jordon Riley is in his second game back from a torn Achilles.
“I think he’s shown a ton of progress,” LaFleur said before practice. “It was good to get him out there last week and get his feet wet a little bit. If he continues to show that progress, then we’ll see where we’re at and he’d be ready to go.”
Riley completed his fifth practice and has been limited in all five.
“It’s really like riding a bike, man,” he said after practice. “So each day, you going to get better. Each day, you going to remember things that you learned in the past, stuff like that. Day 1 stuff. I’m in a better spot than I ever thought I was going to be as far as technical standpoint. Each day, I learned something with my game and each day I’ve been coached up to fix it the next day. So, we doing a good job with that.”
True or false: Josh Jacobs will save the Packers' run game. ⬇️ https://t.co/JseydlPrHE
Center Sean Rhyan has played all 389 snaps this season but there was a brief scare when he was slow to get up after Love’s interception.
“They came to me,” Rhyan said. “I was like, what the f*** do I need to get checked for?”
He had to go through concussion testing, cleared it between series, and was right back on the field.
“They were saying that I got up slow or something,” he said. “When you got [Anthony Belton’s] big body falling on you, sometimes it’s like, ‘Ah, let me just feel myself real quick.’”
As the center of the line, Rhyan will have a big role in helping the offense navigate the noise at Ford Field.
“Just got to listen a little harder, I guess,” he said. “We played there a lot, we kind of know what to expect – real hostile, real loud, kind of dark, on turf. Just keep on going, you know? But at the end of the game, we’re still playing 11 on 11. So, we’re going to go over there and do our thing.”
The update is there is no update. The Lions’ injury report is unchanged from Wednesday, with every player practicing and only one player – cornerback Rock Ya-Sin (hamstring) – limited participation against while safety Brian Branch (Achilles) and center Cade Mays (wrist) were full participation.
All three players are starters. Branch is set to make his season debut following last year’s Achilles injury and Mays is poised to make his season debut, as well, after starting 12 games for the Panthers last year.
Branch will not be on a rep count, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard told reporters earlier in the week.
“Whenever you could gain a player like BB and his caliber back, it’s outstanding. You know what I mean? I’m not big on giving you projections and, ‘Oh, he’s going to do this, he’s going to do that.’ It’s just beautiful to have BB back. There are multiple things, obviously, that player can do to help us, and we’ll find the spots that we feel is right and he feels right for him as we progress here.”

title: Packers Thursday Update From Practice: Latest on Josh Jacobs, Jordan Love
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Josh Jacobs and Jordan Love practiced on Thursday, and the expectation is they will be on the field for Sunday’s game at the Detroit Lions.
Love was listed as limited participation on Wednesday’s injury report with a sore back.
“He was pretty beat up” from the Dallas game, coach Matt LaFleur said before Thursday’s practice. “He took some shots. Saw him in there with the chiropractor postgame, so I knew something was up.”
Love on Wednesday said he had “no” concerns about his availability for the game.
“We talk about it all the time: You want to, obviously, limit me taking hits in the pocket,” Love said.
Meanwhile, for the first time since the end of training camp, star running back Josh Jacobs was participating in a real practice. The team held a jog-through practice on Wednesday; Thursday was the real deal in full pads.
“We’ve been getting him ramped up,” LaFleur said. “He’s been in the building (and) we’ve been doing things with him in terms of our strength staff, our athletic training staff. Certainly, you can’t simulate football until you get out there so I think these next two days are going to be great work for him as we ramp him up.”
Josh Jacobs in slow-mo today at Packers practice. pic.twitter.com/9Ezw8UmxhC
LaFleur said there will be “a lot of conversation and a little bit of the eyeball test” before determining whether Jacobs will play against the Lions. However, Jacobs is in good shape, he knows the offense and he stayed around the team during his six-week stay on the exempt list.
For those reasons, the expectation is Jacobs will be on the field against the Lions in a battle of two-loss teams that could have significant playoff ramifications.
“Last couple months, it’s been weird, man,” he told reporters on Wednesday . “Honestly, it’s been weird. I’ve still been around the guys. Obviously, I couldn’t practice, still could go to meetings, so I’ve been around. So, it’s been weird, like just watching and knowing that you feel good and your body is probably the best that I’ve been since I’ve been here, it’s just weird. Like that’s the only way I could really explain it.”
The Packers have by far the worst rushing attack in the NFL. Jacobs, obviously, would help fix the problem.
True or false: Josh Jacobs will save the Packers' run game. ⬇️ https://t.co/JseydlPrHE
The only player who didn’t practice for the Packers was receiver Bo Melton (back).
Receivers Christian Watson (ankle) and Matthew Golden (shoulder) were limited on Wednesday, but LaFleur had no concerns about their availability for the game.
Cornerback Brandon Cisse, who missed the end of last week’s game against Dallas with a stinger, was limited on Wednesday and practicing again on Thursday.
Defensive tackle Jordon Riley, who was designated for return from injured reserve last week following last year’s torn Achilles, was limited participation on Wednesday and on the field on Thursday. He might be activated this week, which would help Green Bay’s depleted defensive line.
“I think he’s shown a ton of progress,” LaFleur said. “It was good to get him out there last week and get his feet wet a little bit. If he continues to show that progress, then we’ll see where we’re at and he’d be ready to go.”
The Packers will be behind from a preparation standpoint. While LaFleur turned Wednesday into a mental day, the Lions are healthy while coming off their bye.
“I think it’s more about getting our guys’ bodies in the right position,” he said. “I think every team around the league has had an ample number of reps. Certainly reps are at a premium, there’s no substitute for them. But, at the same, you need your guys feeling good when they go out there on the grass.”
Because they’re coming off their bye, the Lions had only three players on Wednesday’s injury report. One of them is star safety Brian Branch, who will be making his season debut following last year’s torn Achilles.
“Well, you get a tremendous football player,” LaFleur said. “I think he’s one of the best safeties in the league. There’s a lot of things he can do that others can’t, and they’re comfortable playing him man to man on wide receivers like we’ve seen in the past, and he adds an element of just physicality, toughness. Just a great player.”
The teams will release fresh injury reports after their Thursday practices. For now, here are the reports from Wednesday. The Packers, who played on Sunday night, have 10 players listed. The Lions, who had their bye, have only three.

title: True or False: Josh Jacobs Will Save Packers’ Historically Feeble Run Game
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – In Week 3, the Green Bay Packers were crushed by the Atlanta Falcons. Part of their problem that night was their offensive line was overwhelmed by the Falcons’ attacking defensive front.
At the time, it felt like the Packers would be just fine if they could get even mediocre play from their offensive line. Changes were made and, sure enough, the Packers will take a three-game winning streak into Sunday’s game at the Detroit Lions.
The Packers are 4-2 but are being held back by an impossibly bad offensive running game. Even a mediocre running game would make a huge difference for Green Bay’s offense.
Enter Josh Jacobs, who is one of the better running backs in the NFL. He can’t single-handedly rescue what’s trending toward being the worst running game in NFL history but, as coach Matt LaFleur said this week, “He’s certainly not going to hurt it.”
Will Josh Jacobs single-handedly save the running game?
The starting point for any offense is, obviously, the starting point of any series, and that’s first down.
Green Bay’s first-down running game is averaging 2.3 yards per carry. To say that’s the worst in the league is accurate. It also doesn’t do it justice. It’s a half-yard worse than No. 31 Las Vegas and a full-yard worse than No. 30 Miami. It’s 1.8 yards worse than the league median.
In 2025, Jacobs averaged 3.9 yards per first-down carry. This year, Pierre Strong leads the running backs with a 2.5-yard average.
Jacobs was stuffed – a run of 0 yards or worse – on 16 percent of his first-down carries last season. By contrast, his first-down success rate – defined as a gain of 4-plus yards – was 44.5 percent.
Compare that to this year’s run game, with 25 percent of the first-down runs resulting in stuffs and 34.2 percent being a success. In number instead of percentage, only the Dolphins have fewer successful first-down runs.
If you can’t run the ball on first down, it’s harder to throw the ball on second down. On second down overall, Jordan Love has completed 63.1 percent of his passes, averaged 7.4 yards per attempt, thrown six touchdowns and three interceptions and produced a passer rating of 94.4. He’s been sacked four times.
Digging deeper, on second-down plays requiring 8-plus yards, Love has completed 63.2 percent of his passes and averaged 9.3 yards per attempt. That’s as good as (or better) than he is overall on second down. However, he’s thrown one touchdown and two interceptions (84.5 passer rating) and taken all four sacks.
On second-and-7 or less, Love has thrown five touchdowns with just one interception (93.1 rating) and has not been sacked.
According to Sumer Sports, teams facing second-and-10 or longer this season have a 46.9 percent chance of eventually getting a first down. A gain of 3-plus yards moves that all the way to 72.5 percent. It’s not quite as extreme for Green Bay, with 50.0 percent on second-and-10 or longer and 67.4 percent on second-and-7 or shorter.
Still, it’s common sense that a first-down running play that gains a few yards is better than a first-down run that gets stopped at the line.
Obviously, Jacobs can’t turn a horrendous rushing attack into a quality rushing attack by himself. According to Sumer Sports, a whopping 81.1 percent of Green Bay’s rushing total has come after contact.
“I think it relies on everybody,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “Whether it’s scheme or blocking or running, I think everyone has to do a better job, starting with me. That’s the biggest thing. That’s a big focus for us as we’re going further into the season. Now, Josh I think will definitely help for sure. He’s an excellent player and he’ll provide some good spark for our offense, so I’m excited about that. But we just all need to do a better job.”
True, but with his toughness and vision, Jacobs will improve the first-down rushing offense – and, therefore, the offense as a whole.
According to Sports Info Solutions, MarShawn Lloyd is averaging 1.8 yards after contact per carry, Chris Brooks is averaging 1.8 yards and Pierre Strong is averaging 1.6. The only productive player has been Kaleb Johnson, who broke a couple tackles on his long run at Tampa Bay and is averaging 2.9 yards after contact. But he wound up in the doghouse after a couple fumbles and played just four snaps last week.
With the Packers, Jacobs averaged 3.1 yards after contact in 2024 and 2.9 in 2025.
“I think he’s an elite-level back,” LaFleur said this week.
More than anything, Jacobs will take what’s there and fight for a little more. Instead of trying to bounce runs around the perimeter, like Lloyd does too frequently, he’ll find the smallest of holes and turn something into something more. Last season, according to Sumer Sports, 80.6 percent of his rushing yards came after contact. Among the 52 backs with 100 carries, that ranked fifth.
Jacobs hasn’t carried the ball since last year’s playoff game. There will be some rust and he’ll need to work his way into football shape.
“Hell, yeah,” safety Xavier McKinney said when asked if Jacobs is ready. “I’ve been watching him work out and getting ready for whenever that moment was going to come. And now that it’s here, obviously, it might be some rust here and there, but a fresh-legged Josh is going to be a monster, so it’s going to be good to see.”
LaFleur wasn’t quite as bullish, saying “the eyeball test” following practices on Thursday and Friday would be the determining factor.
Will Josh Jacobs save the running game? True, if by “save” we mean improve to an acceptable level to help the offense take the next step. It worked on the offensive line with the signing of Laken Tomlinson and the insertion of Travis Glover. Certainly, adding a proven force like Jacobs will have a sizable impact, as well.

title: How Return of Josh Jacobs Will Impact Packers’ Running Game, Depth Chart
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs returned to the practice field on Wednesday. Will he return to the playing field on Sunday at the Detroit Lions?
“My goal is to play,” Jacobs said on Wednesday. “I don’t know how much they’re going to allow me to play, honestly. Especially with having a walkthrough today, I didn’t really get too many reps – real reps. I don’t know what their mindset is. If it’s up to me, I’m going to try to play.”
Jacobs talked to reporters for the first time since his arrest following an altercation with a woman over Memorial Day Weekend, an incident in which he ultimately entered a no-contest plea.
Jacobs spent the first six weeks of the season on the exempt list, meaning he could work out and attend meetings but not practice or play in games.
Coach Matt LaFleur said Jacobs was in good shape, and Jacobs took his time away seriously.
“I’ve been actually practicing with my helmet and shoulder pads, so it’s not like it’s overly different,” Jacobs said. “But just trying to get back to the flow of the guys, simple stuff like being in the huddle, listening to the play call and going out there and executing within that 5-second, 6-second span.”
Here is just about every word of what Packers RB Josh Jacobs said yesterday. ⬇️ https://t.co/3IamXUeG5X
There’s also the matter of building chemistry with the offensive line. He’s never played in a game with Jordan Morgan at left tackle. He’s never played in a game with left guard Laken Tomlinson. Other than the playoff game at the Eagles in 2024, he’s never played in a game with right guard Travis Glover, who was a rookie at the time. He’s played less than 90 snaps with Anthony Belton as the right tackle.
That’s all compounded by the Packers not holding a real practice on Wednesday, with LaFleur navigating a challenging stretch of the Sunday night game against Dallas, a division road game at Detroit and a Thursday night game against Carolina.
Added together, Jacobs has to navigate through close to two months of not practicing and trying to build chemistry with an offensive line that looks a lot different than the one he ran behind the last two seasons or even training camp.
“And also just getting back in the flow of the guys,” Jacobs said. “We’ve got guys even up front that I’ve never played with. That’s another thing. But we’re going to see how it goes. I don’t know where we’re going to be at this week, or if I’m actually going to play or not. All I’m trying to do is get prepared to play if they let me.”
On the other hand, there’s the state of the running game. It’s bad. Really bad. Impossible-to-be-worse ba d. On a history-making-trend bad.
The Packers are last in the NFL – by wide margins – with 59.8 rushing yards per game and 2.87 yards per carry. They are on pace to finish with the fewest rushing yards per game in NFL history.
They haven’t rushed for more than 3.5 yards per carry in a game. The league median is 4.05 yards per carry. If Green Bay’s season average was 3.5, it would rank 30th in the league.
It’s no wonder why quarterback Jordan Love said he’s “happy to have Josh back” with the team.
Can the return of Jacobs cure what’s plagued the rushing attack?
“We’ll see. We’ll see,” Love said. “It’s not really a question I can answer right now. I think, obviously, we know what type of player Josh is and I think he’ll definitely improve [it] just having him out there. But, yeah, we’ll see.”
Maybe nobody on the team knows Jacobs better than Xavier McKinney. They were teammates together at Alabama and signed by the Packers in 2024. Both players have been team captains in Green Bay.
“It was good – good to see him back,” McKinney said. “Obviously, we’ve been waiting on him, but, yeah, it’s good to see him back, man. He brings that energy. We know what type of player he is, and, sh**, we’re happy to see him back, dawg, for sure.”
The Packers the last two games have leaned on MarShawn Lloyd and Pierre Strong in the backfield due to Kaleb Johnson’s two fumbles and Chris Brooks’ injury. Lloyd, who leads the team with 48 carries, is averaging 1.96 yards after contact per carry, according to Pro Football Focus. Strong, who got most of the work against Dallas, is averaging 1.88 yards after contact.
Jacobs last season averaged 3.06 yards after contract. In 2024, when he rushed for 1,329 yards, he averaged 3.45 after contact.
That’s where Jacobs can save the running game – with his ability to turn nothing into something.
The NFL gave the Packers a one-week roster exemption for Jacobs. They have only 50 players on the 53-man roster, so no corresponding roster move will be needed once Jacobs is officially back on the roster.
The depth chart is another matter.
With Chris Brooks spending a second week on injured reserve, the Packers against Dallas had Pierre Strong on the field for 41 snaps. MarShawn Lloyd played 30 snaps, the third consecutive week around that number. Kaleb Johnson played only four snaps; he’s gone from 16, 24 and 17 to nine and four.
Lloyd was drafted in the third round in 2024. After playing in only one game in two seasons, he’s been healthy all year but hasn’t made much of an impact.
Strong seemed to be trending toward a spot on the roster during training camp but was the odd man out after the trade for Johnson. After Brooks landed on injured reserve after the Tampa Bay game, Strong was promoted from the practice squad. He hasn’t done much as a runner but was impressive by breaking a few tackles during a pair of third-and-13 conversions against Dallas.
Johnson was a third-round pick by Pittsburgh in 2025 but quickly fell out of favor; the Packers acquired him for a 2028 sixth-round pick. That’s not a huge investment if the Packers wanted to switch gears.
For now, because they have openings on the roster, the team can go to Detroit with all four players on the 53-man roster and make Johnson a gameday inactive.
In the long run, Jacobs – assuming he avoids a suspension that puts him back on the sideline – will reclaim his role as the No. 1 running back and Brooks will return from injured reserve and be back in the third-down role in which he was so valuable last year. The Packers probably aren’t going to give up on Lloyd.
The question from there is whether the Packers will roll with three running backs on the 53 – Jacobs, Lloyd and Brooks – or if the state of the roster will allow them to keep four. Four running backs is a lot; only five teams have more than three on their 53-man roster.
If they keep four: Strong has shown his value and versatility, though the team might see something in Johnson worth developing. Will general manager Brian Gutekunst value short-term production (Strong) or long-term upside (Johnson)? The ability to get one or both to the practice squad could factor in the decision-making.
What is absolutely certain is the Packers’ No. 1 running back will be back in the lineup, perhaps as soon as Sunday’s game against the rival Lions. He is an impact player on the field and in the locker room.
“Leadership, playmaking ability, all of the above,” Xavier McKinney said. “I mean, a great teammate, great dude. I’ve known him for a little while now, so I know the level of impact that he makes on the game and also the level of impact that he can make on a team, as well.
“So I understand every component of it, just how a lot of these guys do in this locker room, and we know that he was eager to get back out there with us. And now that he’s out there with us, he’s happy and he’s ready to put into work.”

title: Here’s Everything Josh Jacobs Said About Return to Packers, Re-Evaluating Life
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – For the first time since the Memorial Day Weekend incident that led to missing the first six games of the season, Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs talked to reporters about the arrest, punishment and return to the team he had captained the previous two seasons.
“Obviously, you never want to be in this situation, but just me being honest, for my life, it was probably one of the best things to ever happen to me,” Jacobs said outside the locker room at Lambeau Field on Wednesday afternoon.
“I say that because it gave me a chance to sit down and re-evaluate what’s important and what I want my life to look like, and what do I want people to know me for. When they think of me, what are they going to say? Another thing that it showed me was the people that were in my corner. A lot of people I didn’t even know or even expect to be in my corner, they showed up. So that was huge for me. It just gave me more appreciation, more love honestly for this organization and this team.”
It was his most powerful statement of the day. Since the NFL is continuing to investigate, Jacobs was limited in what he could say. So, there was no explanation of what happened on May 23.
But he expressed remorse for putting the team through the ordeal, gratitude for the team for standing by him and an eagerness to return to the football field.
Throughout the 9-plus minutes with reporters, he spoke nervously. His lips quivered at times and he frequently rubbed his chest.
Here are the highlights of what he said.
Jacobs did not speak from notes or read a statement. Instead, he spoke for 1 minute, 23 seconds to open the conversation.
“First, I’m excited to be back with the team, with the guys. I want to say thank you to the organization, really, for supporting me throughout this whole process and how everything played out. With that being said, I can’t get into a lot of things like specifics of things but, obviously, man, I’m remorseful and sorry for putting this team in this situation.
“Sometimes when you go through life, situations occur and a 4-second, 3-second decision can alter your life, honestly. But with that being said, still a human being, man, still trying to learn, still trying to grow from the whole process. Actually learned a lot throughout this process legally and just personally. But going forward, man, I just try to be better.
“I know for some people this might be a stain on me and my character. I feel like I don’t have to really speak on my character. A lot of people that know me in this locker room or that’s been around me, I’ll let them do that. But for me, man, I’m just trying to come back in here and play ball, learn from this mistake and move forward.”
Jacobs said he wasn’t “overly concerned” about his career being over because “in my heart, I know what happened and what didn’t happen.”
Jacobs spent the first six games of the season on the exempt list, meaning he could not practice or play with the team but could attend meetings and workout.
“I think six games was a lot, honestly, but that’s not really up to me to decide,” he said. “I’m grateful to be playing, so that’s not even something that I’m like arguing or petitioning with. I’m just happy to be back on the team.”
The NFL is continuing its investigation. A suspension is the expectation; the question is whether it will sideline him for more games.
“Honestly, I thought it would be sooner,” he said. “I thought it’d be sooner. I thought I’d be playing sooner. But, you know, the optics of everything, I understand the other side. For me, like I said, I’m just grateful to be able to play. It was one of them things where I didn’t want to sit the whole year and then figure it out. I’m just grateful to be back on the team and to be back playing.”
Josh Jacobs on the possibility of not playing again. pic.twitter.com/ErkJELwnNt
Jacobs was arrested over Memorial Day Weekend and addressed the team shortly thereafter.
“I was just apologizing to the guys because I know a lot of guys look up to me, a lot of guys come to me about real-life issues and things that go on in their lives. And so for me, being that guy for a lot of people, it’s weird when you take that fall. For me, it’s just trying to show everybody like, you know, I’m not better than the next person. I still deal with my own personal things.
“But, at the end of the day, just know that I’m still be here, I’m still show up and I’m still be the same guy. But really the main story was for me, when we had that meeting, was me being apologetic for the attention that it’s brought to this team having the guys have to answer or watch what they say when it comes to that, so that’s just something I had to take accountability for.”
For Jacobs, his focus has been on the team – the players, coaches and front office – and not about winning over fans who turned on him following whatever happened almost five months ago, which concluded legally with him pleading no contest to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property.
“No, I don’t think I had to earn respect back from the guys because I’m the same person every day. Like I said, at the end of the day, we human. We all make mistakes. It’s just different for me because I’m in the public eye.
“Like I said, I’ll let other people speak to my character and who I am and who I consistently have been. When it comes to earning the respect for the fans, I mean, for me, it’s more of a thing of not trying to put this organization in a position where it looks negative in any type of way. At the end of the day, people are always going to have they opinion. People are going to believe what they believe, and it’s not really my job to try to explain or discount certain things. All I can try to do is control what I can control and move on from there.”
Later, he made the same point about the fans, who have formed their opinion based on the facts made public and are unlikely to be persuaded one way or the other.
“I’m not trying to win nobody back, and that’s just me being all the way honest because, at the end of the day, like I said, I know what happened and if you feel some type of way – obviously, I feel bad because it’s still a situation occurred and it should’ve never even happened, so that’s something that I still will understand if people feel some type of way about it.
“But, like I said, all I can do is keep showing up and being who I am, being a leader for this team, being a leader in this community and that’s really all I can control.”
Jacobs will practice this week before a determination is made about his availability for Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions. While he hasn’t been practicing with the team, he’s been in meetings and has been working out.
“I’ve been actually practicing with my helmet and shoulder pads, so it’s not like it’s like overly different,” he said. “But just trying to get back to the flow of the guys, simple stuff like being in the huddle, listening to the play call and going out there and executing within that 5-second, 6-second span.
“And also just getting back in the flow of the guys. We’ve got guys even up front that I’ve never played with. That’s another thing. But we’re going to see how it goes. I don’t know where we’re going to be at this week, or if I’m actually going to play or not. All I’m trying to do is get prepared to play if they let me.”
Jacobs isn’t sure if he’ll play, but that’s his goal.
“If it’s up to me,” he said, “I’m going to play.”

title: Packers-Lions Wednesday Injury Report: Here’s What Jordan Love Said About Sore Back
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Jordan Love has taken a beating at times this season. For the first time, it’s shown on the injury report.
The Green Bay Packers’ star quarterback, who has carried the load for most of the team’s 4-2 start, was deemed limited participation on Wednesday, the first day of on-the-field work before Sunday’s NFC North showdown at the Detroit Lions.
He said “no” when asked if he was concerned that he will not be in the lineup against Detroit.
Coming off a Sunday night game and with a Thursday night game looming against the Panthers, coach Matt LaFleur conducted a “jog-through” practice on Wednesday but will put the team in pads for a “really good” practice on Thursday.
That was welcome news for Love. After two games of strong pass protection in wins over Tampa Bay and Chicago, it was another painful week for Love in the win over Dallas.
“It’s just dealing with a sore back from the game,” he said. “Just some lingering effects from that. One of those things, we’ll just take it day by day but, obviously, it was nice to have a jog-through day, a little bit more mental day, and just recover.”
By the official stats, Love and Cleveland’s Deshaun Watson have absorbed a league-high 45 hits through Week 6.
He was hit eight times and sacked on three against the Cowboys.
“Obviously, just with the back, I don’t know exactly what play it happened on, when it happened,” Love said. “We talk about all the time: You want to, obviously, limit me taking hits in the pocket. That’s something that we’ve talked about, we harp on, and there’s been some better efforts to do better and protect better. I think guys are responding to that. It’s one of those things, yeah, you want to be able to limit as many hits as I take.”
Only one player, receiver Bo Melton (back), would not have practiced. Nine players were limited, including Love and receivers Matthew Golden (shoulder) and Christian Watson (ankle).
Running back Josh Jacobs, who is returning after six weeks on the exempt list, is not on the injury report.
“I’ve been actually practicing with my helmet and shoulder pads, so it’s not like it’s overly different,” Jacobs said. “I don’t know where we’re going to be at this week, or if I’m actually going to play or not. All I’m trying to do is get prepared to play if they let me.”
Fortunately for the Packers, while they have a long injury report, just about everyone practiced, which will help the team get ready for the deafening environment at Ford Field.
“It pretty much is you try to simulate that crowd noise as best as possible but that place is usually rocking pretty good and it’s hard to [communicate],” LaFleur said. “Good thing is we’ve had a couple road games where we’ve had to deal with that. So, you get some practice with that. That’s something that we train all offseason. We have days where we go on the silent count and all that. So, I think our guys will be ready for it.”
The Lions are coming off their bye. Every player on the roster practiced, including safety Brian Branch, who is set to return from last year’s torn Achilles.
“Here's what's great about getting BB back,” Lions coach Dan Campbell told reporters. “BB gives you the flexibility – is what do you want to do with anybody else? Because there are things you're going to want to do with BB high, let him play top-down, and then there are things you want him to play underneath. And that doesn't require somebody else playing off of him necessarily. He'll make it right.“
Did not participate: WR Bo Melton (back).
Limited participation: LG Aaron Banks (knee/toe), DT Anthony Campbell (ankle), CB Brandon Cisse (hip), WR Matthew Golden (shoulder), QB Jordan Love (back), DT Jordon Riley (Achilles), CB Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring), WR Christian Watson (ankle), WR Savion Williams (ankle).
Riley has been designated to return from injured reserve and is within his 21-day practice windows.
Limited participation: CB Rock Ya-Sin (hamstring).
Full participation: S Brian Branch (Achilles), C Cade Mays (wrist).

title: Jordan Love Getting Crushed by Drops; Why Aren’t Packers Crushing Panic Button?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are dropping the ball on what should be a blockbuster season for quarterback Jordan Love.
With Week 7 of the NFL season on the horizon, Love has been victimized by a league-high 19 dropped passes, according to Pro Football Focus. No other quarterback has had more than 11 passes dropped. The six quarterbacks who’ve played for the other NFC North teams have had 15 passes dropped.
According to Next Gen Stats, which has counted 18 drops, Love is second in passing yards lost due to drops.
Most pass yards lost due to drops this season, per @NextGenStats : 1. Drake Maye – 161 2. Jordan Love – 158 3. Justin Herbert – 127 4. Trevor Lawrence – 111 5. Aaron Rodgers - 106 6. Joe Burrow - 103 7. Bo Nix - 101 8. Geno Smith - 100
New England’s Drake Maye has lost 161 yards with Love next at 158. Those are air yards only and don’t include potential yards after the catch.
Love enters Sunday’s game at the Lions ranked third in the league with 1,684 passing yards, behind only the Rams’ Matthew Stafford (1,794) and the Texans’ C.J. Stroud (1,714). If you add the drop yardage to Love’s tally, he would lead the league with 1,842 passing yards.
Using the numbers from Fantasy Points Data and understanding that drops sometimes are in the eyes of the beholder, Love has been plagued by a drop rate of 8.0 percent, which is the fourth-highest among quarterbacks who’ve thrown more than 50 passes. New England’s Drake Maybe has lost 206 yards to drops with Love fifth with 128.
According to Pro Football Focus, Love has had a league-worst 12.2 percent of his passes dropped; Tampa Bay’s Baker Mayfield (10.3. percent) is the only other player at more than 9.2 percent.
“What do you want us to do to address the drops?” coach Matt LaFleur said on Wednesday. “It happens. It’s football. It happens. As long as guys are using the right mechanics and attacking the football, they happen.”
Among the 32-or-so quarterbacks with at least 275 dropbacks in a season during his tenure as the starter, Love was 18th in drop percentage in 2025 (5.8 percent), fifth in 2024 (8.2 percent) and 19th in 2023 (6.1 percent).
Using the numbers at Stathead, 46 quarterbacks have thrown at least 400 passes since Love took over as the starter, He has been victimized by the third-highest drop percentage, 6.0. Only Patrick Mahomes (98) has had more passes dropped than Love (96).
So, while Green Bay’s receivers have never been particularly sure-handed, this season is at a whole other level on a butterfingers scale. According to PFF, he had 24 passes dropped in 2023, 24 passes dropped in 2024 and 18 passes dropped in 2025. With 19 this season, he’s on pace for 54.
“The one thing is you’ve just got to trust yourself,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “Things like this happen. There’s been other guys – (Dontayvion) Wicks a couple years ago sticks out where he had the case of some drops. But the one thing is you’ve got to work hard, keep working on the JUGS, keep catching ball and just trust your hands and trust yourself, and he’ll keep making those spectacular plays.”
According to PFF, Matthew Golden leads the NFL with seven dropped passes. Of the 68 receivers have been targeted at least 20 times, Golden has the second-highest drop rate at 18.9 percent; former Packers receiver Romeo Doubs is first at 22.2 percent. Christian Watson, who has three drops, is tied for 15th at 9.4 percent.
At tight end, 27 players have been targeted at least 20 times. Tucker Kraft has the third-highest drop rate at 10.7 percent. He’s dropped three passes; Baltimore’s Mark Andrews leads in both categories with four drops and a 14.8 percent drop rate.
Green Bay’s backs have combined for four drops: two for MarShawn Lloyd (16.7 percent), one for Chris Brooks (25.0 percent) and one for Pierre Strong (11.1 percent).
Golden’s drops are dumbfounding. He caught everything in sight during his two training camps but has been plagued by big ones this season.
“No, no, I’m not concerned, just because I know the type of player that he is,” Stenavich said. “Again, just one of those things that you can’t lose trust in yourself. You got here for a reason. You are the player who you are for a reason. We all trust him. Jordan trusts him. I know he’s going to make those plays. The ball’s going to keep coming his way, so it’s just one of those things. You just got to work through it, trust yourself and keep your confidence.”
Love had five passes dropped last week against Dallas, according to PFF. Fantasy Data Points had Love losing 60 passing yards.
Love took it in stride as much as possible. Among 33 quarterbacks who’ve dropped back 100 times, Love is 28th in completion percentage. With drops turned into completions, he’s still only 28th. But it’s the big plays such as touchdowns that must be rectified before they cost the team in big moments in big games.
“It’s tough,” Love said after the game. “It’s football. I want to see us make every play. I want to make every throw. I want these guys to make every catch. That’s the expectation. Stuff happens. Drops happen.
“Obviously, I want those guys to make those plays, and we’re capable of making those plays. But for me, it’s got to be the next play mindset. You’ve got to move on. You’ve got to try and fight back and continue to make good plays. Yeah, it sucks and is something we’ve got to continue to get better at.”
Added together, the Packers somehow are 4-2 with a three-game winning streak with inconsistent pass protection, a penchant for penalties and far too many drops.
From his perspective, LaFleur understands that his receivers have missed too many opportunities. He also believes his players are doing things the right way, so there’s no sense of panic.
“Do we want them to happen? No,” LaFleur said. “If they’re using poor fundamentals, letting the ball get in their body, letting the ball cross their eyes, then, yeah, you work on that stuff. But it’s the same stuff we do every day. We go out there and we hammer fundamentals. Sometimes we make plays and sometimes we don’t. But I think that’s everybody in the league.
“I have a lot of confidence in our guys that when called upon, they’re going to make the plays. If they drop the ball, you know what I want them to do? I want them to reset and go play the next play.”

title: Packers Have Roughing-the-Passer Problem And It Goes Back Years
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – According to NFL Penalties , the league average for roughing-the-passer penalties this season is 1.38 per team. The Green Bay Packers have been guilty of a league-high six.
Meanwhile, eight teams have not had their quarterback on the receiving end of a roughing-the-passer penalty. The Packers are one of those teams.
Added together, the Packers are down 6-0 on roughing penalties. No other team is worse than minus-3 in net roughing calls. Either the Packers’ defense is filled with a bunch of cheap-shotting jerks or their opponents are leading with their halos rather than the crown of their helmets when they hit Jordan Love.
After Sunday night’s victory over the Dallas Cowboys, when the Packers were guilty of three roughing-the-passer penalties, coach Matt LaFleur said he left Lambeau Field “a lot later” than he wanted. Part of burning the midnight oil was looking at the infractions.
“I think just in regards to all that stuff, at the end of the day, you just want it to be called both ways,” LaFleur said. “So, if they’re going to call it one way, it should be called for the other team, as well, and I feel like there’s been a lot of times when Jordan’s taken some close to potential roughing calls, and he’s not getting the calls.”
It was quite the diplomatic choice of words by LaFleur as he walked the fine line of trying to make a point while not trying to lighten his wallet.
“I think (Love) needs to be more of an a-hole to the officials and lobby for some of those calls,” LaFleur said, somewhat lightheartedly. “You see some guys do it, and it works.”
But what about LaFleur? NBA coaches are famous for working the referees, especially during a playoff series, when a perceived lack of calls in one game is harped on after and between games in hopes of getting the calls the next game.
“You saying I’m not working them good enough?” LaFleur said to that example.
Only LaFleur would know how much he lobbies the officials during the game or the league during the week. With a contract extension, he probably can afford the fine for criticizing the officials for letting Love get blasted after the throw.
“I’m going to tell them next week, I’ll say, ‘Bill Huber told me that I need to get on you guys.’”
All joking aside, it’s wild that the Packers have been flagged six times compared to zero for their opponents. The Packers have been flagged for some legit fouls. Others, such as Lukas Van Ness’ two-handed shove of Dak Prescott, looked incredibly weak – even for this era of protecting the passer at all costs.
“We can only control our actions out there, and there were a couple hits like you cannot go high on a quarterback,” LaFleur said. “You’ve got to make sure that you’re going in the strike zone and then, obviously, if you do have him wrapped up, you’ve got to make sure you don’t land on him with your body weight.”
LaFleur said opinion among the coaches was split on Karl Brooks’ body-weight foul on Prescott, though he seemed to agree that was the right call.
“As far as some of those other calls,” he continued, “I thought Van Ness’ wasn’t. You get a step before you have to hit the quarterback, and I didn’t think it was a forceful hit to the quarterback.”
Part of the weekly postmortem is sending in clips to the league to question or gain clarity on penalties that were called or not called. Shots on the quarterback probably have been a theme.
“We’ll see what they say,” LaFleur said. “And then I obviously can’t tell you guys about what they say, but it helps us educate our players and at the end of the day that’s our job. We got to educate them on what they can and cannot do and make sure that we try to coach them up and they got to control themselves in the moment.”
No team has reached double-digits for roughing penalties since the Jets were flagged 14 times in 2020. The Packers, who have been guilty of 14 percent of the league total through six games, are well on their way.
“We can’t foul,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said, choosing to stay out of the public fray. “I always say, like it’s continuing to educate, continuing to talk technique and then decision-making. We got to make sure that we’re making correct decisions in real time, which I know is not easy to do, but good defenses don’t beat themselves.”
Using data from Sumer Sports, the Packers were flagged only once for roughing while opponents were penalized four times, so Green Bay was plus-3. In both 2023 and 2024, Green Bay was flagged three times and its opponents once.
That means during the three-plus seasons with Love at the controls, officials have called six roughing penalties against Green Bay’s opponents. The Cowboys’ opponents have been flagged 20 times during that span, three more than any other team. The Bills have been the second-largest beneficiary with 17.
The Chargers’ opponents have been flagged six times this season alone.
In the NFC North, Green Bay’s division rivals have been flagged for roughing one time apiece this season.
Due largely to this year’s 6-0 disparity, the Packers are minus-7 on roughing calls during the Love era. Only the Eagles at minus-8 have seen more lopsided officiating. For Green Bay during that span, only four teams have been flagged more for roughing the passer and only two teams (the Rams and Texans) have benefited from fewer roughing penalties.
Dallas is a staggering plus-13. Buffalo (plus-11) and Cleveland (plus-10) are the only teams that are double-digits positive.

title: Packers-Lions Matchups: Just One Advantage, But It’s Huge
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have won three games in a row. As fictional manager Lou Brown from Major League II once said, that’s called a winning streak.
Can the Packers extend their streak to four? They will face a big challenge in Detroit against the Lions at 3:25 p.m. Sunday. It will be the first of five consecutive games against teams that would qualify for the playoffs if the season were to end today.
The Packers swept the Lions last season, including a 31-24 in Detroit on Thanksgiving. The teams are different now. Some key players are back. Others are on the shelf due to injuries. The Lions are coming off their bye week, while the Packers played Dallas on Sunday night.
While the Lions have the rest advantage, who has the advantage on the field? We go through that in our weekly matchups.
The talking point last week was that the Packers were playing well on defense but that they had not faced a real quarterback.
Now they have, and the Packers beat up Dak Prescott on Sunday night. This week? They’ll face another high-powered offense with a quarterback who has been mostly flawless this season.
Jared Goff does not get the league-wide respect that he deserves, but he’s been nothing short of excellent since coming to Detroit.
This year has been no different. He has completed 67 percent of his passes. His passer rating is 111.3. He’s thrown 12 touchdown passes and has yet to be picked off.
Perhaps Detroit’s offense was summed up best by Green Bay defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon.
“They’ve scored 30 any time they’ve touched the grass,” Gannon said on Tuesday .
Four out of five games but, with a second-ranked 32.8 points per game, close enough. Detroit’s offense is dangerous. They’re loaded with weapons. Receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams and tight end Sam LaPorta can all hurt the defense in different ways.
Last week, the Packers handled their matchup against George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb well. This group is deeper, and more dangerous.
The key to slowing down the Lions is pressuring Goff. The Packers beat him up last year at Lambeau Field and held the Lions to 13 points.
Can the Packers get enough pressure? Will Gannon have another masterclass up his sleeve?
As good as Green Bay’s defense has played early in the season, this matchup is closer than you would think at first glance.
Jonathan Gannon was asked what makes Jahmyr Gibbs, Jahmyr Gibbs. He sighed, before saying, “Woah.”
Gibbs is the fastest player on the field every week that he steps on it. He’s a dominant force in a Detroit ground game that remains its identity even with the loss of some of the personnel that made it such a powerful unit in 2024.
Green Bay’s run defense has truly only struggled once this season. The problem? That came against the Falcons, who employ a back with a similar running style to that of Gibbs. There’s an argument to be made that Gibbs is a better running back than Bijan Robinson, but it’s those two at the top of the league with everyone else fighting for a seat at the table.
Either way, Gibbs makes this group go.
The Packers did a good job against him last year. Gibbs was held to 19 yards on nine carries at Lambeau Field. He added 10 catches for 31 yards. If the Packers can hold him to 50 yards on 19 touches, they’d be thrilled.
In the rematch at Ford Field, Gibbs was more productive, but not up to his usual standard. He touched the ball 20 times for 86 yards. The Packers held him in check, but will be missing both linebackers from those games. Quay Walker is playing in Las Vegas while Edgerrin Cooper is rehabbing a torn Achilles.
Regardless, Gibbs’ excellence and the Packers’ recent history against a back of his caliber gives the nod to Detroit.
The Lions can make things difficult with their pass rush. Their front boasts two really good players in defensive tackle Alim McNeil and defensive end Aidan Hutchinson. D.J. Wonnum is sixth in the lead with five sacks. Hutchinson has four and McNeill has 3.5.
Added together, the Lions lead the league in sacks – even while playing one less game than most teams.
So, why does their defense stink?
Once the ball goes in the air, the Lions have had significant problems. Their defensive backfield was in flux before the season even began. Their once elite safety tandem of Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph have missed the entirety of the season with injuries. Following last year’s torn ACL,, Branch is likely to return this week, which should give them a boost.
The cornerback spot has been an issue. D.J. Reed has not worked out as a free agent signing, and they’ve been struggling to find someone to give them consistency. Keith Abney is the only cornerback with an interception.
The Lions are allowing 297.4 passing yards per game. That’s the worst in the NFL this season and on track to be one of the worst in NFL history. The Lions are on track to allow 5,056 passing yards over 17 games. The 2011 Packers allowed the most passing yards of all-time with 4,796 yards over 16 games. That’s 299.8 per game.
They are 29th in opponent passer rating (106.3) and opponent completion percentage (68.1).
That’s good news for the Packers as they come in rolling. Jordan Love’s stats won’t show how well he played on Sunday against the Cowboys, but he was three drops away from throwing four touchdown passes.
Matthew Golden has back-to-back 100-yard receiving games, the first for the Packers since Davante Adams, and is turning into a star. Will the Packers be able to protect Love long enough to exploit a leaky pass defense? That’s the million-dollar question.
With the advantages Green Bay has, especially at quarterback, where Love has thrived almost regardless of the situation, the nod here goes to the visiting team.
Green Bay’s run game stinks. If there was any doubt about that, Sunday’s results against the Cowboys, who were 32nd in the league against the run, should have answered any remaining questions.
As has been the case all season, the Packers were terrible on the ground. Their leading rusher was Pierre Strong. He had 28 yards on 11 carries. Their starting running back was MarShawn Lloyd. He had negative yards rushing at halftime and finished with 10 yards on eight carries.
Their most efficient runner was Savion Williams, and those runs were on plays in which Jordan Love threw the ball behind the line of scrimmage.
They could be getting a boost this week. Josh Jacobs is off the commissioner’s exempt list, and looks to be on track to play this Sunday. How much can he play? He can help, but how much?  Those are questions we don’t know the answers to yet.
Until we know, it’s impossible to give the Packers the edge, against any opponent, let alone one that has been a decent 13th in rushing yards allowed per game and 12th in yards per carry.
From a special teams perspective, the Lions have some stability at kicker and punter. Jake Bates has been perfect on field goals this season and Jack Fox is averaging 47.2 yards per punt.
There is a slight transition in their return game with Tom Kennedy taking over for Kalif Raymond, who joined Ben Johnson in Chicago.
Green Bay’s special teams entered the Dallas game struggling. Trey Smack missed three kicks against Chicago and Skyy Moore is missing from their return game due to a high-ankle sprain that landed him on injured reserve.
Coleman Owen was elevated from the practice squad last week to return punts in Moore’s place while J. Michael Sturdivant and Bo Melton returned kickoffs. Neither did much to stand out, but they protected the football. Matt LaFleur noted that he thought Owen did a nice job returning punts other than calling for a fair catch inside the 10. He will likely be elevated again this week.
Smack shook off some struggles against Chicago with a 5-for-5 night against the Cowboys. This game is in a dome, which should remove the degree of difficulty for kickers to some degree. Having said that, two of the worst games of Mason Crosby’s career came at Ford Field.
Detroit’s excellence at kicker…

title: Texans' Week 7 Odds Point to Potential Blowout vs. Giants, J.J. McCarthy
full_text:
The Houston Texans head into their Week 7 contest against the New York Giants riding the high of logging two straight wins over their last two matchups, and now hope to extend that streak to three in their last game before the bye.
And the pieces could certainly be in place for the Texans to make that third consecutive win become a reality.
Their offense is looking the best it has all season after another strong performance from C.J. Stroud. The defense will have the task of facing a new starting quarterback on the other side in J.J. McCarthy , and all of that coming back on Houston's home field tends to make their chances look even better.
And when looking at the Texans' betting odds heading into Week 7, it's becoming pretty clear that the sportsbooks have one obvious favorite in mind for this weekend's action in Houston.
According to recent odds from FanDuel Sportsbook , the Texans are now listed as 10.5-point favorites (-550 ML) over the Giants in Week 7.
That's by far the Texans' highest spread heading into any week they've played this season. And when looking around the league's Week 7 matchups, Houston is currently the only team listed as a favorite by more than a touchdown––let alone being a favorite by double digits.
The projected point-total for these two teams doesn't look favorable for the Giants either. Houston and New York have an over-under sitting at 43.5, which comes in tied for bottom-five among the NFL in terms of projected totals for Week 7.
So if the Texans are projected to win by double-digits, and the total score isn't expected to reach above 43 points, that's not much of an optimistic statement from the books on how this Giants offense could fare against a Houston defensive unit that many considered among the best in the NFL heading into this season.
Now, projections are one thing. Clearly, the consensus is starting to lean in one clear direction for this one between the Texans and the Giants.
But does Houston actually have what it takes to make that double-digit victory come to fruition?
Really, it all relies upon the defense.
Last game against the Jacksonville Jaguars showed that the Texans' offense is starting to get into a bit of a rhythm . A ton of receivers are getting involved and making plays, the run game showed signs of life against one of the best rushing defenses in the NFL, and the offensive line even held up to zero sacks.
But the Texans' defense just hasn't been as consistently elite as this team proved to be last year. That's not saying they can't find their way back to that level–– because the personnel looks virtually identical to last year outside of a select few changes. But we still need to see Houston have multiple strong weeks defensively to really have this level of confidence in their chances on Sunday.
After all, the Giants have won three games as is this season. That's more than the Texans can claim for themselves, and New York sits atop the NFC East because of it.
So as 10.5-point underdogs, they seem just a slight bit underrated here, simply when considering Houston's inconsistencies on defense. Maybe the Texans wind up crushing those projections anyways, but perhaps the Giants can make this game just a little bit more interesting than the odds tend to show.

title: 3 Texans Matchups to Watch Closely Against Giants in Week 7
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into Week 7 against the New York Giants with hopes of firing off their third straight win after back-to-back encouraging wins being stamped in the books.
However, for this matchup against the Giants in particular, there's going to be a handful of matchups for the Texans to keep an eye on so that they can check off that aspired third straight victory.
And even for a Giants team that might not have as much talent on paper as the Texans do, their 3-2 record, along with their current first-place standing in the NFC East tends to show that this team isn't one that should be overlooked for this wekeend whatsoever.
So with that in mind, let's break down three key matchups to keep an eye on for the Texans in their Week 7 matchup back at home against the Giants:
The biggest source of the Giants' offense is undoubtably their star wideout, Malik Nabers, who's done nothing but see his stock rise even further than it was throughout the past two weeks. Through Weeks 5 and 6, Nabers has seen 35 targets to turn those into 23 receptions, 286 yards, and a touchdown.
But this week, Nabers will be tasked with one of the most talented corners in the NFL in Derek Stingley Jr.–– someone who's come off of back-to-back All-Pro appearances in 2024 and 2025, and could be one of Nabers' toughest individual matchups of this season so far.
The Texans' secondary has been less than stellar over the past several weeks. It wasn't too long ago that this same Houston defense allowed CeeDee Lamb to have a dominant 17-reception game for 189 yards and a touchdown. But if Stingley and Co. can hold down Nabers for a limited performance, the road to victory can become a whole lot easier.
The Texans' pass rush wasn't quite as dominant as we know them to be this past weekend against the Jacksonville Jaguars . Houston combined for zero sacks throughout the contest, even while both Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter were at full strength.
For reference, there wasn't a single game in which Houston didn't log at least one sack over the course of the 2025 season, and it hadn't happened over the course of 2026 through five weeks. So that was pretty uncharted territory for this defense.
This week, the Texans will be back at home on their own turf, and might have a much better chance of gaining some traction in terms of getting pressure on the quarterback. And when Houston starts racking up sacks, the task becomes immensely more challenging for the opposing offense.
The name I'll be watching closest in Houston's efforts to build a better pass rush will be Danielle Hunter, given that he has the tougher task of lining up against Andrew Thomas on the left side of the line, and could end up being a force multiplier if Will Anderson continues on his DPOY pace.
It was too tough to single out just one player on the Texans' side of the equation here, but seeing how this defense takes on the task of facing Giants starting quarterback J.J. McCarthy will be fascinating to watch unfold.
McCarthy has had nothing short of an up-and-down first three years in the NFL. From a season-ending injury to terrible play with the Minnesota Vikings, to now being traded to and starting for the New York Giants in Week 7, there's a wide range of outcomes for just how McCarthy's day goes here against a Texans defense that many have touted as among the best in the NFL.
If the Texans' defense played like it did last weekend against the Jaguars— a game in which Trevor Lawrence threw for over 300 yards and four touchdowns— then maybe McCarthy can find his way to some steady production to keep the Giants and their scoring attack.
But if the Texans can revert back to defensive output closer to what was seen against the Tennessee Titans and Cam Ward, then this could quickly become a long day for McCarthy and this Giants offense.

title: Everything Texans WR Tank Dell Said Ahead of His Long-Awaited Return
full_text:
The Houston Texans are finally going to be getting fan-favorite wide reciever Tank Dell back in the lineup this weekend against the New York Giants.
After a long, near two-year recovery process after Dell had first suffered his devastating knee injury in December of 2024, the time has finally come for the wideout to get back on the field in Week 7, and catch some passes from C.J. Stroud as one of his top playmakers in this offense.
And ahead of Dell's long-awaited return to the field, he fielded some questions from the media a few days out from the Texans' Week 7 contest against the Giants .
Let's take a look at seven quotes from Dell leading up to him officially suiting up for this weekend's matchup.
On Wednesday, Dell was first asked about how he's feeling in the days ahead of his first time back on an NFL field in nearly two years. And overall, he's seemingly not feeling too overwhelmed. Above all, he's feeling a lot of gratitude.
"First off, I'm blessed. I want to thank God for getting me back in this position," Dell said. "I don't think I'm overwhelmed. A lot of people have been hitting me up, but I don't think I'm overwhelmed. I'm anxious, of course."
"It's been two years— well, dang near two years— but I don't think I'm overwhelmed. I'm anxious to get back out there and play some football, but I'm blessed, man. That's all I can say."
The Texans won't be setting any crazy expectations for Dell this weekend , and neither will Dell himself. Of course, his competitive drive will continue to have a nose to make plays, but he's looking to live in the moment more than anything.
"Go out there and have fun, man. First game back, I'm just trying to go out there and have fun," Dell said of his expectations.
"Of course, y'all know I'm competitive, so I want to make some plays. A lot of plays. But my main thing is just to live in that moment, be where my feet are, have fun, fly around and just try to be who I am. Not try— be who I am.
Stroud is going to find Dell to make a play at some point over the course of Week 7's game against the Giants. But how does Dell envision that first catch going?
No matter how big of a play that catch ends up being, he's sure to have a pretty passionate celebration.
"I don't care if the first catch is two yards, five yards, I'm spiking the ball. I'm doing what I got to do, man," Dell said.
"It's going to feel good. I know there's a lot of questions about how I'm going to look when I get tackled. I don't care about none of that. I'm ready to get tackled. I'm going to be joyful. Y'all are going to see the passion I have after I have that first catch."
Dell has been stuck on the Texans' sidelines for over 650 days now, including throughout all of the 2025 season. And such a traumatic experience is bound to have a huge impact on anyone more than just what happens on the football field.
As to how the injury recovery process changed Dell as a person, it taught him how to truly live in the moment.
"It just made me live in the moment and be grateful for everything," Dell said of what his recovery taught him. "People say that repetitively all the time, but when you actually go through it and have to be the one who pulls yourself out of it, I feel like it makes you grateful and thankful that it could have been way worse, even though it was a crazy, traumatic incident."
"There are people out here going through things way worse than me. I got injured in a football game, but somebody else is fighting for their life for real. It's just about being grateful and thankful to be where I'm at, man, and having fun."
After Dell first went down with his knee injury against the Kansas City Chiefs in 2024, there were serious questions regarding whether or not the Texans' wideout would ever be able to play in an NFL game ever again.
Fast forward to this week, and Dell has defied those odds. But did he have any doubts himself about being able to make it through the long journey back? It certainly doesn't seem like it.
"I think I made a post a couple of days after it happened where I said, 'I'm going to be back.' In my mind, it was never a question of whether I was going to be back," Dell said. "Of course, throughout the process, you question yourself, but you have to have faith in God. I never doubted that I was going to work myself back to being able to get on the field."
"I already knew I was going to put in whatever work I had to put in. Even on the days when I woke up and didn't feel like doing anything, I still gave it my all, came in here and did everything. I was in the facility every day throughout the year and offseason. I was just making sure I put my best foot forward to come back and play football."
Compared to the last time that Dell took the field alongside the Texans' offense, today's wide receiver room in Houston is looking a whole lot different than it did then. No Stefon Diggs, no Jared Wayne, but guys like Kayshon Boutte, Marvin Harrison Jr., and Jaylin Noel have been brought into the mix.
And while on one hand, it puts Dell in an offense with a lot of mouths to feed, he's confident that in a deep wide receiver room like this one, getting everyone involved and making plays will allow everyone's energy to feed off one another.
"I think it's great, Dell said of the Texans' wide receiver room. "If you look back at last year, we had a lot of receivers and tight ends down in a big game. Just having more guys in the room who can go out there and make a play helps us.
"We feed off each other's energy and making plays, and I feel like we're competitive. If I see Nico make a play, in a non-selfish way, I want to go out there and make a play, too. I'm going to be happy for him, and I want to go out there and make a play. It's the same with Marvin, Kayshon, Hutch, J-Noel, everybody."
"It's exciting to have that type of room. The cream is going to rise to the top. If you're a competitor and know how you can play football, just have fun doing it. Don't be selfish or look at it as a bad thing. When there are blessings in the neighborhood, you'll get blessed, too. Just go out there, work hard and make the play when the ball comes."
Given that the Texans are going to be back at home for Dell's long-awaited return, there's no doubt that all of Reliant Stadium will be fired up the second they see their fan-favorite wideout run out of the tunnel for his first game back since 2024.
And so of course, Dell has no doubts that the environment on Sunday will be unmatched.
I feel like they're going to go crazy. I'm excited for that, too. That's what I'm saying — fill the stadium up, please," Dell said. "It's great to have that support from Houston, getting drafted by the Texans and being part of this organization. It's a beautiful organization, the same with the University of Houston. I feel like I'm a Florida boy, but, like I said before, I feel like this is home for me, too."
"It's great, and I know it's going to be a great feeling when I run out of the tunnel."

title: Texans' First Injury Report vs. Giants Features Several Concerns for Week 7
full_text:
The Houston Texans have dropped their first injury report of the week heading into their upcoming matchup against the New York Giants .
And after their first practice, there's a good chunk of players on the roster listed as either a DNP or a limited participant.
Let's break down everything to know about the Texans' Wednesday injury report:
LB Azeez Al-Shaair (knee) S Jalen Pitre (shoulder) S Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand) RB David Montgomery (groin) OT Blake Fisher (thumb) OT Trent Brown (wrist) TE Dalton Schultz (calf)
WR Nico Collins (rest) LB Henry To'oTo'o (shoulder) DE Will Anderson Jr. (rest) DE Jadeveon Clowney (knee) DE Logan Hall (knee)
The Texans have been dealing with injuries to both running back David Montgomery and defensive back Jalen Pitre since their Week 5 game against the Tennessee Titans. Both of them missed the trip to London against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and they've both now missed their first of three practices heading into this weekend against New York. Both of them were considered week-to-week upon the announcement of their injuries a couple of weeks ago, and thus could provide a bit of optimism for their availability vs. the Giants. However, don't be surprised if either or both are due to miss another game.
As mentioned by DeMeco Ryans earlier this week, veteran safety Reed Blankenship is in concussion protocol , and therefore didn't practice with the team on Wednesday. It also seems as if he's dealing with a hand injury that's limiting him as well. So if things continue to trend in this direction for Blankenship, he could be forced out for Week 7, and instead return after the Texans' bye in Week 9. If that's the case, expect M.J. Stewart to be the next man up to start at safety next to Calen Bullock.
One noteworthy name to keep an eye on within the Texans' injury report heading deeper into the week is tight end Dalton Schultz, who seemed to suffer a calf injury in the middle of their trip to London against Jacksonville, but wound up finishing the game anyways. Given that he did finish the game out against the Jaguars, that tends to be a good sign that he'll be able to play this coming weekend. But in any event, he is forced to miss time; keep an eye on Foster Moreau, fresh off of his two-touchdown day.
Tank Dell is officially set to make his return to the NFL field this weekend. He's now logged multiple full practices over the past three weeks and will be designated for return from injured reserve for his first game in over 650 days. Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans spoke about Dell's pending return earlier this weekend: "I expect Tank just to be himself, and just play the offense the right way," Ryans said. "No huge expectations for what he needs to do. We're all just going to be excited... I'm just thankful, grateful for him to have this opportunity to return." "I don't have any expectations, I'm just happy to see him out there. And that's the only thing that matters."

title: Texans' DeMeco Ryans Shrugs Off Giants' Decision to Start J.J. McCarthy
full_text:
Heading into the Houston Texans' Week 7 matchup against the New York Giants , the opposition has made an eye-catching shake-up at their quarterback position.
The Giants have been rolling out Jameis Winston as their starting quarterback ever since Jaxson Dart went down with a knee injury in Week 2. However, New York head coach John Harbaugh announced Wednesday that J.J. McCarthy would start under center against Houston.
McCarthy had previously made an appearance at the end of the Giants' Week 6 game against the New Orleans Saints, in which he performed relatively well in the reps he was given: he completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards with a touchdown, an interception, and had two rushing attempts for 26 yards.
So now, the Giants have seen enough out of the 23-year-old quarterback from that showing to warrant another start in Week 7 on the road against Houston.
However, heading into that Week 7 duel against the Giants, it doesn't seem like Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans is too concerned about who's starting at quarterback for New York.
Ryans was asked during his Wednesday presser about his thoughts on the Giants starting J.J. McCarthy for their Week 7 matchup against Houston.
But overall, the focus remained more upon the Texans' defense being better prepared for the week ahead, no matter who the opposing quarterback is.
"For us, it really doesn't matter who plays quarterback," Ryans said of the Giants' quarterback decision. "For us, defensively, it's been about our process, and how do we do things that we do the right way, and do them well."
"So, whoever's at quarterback doesn't really dictate what we're going to do defensively. It's about us. We got to play better defensively, because it wasn't good enough in our last outing."
Of course, Ryans and the Texans won't be heading into this game without doing their due diligence scouting and studying film on McCarthy.
Knowing that he will be the guy under center could make Houston's preparation a little bit easier by having a bit more clarity on how New York's offense will look. Or, perhaps that pre-game prep can be a little more challenging without having as vast of a sample size with McCarthy as the Giants' starting quarterback.
But no matter what the Giants' quarterback looks like, that's not where Ryans head is sitting at a few days out from their Week 7 matchup. More than anything, Ryans clearly wasn't too satisfied with the output his defense showcased last week against the Jaguars –– and he wants those lapses ironed out ASAP.
In Week 6, Houston allowed Jacksonville to become the third team to score 30-plus points on them in a single game on the year. For reference, that feat only happened once over the course of the 2025 season in their Week 18 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts .
So rather than putting a ton of focus on the external factors in terms of who the Giants will have under center, Ryans is taking a different approach. He's more locked in on how he and his team can take the necessary steps forward to be the elite defense that they proved to be capable of all of last season.
Maybe this game can present a get-right opportunity for the Texans' defense and their hopes of lifting back to that elite level they stood at all of last season. But if it isn't, the conversations around exactly what's happened to this side of the ball in Houston will only continue to get louder.
