title: Jaguars Rookie Rankings Entering Bye Week: Who Are James Gladstone's Early Hits?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jaguars are about a third of the way through the 2026 season, and we have learned a good bit about their rookie class thus far.
There are a handful of rookies who have played big roles for the Jaguars during their 4-2 start, while other rookies have mostly stayed on the sidelines. So, where does each rookie stand entering the bye week, and who can continue to progress toward a larger role? We break it down below.
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen shouted out Wesley Williams, along with Albert Regis, for his work on the practice field last week. That is about as much as we have heard about Williams during his rookie season, however. The fourth-round Duke product has yet to be made active, which feels unlikely to change with B.J. Green coming off the injured reserve sooner rather than later. As a whole, though, this is a redshirt year for Williams as he develops behind the Jkely that he wikl aguars' veteran defensive ends for the 2027 season.
CJ Williams has been inactive in each Jaguars game other than Week 1, so there is not exactly a large sample size to go off of. He did good things during training camp and the offseason program, but it feels unlikely that he is going to get much playing time this year unless the Jaguars sustain some injuries at wide receiver. Perhaps that changes if the Jaguars end up trading Brian Thomas Jr. before next month's deadline, but it feels unlikely he gets an active game day jersey otherwise.
The second player drafted in the Jaguars' 2026 draft class, Albert Regis has missed three games this season: one in Week 3 due to injury, and then the last two weeks as a result of being a healthy scratch. Regis has played just 22 snaps and recorded two assisted tackles this season thus far, so it has been a quiet rookie year for the third-round pick. The most likely explanation is that the Jaguars feel good about their top-four defensive tackles and do not have the room in the rotation right now for Regis.
This is the one right now that just isn't making much sense to me. Jalen Huskey has only been active in one game this season, and in that game all he did was play four special teams snaps. Even with an injury to Caleb Ransaw, the Jaguars have gone with Kaevon Merriweather over Huskey now two weeks in a row, which makes it clear that we are not going to see Huskey with a role on defense for some time. Huskey needs to play more if the Jaguars keep getting dinged up at safety, but it hasn't happened yet.
Bryan Thomas Jr. is this high because of the snaps he has played, but not because of the impact he has made. The Jaguars rolled the dice with young undrafted talent at the defensive end position, and it just has not paid off yet. Thomas has one pressure on 28 rushes and his 3.6% pressure rate is the second-lowest on the team, ahead of only Danny Striggow's 2.3%. Thomas looked the part this preseason, but it has not led to many plays on the field this season.
Tanner Koziol has played just 30 offensive snaps this season and has yet to see a pass come his way, though he has seen his snaps increase some in recent weeks. He has been on the field for some big plays out of 13 personnel, but we have yet to really see what he can add to the offense via the passing game. It feels like we could eventually, though, considering how often he has been on the field recently.
Josh Cameron had another big kick return against the Texans to display his special teams value, and it is clear he is making a big impact early on. His production as a pass-catcher varies week-to-week right now, but that could always change if the Jaguars opt to trade Brian Thomas Jr. during the trade deadline next month. For now, though, Cameron is a very valuable depth piece and a masssive 6th-round draft hit.
Nate Boerkircher caught the first touchdown of his NFL career against the Texans, showing off the strong hands in the red-zone that made the Jaguars big fans of his during the draft process. He has been a strong run-blocker and has shown up each time in his limited chances in the passing game, which means the Jaguars should feel pretty happy about what they are getting from him thus far. He should keep getting better, too.
Emmanuel Pregnon has had the top spot in these rankings since he became a starter at the end of training camp, and I do not see that changing anytime soon. Pregnon has had some penalty issues in the form of holding calls in recent weeks, but he has been strong in the running game and has been far from a liability as a pass-protector. He should keep getting better, too.
"Pregnon, I thought he had one of his better outings yesterday. He had the one hold and we'll continue to work with him as he goes on the second level and getting up and getting in space but I thought he played really well on the inside for us yesterday," Coen said Monday.

title: Jaguars Stock Report: 3 Risers, 3 Fallers After Week 6's Eye-Opening Texans Loss
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars still have some work to do.
That is the biggest takeaway from the Jaguars' 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans on Sunday. The Jaguars made far too many self-inflicted mistakes, though, and dropped to 4-2 to give the Texans some life in the AFC South as a result.
So, which Jaguars played well and have rising stocks after the close loss, and whose stocks are falling after the eye-opening loss to Houston? We break it down below.
I mean ... this one is obvious. For the first time in his NFL career, Travis Hunter was able to make a game-changing play on both sides of the ball. He produced four catches for 59 yards and a touchdown despite only playing nine offensive snaps, while he played 98% of the Jaguars' defensive snaps and recorded a red-zone interception. Hunter is a special player, and it sure seems like the Jaguars are willing to continue to let him show off why. It will be fascinating to see how his role develops over the final two-thirds of the season.
"Yeah, that's kind of who he is. We got to continue to get him the ball and keep building off of it and make sure it fits within the rhythm and flow of the game, but he definitely helped put us in a position to win that game today," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game Sunday.
This game felt like the end of an era for Brian Thomas Jr. The Jaguars' third-year receiver was targeted twice in the first-half on plays that would have put the Jaguars in field goal position, but both passes ended up incomplete after hitting his hands. Thomas played 15 snaps in the first half but did not play a single snap in the second half, and Coen did not give Thomas a vote of confidence when asked about him after the game. This felt like the game that we will look back on and say it led to the final straw in Thomas' tenure with the franchise.
Jaguars running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. had his best game of the season in Week 6, rushing 11 times for 55 yards and consistently showing off the ability to break tackles and get yards after contact. Rodriguez has quickly picked up his play over the last few weeks after a slow start to the season, and it has increasingly felt like he and Bhayshul Tuten are forming the 1-2 punch the Jaguars pictured when they signed him.
“What we’ve excelled at I feel, honestly, is a new line of scrimmage. We say that from the O-lineman standpoint. The best runs are when you can get those guys off the ball and create a second line of scrimmage. I feel like we've done a pretty good job of that. And, for me, I’d just say running downhill, trying to get back into a rhythm and flow of being who I am and being who got me here, essentially," Rodriguez said this week.
Jarrian Jones has had some strong moments this season, but he has also been at the mercy of being the marked man in the Jaguars' secondary. Quarterbacks are simply not testing Travis Hunter very much, which means Jones has been the most-targeted cornerback in football through six weeks. He has fought through this for impressive performances some weeks, but this was not one of them. Jones had some penalty issues, gave up an explosive play, and had a missed tackle on a Texans touchdown run.
Despite playing the best defensive end duo in the NFL in Week 6, Walker Little had very few issues. The Jaguars' veteran offensive tackle was up to the task of slowing down Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, and accoding to Pro Football Focus he recorded just two pressures on 44 pass-blocking snaps. Little will be needed for at least the next few weeks, if not longer, and Sunday was a strong step in the right direction for the long-time Jaguars offensive lineman.
It is starting to feel like Jarrian Jones might be better off in the slot for the Jaguars. If that is the case, then the Jaguars have a question to answer with veteran cornerback Jourdan Lewis, who had a tough game against the Texans. Lewis allowed the 3rd-and-10 touchdown to Jaylin Noel at the start of the second-half, and he was also at fault for the third-down completion to Woody Mark's on the game's final drive that put the game away. He might have seen his best days in the defense already.

title: Jaguars Week 6 Snap Count Analysis: Travis Hunter's Path is Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to move past their Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans and move into the bye week, but first there are a few loose ends to take care of.
Amongst those loose ends? Finding out what the Jaguars' snap counts from the last-second lass to the Texans mean, both for last week and moving forward.
So, which snap counts stood out to us when the Jaguars took on the Texans , and why? We break it down below.
Travis Hunter's performance against the Texans made it very clear how he should be used moving forward. Hunter played 98% of the defensive snaps with 62 snaps, just one away from playing all 100%. Hunter made one of the game's biggest plays with an end-zone interception of C.J. Stroud, becoming the first defender to pick off Stroud this season. He also was matched up with Nico Collins frequently, providing strong coverage throughout the day with his lone big play given up being the double-move to Collins in the first-half.
Offensively is where things got interesting, with Hunter catching four passes for 59 yards and a touchdow ... on just nine offensive snaps. This was the first game of Hunter's career where he truly made game-changing plays on both sides of the ball in one game, and the Jaguars now have the blueprint: keep him as a full-time player on defense, while preparing him for certain packages and situations on offense. Hunter just proved he can handle doing it, and the Jaguars must now lean into his special traits as a result.
Despite picking safeties in the top-100 in back-to-back seasons, the Jaguars appear to have a safety issue moving forward. The Jaguars have actually drafted three total safeties in the last two drafts, but none of them took a snap against the Texans. Caleb Ransaw, of course, is on injured reserve for the foreseeable future, but Jalen Huskey was once again a healthy scratch and Rayuan Lane did not get any defensive snaps despite Antonio Johnson going down with an injury in the Texans loss.
When Johnson went down, the Jaguars opted to put former practice squad safety Kaevon Merriweather
 on the field, with Merriweather playing 43 snaps (68%). With the amount of coverage busts the Jaguars had, and with Eric Murray allowing two touchdowns, the Jaguars simply need to lean into their young talent or find other safety upgrades. Huskey getting zero defensive snaps over the last two weeks makes very little sense.
The Jaguars' defense was simply not good enough against the Texans, but there were still some good flashes. Amongst those flashes came from third-year defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro, who has started to pick up some momentum over the last month after a slow first few weeks of the season. Orhorhoro was one of just two Jaguars defensive linemen to record multiple pressures against the Texans, and he had the best pressure rate of any Jaguars' pass-rusher. He did all of this while playing 24 (39%) of the snaps.
Orhorhoro has now collected multiple pressures in four straight games after just one pressure in the first two weeks. He is starting to heat up, and the Jaguars would be wise to let him start getting some of the snaps that have been earmarked for Arik Armstead, who has been more up-and-down in his week-to-week consistency.

title: 5 Realistic CB Trade Targets for the Jaguars Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline isn't for another few weeks, but needs are starting to creep up for the Jacksonville Jaguars that very well could be addressed near the deadline.
We mentioned cornerback as one spot the Jaguars should consider investing some resources in by the trade deadline, but what are some names who could make sense? We break it down below.
The Eagles' season is over for all intents and purposes following the news of Jalen Hurts set to miss the rest of the season, which should make Tariq Woolen an interesting trade option for multiple teams, including the Jaguars. The Eagles will likely go into sell-mode sooner rather than later, and Woolen is one of their most tradeable players considering the fact he only signed a one-year, $12 million deal with the Eagles this past offseason.
Woolen is a good player who fits the Jaguars' need for an outside cornerback, and he would likely come cheap. I could see Howie Roseman flipping Woolen for a run-of-the-mill Day 3 pick, which would be a smart rental for the Jaguars. Since he is a pending free agent, Woolen could also nab the Jaguars a future draft pick if he departs in free agency next March. The Jaguars need to be aggressive, and he would fit that bill.
Another team that should quickly become sellers are the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Todd Bowles is on his last leg as a head coach and they are 1-5 through six weeks, which means they are likely just a few more losses away from burning it all down and starting over. And when they do that, Zyon McCollum is one of the names that makes the most sense for them to move on from. McCollum still has a few years left on his three-year, $48 million deal with the team, but that barely places him in the top-25 among highest-paid cornerbacks.
McCollum is having one of the best years of his career so far in 2026, and he is not one of the reasons the Buccaneers have struggled. He could help the Jaguars stabilize a secondary that badly needs it, giving the Jaguars a reliable outside cornerback duo and the depth needed to make a run. He would be the most expensive option on this list, but there is a reason for that.
We have mentioned Brandon Stephens before, and for good reason. The sixth-year cornerback has a ton of experience playing both zone and man coverage, and he had a solid season thus far for the Jets outside of a few touchdowns allowed. But the Jets keep losing games and it is becoming easy to see that, eventually, they need to start becoming sellers. When they do, Stephens would make a ton of sense to make available.
The Jets have younger cornerbacks on the roster they have invested in, and there is no real point for the Jets to do anything other than continue to load up on draft picks. The Jaguars need help at the outside cornerback spot, and Stephens would give them a higher floor while not doing anything to change the role that Travis Hunter plays for Anthony Campanile's secondary moving forward.
Yet another pur outside cornerback, Kristian Fulton has been one of the best cornerbacks in football this season. He has allowed just 19 yards on nine targets, giving him a 12.0 passer rating allowed in coverage. He has not exactly been a full-time player, though, with the Chiefs giving more snaps to Nohl Williams, L'Jarius Sneed, and first-round pick Mansoor Delane. As a result, it would make sense for Fulton to be available.
Would the Chiefs want to trade with a team that is set to compete with them for the top spot in the AFC? Maybe, maybe not. But Fulton would check a lot of boxes for the Jaguars considering the state of their outside cornerback spot. He is just 28, and theere is still plenty of good football left in his tank moving forward.
Perhaps the New York Giants will be hesitant to become sellers since they are 3-2-1 in a very winnable NFC East ... but they shouldn't. The Giants have an absolute mess of a quarterback situation moving forward, and they still have to face the Texans, the Jaguars, the 49ers, the Lions, and the Seahawks over the next few months. The Giants would be wise to get picks where they can, and an expiring contract in Deonte Banks could make sense to move.
Banks is having pretty easily the best year of his career, and the former first-round pick is strictly an outside cornerback, which the Jaguars need considering Montaric Brown is hurt , Travis Hunter deserves more offensive snaps, and Jarrian Jones might be the Jaguars' best slot cornerback after a few struggles outside in recent weeks. Banks would help transform the room, and he could also give the Jaguars a chance to get compensatory picks thanks to Banks' free agency future next March.

title: The Biggest Decision Jaguars' Liam Coen Got Wrong Against the Texans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Hindsight is always 20/20, especially after a loss in the NFL.
With that said, it didn't take the benefit of hindsight to dive into one of Liam Coen's biggest decisions in the Jaguars' 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans in Week 6. Coen and the Jaguars had a chance to put themselves in a position to beat the Texans and improve to 5-1, but that was before this critical decision.
Coen has bgeen an aggressive coach when it comes to fourth-down decisions since he was hired, and it has helped the Jaguars more than a few times. He was even aggressive against the Texans in the first-half, passing up a potential field goal for a fourth-down attempt that would end in an incompletion.
That is what made his decision to kick a 60-yard field goal with 1:55 left a difficult one to understand in the moment. The Jaguars were down by three and had the ball at the Texans' 42-yard line, facing a 4th-and-4 with the game on the line. Going for it would have meant risking the chance of giving the Texans the ball back near midfield, but it also would have given the Jaguars their only real chance to win the game considering the performance C.J. Stroud had.
The math, though, was clear. There were four potential scenarios with the decision, and only one of them would have led to a likely Jaguars win; kick it and make it, and the Texans get the ball back with three timeouts and nearly two minutes to kick a field goal and likely lose, which is what happened; kick it and miss it, and lose; go for it and do not get it, and likely lose; go for it and get the first down, which would have likely led to, at worst, overtime.
For the Jaguars to win this game, they needed to be aggressive one more time instead of trusting their kicker. But they didn't, and the Texans drove down the field and won the game as a result.
"Look, every decision like that, it's a coach's decision. I ended up doing that and there's always hindsight. And you look, alright, if we don't get it, we're going to need a stop either way," Coen said on Monday. "If we go down and you're down by six points, now we have got to go score a touchdown. I felt like we had just got the turnover, maybe we put a little pressure on them on the other side of the ball."
Little, of course, made the 60-yard field goal. The Texans then drove into field goal range in six plays, finishing the drive with a 49-yard field goal as time expired to give themselves the win -- a win that the Jaguars could have had with a different decision and, of course, the proper execution.
But having Little's big leg plays a factor. The Jaguars knew he could make the field goal, and that is exactly what he ended up doing.
"But he gives you so much confidence to be able to be in those moments regardless of end of game, end of half, you feel like he got a shot and that's why we were able to be aggressive at the end of the half was to try to put us in a position to get points and he's such a weapon," Coen said. "Sometimes it makes some of these decisions challenging when you have a guy that's so dynamic that he can make kicks from so many different spots on the field, but very proud of Cam in the last few weeks that he's had, just continues to give us a chance to win.”

title: 2 Jaguars Foes Have Suddenly Emerged as Logical Brian Thomas Jr. Landing Spots
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jagyars are clearly heading in one certain direction with third-year wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. and now a few more teams have emerged as logical landing spots.
With the trade deadline still several weeks away, a lot can change around the NFL to shift the wide receiver market. We saw that over the last two days, with the Los Angeles Rams and Washington Commanders each suddenly having significant receiver injuries pop up over the course of Week 6.
As a result, there is a case to be made for both franchises as landing spots for the embattled former Jaguars' first-round pick , and here is why.
The Rams are in serious trouble at 2-4, with their Super Bowl and dream team aspirations from the offseason looking like a distant memory. The Rams need to quickly rebound over the next 11 games,and the reality is they can likely only afford to sustain three or so losses during that time. To make matters worse, the Rams have now have gotten the injury bug in a big way.
Amongst the injuries the Rams are now facing is one to star wide receiver Davante Adams, who Rams head coach Sean McVay said would be out for the next 6-to-10 weeks after sustaining a lower-body injury in their woeful loss to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 6. Adams has 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns already this season, and he has a high target share of 20.2%, behind only Puka Nacua amongst the Rams' targets.
With Adams out for potentially most of the rest of the season, the Rams will have to rely on a receiver room made up of Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, Jordan Whittington, and Xavier Smith. Outside of Nacua, this is one of the worst wide receiver depth charts in the NFL, and they could use a big boost.
Naturally, Thomas could be that boost. He has had serious issues with drops with the Jaguars over the last two seasons and it seems like the only logical solution is to let him hit the reset button somewhere else while the Jaguars get draft picks in exchange. The Rams need a big-play threat to help the offense get by until Adams returns, and Thomas could certainly be that since he would have more opportunity in the Rams' receiver room than he does in the Jaguars' deep one.
There is a question of whether the Rams would be interested in Thomas since they already gave up picks for Myles Garrett and since they have close ties with a Jaguars' staff that has had their own issues making it work with Thomas. But the Rams need receiver help now to turn around their season and get them to the playoffs, and Thomas would certainly give them a dangerous weapon to pair Nacua with for the long-term.
The next team that suddenly has a massive wide receiver need is the Washington Commanders, who saw wide receiver Terry McLaurin sustain a serious injury on Monday Night Football that NFL Network's Ian Rapoport said is likely a season-ending injury that will sideline him for the rest of the 2026 season. The Commanders are a bad team that is sitting at 1-4-1 and does not have much going for them, but this still makes sense for a few reasons.
#Commanders WR Terry McLaurin, who was carted off in an air cast last night against the #49ers , is feared to have suffered a serious and season-ending knee injury. He’ll have an MRI today. pic.twitter.com/TOs0bxGoNu
While Commanders head coach Dan Quinn will likely be fired this year, it does not feel like the Commanders will dump general manager Adam Peters. The easiest way for Peters to keep his job in the long-term is via Jayden Daniels -- if Daniels can improve his play and get back to his rookie year form, that will look pretty good for the general manager who drafted him a few years ago.
So Thomas is not a trade that would make a ton of sense for a Commanders team that might be losing a ton of games and needs their picks to rebuild ... but it would make sense for a general manager who needs to keep his job to give his quarterback a familiar and talented target. Daniels was Thomas' quarterback during their final seasons at LSU, and the connection between the two could go a long-way toward solving some of Washington's long-term issues at the wide receiver position.
If the Jaguars truly are comfortable with moving on from Thomas this season, there should be no shortage of potential suitors. Two more have hit the radar this week, and more could join as the season goes on.

title: ESPN Matchup Predictor Analyzes Chiefs vs. Seahawks Sunday Night Showdown
full_text:
Following a gritty 22-6 victory over the Chargers last week, the Kansas City Chiefs are set to return to the primetime stage for the first time since Week 2. They will compete in a Sunday Night Football matchup for the second time in 2026 as they head to Seattle to take on the reigning Super Bowl champions.
While Andy Reid's squad has yet to drop a game, the Seahawks have struggled to get their offense going in the post-Kenneth Walker era . Amid their two-game losing streak, quarterback Sam Darnold has tossed four interceptions, including one that ultimately gave the Broncos a free victory last week in overtime. Sportsbooks have labeled Seattle as a slight home favorite, but what does the ESPN Matchup Predictor think? Here's what their computer model projects a few days before kickoff.
This is technically the second meeting between these two teams this year, following an ugly preseason tie in August that featured mostly second and third-string players.
ESPN Matchup Predictor Chances at Victory: Chiefs 52.8%, Seahawks 46.8%.
While Seattle boasts one of the best home-field advantages in the sport, the matchup predictor still gives the undefeated Chiefs a slight edge to maintain their perfect record.
Usually, the matchup predictor closely mirrors what traditional betting lines are forecasting. However, that isn't the case for this contest.
This was undoubtedly circled as one of the more difficult challenges on the Chiefs' schedule heading into the season, and that stands true despite Seattle's early shortcomings. They have the same defensive playmakers who made them a force to be reckoned with in last year's postseason. Even with Darnold's inconsistencies through the air, Jaxon Smith-Njigba remains a premier wide receiver in the league. He leads the NFL in receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns in spite of the shaky quarterback play.
Seattle's passionate 12s will undoubtedly come out in full force, as this game means a lot more to them than it does to the Chiefs. Kansas City obviously wants to preserve its flawless record, but a loss that drops Seattle to 3-4 would likely take the Seahawks out of the division race moving forward.
Walker's homecoming to the team he spent his first four years with is a major storyline. He'll be looking to prove why Seattle should have paid him as he continues to establish himself as one of the best running backs in the NFL.
The Chiefs have had plenty of breaks go their way and won't stay undefeated forever, but the Seahawks will have a tough time overcoming turnovers from Darnold if they want to win. Unlike some of their past opponents, Patrick Mahomes will make them pay.

title: Three Takeaways From Chiefs' Announcement of Josh Simmons Going on Injured Reserve
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs face their toughest test yet on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks, and making matters worse is that the club will continue to be without the services of left tackle Josh Simmons.
Last year's first-round pick hasn't played in a game all season since sustaining a back injury in August , although he did return to practice last week on a limited workload. Unfortunately, that didn't wind up parlaying into getting on the game field, as the former Ohio State standout is set to miss even more time.
Speaking to the media on Thursday, team vice president of sports medicine and performance Rick Burkholder provided a complete breakdown of the Simmons situation. The star tackle has since been placed on the injured reserve list, meaning he's out for a minimum of four additional games.
A clip of Burkholder's statement is below — let's dive into it with three key takeaways.
The #Chiefs , when they have a health situation that requires more context, send out head trainer Rick Burkholder to explain it to the media. He did that today with LT Josh Simmons. Here’s his full explanation: https://t.co/pYCEWuZHtE pic.twitter.com/FHNcMQRh5n
Burkholder opened his media availability by pinpointing when Simmons first got hurt. It's now been over two months since the sophomore tackle first reported a calf issue that turned out to be a back one.
"On August 17, Josh came to me with calf discomfort and feeling that he couldn't post on a single leg in training camp practices," Burkholder said. "This was the same leg that he had knee surgery on in 2024. He was evaluated by our physicians who, thankfully, suspected a low-back injury instead of a lower-leg or knee ailment.
"We obtained an MRI in St. Joe that confirmed that he had a bulging, herniated disc in his lumbar spine. That disc problem was higher up than what we normally see in our offensive linemen, which complicated the case. We recommended a second opinion, as we always do with all of our injured guys and, through his agent and Josh, they selected a spine specialist in California that we have used previously and is really well-known in the NFL.
"He went there and was evaluated, and the recommendation was to do rehabilitation — not surgery — with the intent that we would do an MRI in the near future to see what that disc looked like. Josh continued to progress, and the repeat MRI a few weeks later showed that the disc improved, so no surgery was recommended and rehab would continue."
Head coach Andy Reid acknowledged the bulging disc late last month after previously being noncommittal — and even a bit mysterious — about a recovery timeline or return-to-play window. We now know what triggered Simmons' injury, how it was managed and why he didn't start the regular season on IR.
When Simmons got on the practice field last Wednesday, it was indeed in an effort to evaluate his readiness and continued ramp-up period. It also got many in Chiefs circles buzzing about the much-anticipated season debut for one of the franchise's top young players.
Given that Simmons was a limited participant from there onward and then didn't get any work in this week, something appeared to be up. Burkholder revealed that Simmons simply isn't where he needs to be progress-wise.
"Throughout this process, we've had frequent communication with the second opinion, with our doctors and Josh and his agent," Burkholder said. "Josh worked his tail off. He worked diligently with my staff every day and has improved to the point where he returned to practice in a limited capacity last week. However, we feel that he's plateaued in the rehab process as he's trying to get to the final steps in recovery with return to competition. He's just not there yet."
Everyone then opted to take a break and come up with the best course of action for Simmons' health and eventual on-field viability.
"After discussion with Josh yesterday, we gave him some time to talk with his family and his representatives to investigate next steps as he goes through this process. That's why he was listed yesterday as both personal and with the back injury as we determined these next steps. He took the day off to get with his people."
All of this culminated with Burkholder announcing that Kansas City would be putting Simmons on IR, which the club formally did later on Thursday. As a result, Simmons is ineligible to play versus the Seahawks or in upcoming contests against the Denver Broncos, New York Jets or Atlanta Falcons. The earliest he can return is Week 11 against the Arizona Cardinals.
It wasn't solely Simmons' call. Burkholder emphasized that the IR decision was a collaborative effort that included multiple medical teams, the Chiefs' coaching staff, the front office and, of course, Burkholder and Simmons themselves.
"It was decided and agreed upon by everybody — his people, his agent, him, myself, Andy (Reid), (Brett) Veach — that he should be placed on IR to give him more time to return to full function," Burkholder said. "He'll continue with the rehab process with the goal of returning to play at the high level he achieved in the past."
The organization's hope is now that Simmons will be able to play during the stretch run of the 2026-27 campaign. Surgery still isn't the optimal route, which is a silver lining in what's otherwise still a far less than ideal set of circumstances.
"I give a lot of credit to Josh, my docs, my physicians and my staff," Burkholder added. "I just give them a ton of credit for navigating through this injury to the point where surgery is not recommended and he just needs more time to return to full function."

title: Chiefs Injury Report: Latest on Rashee Rice, Josh Simmons, Jaylon Moore Ahead of Primetime Showdown in Seattle
full_text:
Ahead of the Kansas City Chiefs' Week 7 showdown against the Seattle Seahawks , the team has a mixed bag of injury news.
On Wednesday, head coach Andy Reid indicated that wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) and right tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) would not practice today, while left tackle Josh Simmons (back) is expected to participate to some extent.
Afternoon update: Despite not receiving a pre-practice designation from Reid, Simmons was not seen at practice, according to numerous reports . Later in the afternoon, Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest reported that Simmons would be listed as "DNP (back/personal)."
The story continues below as originally published.
Rice suffered a hamstring injury in Week 4 against the Las Vegas Raiders and has been sidelined since. Even with the benefit of the team's Week 5 bye, Rice was not ready to practice in the team's lead-up to Week 6.
"Rashee's getting better as we go, by the day, so that helps," Reid said on Wednesday.
Simmons returned to practice in a limited capacity last week as a part of his recovery and ramp-up process from his back injury— later described as a bulging disc —that first appeared late in training camp . Simmons participated in all three practices last week but was a limited participant each time.
Moore left Sunday's win over the Los Angeles Chargers due to a concussion that kept him out for the game's second half . While Moore navigates the concussion protocol, offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu is expected to be the first man up at right tackle, as he finished the game in Moore's place against LA.
The Chiefs made a flurry of linebacker-based roster moves on Wednesday, designating linebacker Cooper McDonald to return to practice after a short stint on the injured reserve list. McDonald was placed on IR due to a knee injury suffered early in KC's Week 1 win over the Denver Broncos.
The Chiefs also signed linebacker Aiden Fisher to the practice squad, adding the rookie seventh-round draft pick to their developmental plans. Fisher played for James Madison and Indiana before being drafted by the Houston Texans in April.
In corresponding moves, the team waived linebacker Cam Jones and terminated the practice squad contract of running back Nate Carter.

title: Chiefs vs. Seahawks: Kenneth Walker Looking to Prove Why Seattle Should’ve Paid Him
full_text:
Running back Kenneth Walker III has been nothing short of magnificent since arriving in Kansas City this offseason. Even after the Chiefs' bye week passed, he still leads the NFL in rushing yards despite having played in one fewer game than the next five guys behind him.
"K9" was perhaps the most significant acquisition that general manager Brett Veach made in the winter. It didn't come without its criticisms, though. The age-old argument about whether it's worth it or not to pay a running back big money led many to believe the injury-prone Walker would be a signing KC would soon regret. Through the first couple of months of his tenure in the red and gold, that couldn't be further from the truth. Walker looks like one of the best running backs the Chiefs franchise has ever seen and is making a legitimate case to compete for AFC Offensive Player of the Year. His impending return to his former team could provide another opportunity to show just how valuable that investment has been.
When the Chiefs travel to Seattle for this week's edition of Sunday Night Football, Walker will be making a homecoming to the team he spent his first four years with. He played a huge part in the Seahawks' 2026 Super Bowl run and took home the MVP award in the big game with a 135-yard performance on the ground.
The split between both parties was far more amicable than some departures. Walker left Seattle on decent terms after winning his first Super Bowl ring, forever cementing his place in franchise history as a result. However, he still has plenty to prove to the organization given how his contract situation unfolded this offseason.
When head coach Andy Reid was asked whether Walker would take this game a little more seriously than the others, he refuted those claims and said it'd be business as usual for the superstar tailback. That may be true from Walker's perspective, but it's hard not to wonder if facing the team that drafted him will bring out a little extra motivation.
#Chiefs HC Andy Reid on Kenneth Walker returning to Seattle Sunday evening to take on his former team #Seahawks “I don’t think he’ll have an issue with that, he’s plays aggressive, physical football anyway, that part isn’t going to change—he’s going to bring it even if he’s…
In the offseason, Walker inked a three-year, $43.05 million deal with the Chiefs, but finding a new home was never something he necessarily planned on doing. The Seahawks had expressed interest in keeping him, but they couldn't meet his contract demands, sending Walker into free agency and eventually to KC. The Seahawks chose to allocate that money elsewhere and pursue a new running back in the draft by selecting Jadarian Price in the first round. It's safe to say that hasn't panned out for the reigning champions so far.
Putting aside Walker's success for a minute, Seattle's running game ranks 21st in the NFL in yards per carry and 30th in EPA per play. A slow start from the Notre Dame rookie Price and an early-season injury to Zach Charbonnet forced Seattle to turn to Emanuel Wilson. Charbonnet is actually expected to return from his lingering knee injury for his season debut this week, but there's even a story there.
Throughout his entire time with the Seahawks, there was always an ongoing joke that whenever Walker would put together a strong drive, his rhythm would be disrupted when Seattle's coaches put Charbonnet in at the goal line. Walker never got the full opportunity he deserved in Seattle, and hours after he announced he was heading to the Chiefs, the Seahawks chose to pay return specialist Rashid Shaheed more money annually instead.
Now, the Chiefs have let Walker play out to his full potential as a bell-cow back. He's on pace for 400+ touches, and for perspective, he never surpassed 255 touches from scrimmage during his time as a Seahawk.
It's almost become cliché to keep talking about Walker because of how good he's been. Seattle's run game has faltered without him, and the Chiefs have given him the freedom to establish himself as one of the league's premier backs. On Sunday, he has a chance to make a statement against the team that ultimately decided he wasn't worth the contract he deserved.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Who's in for a Big Post-Bye Stretch?
full_text:
Another week, another Kansas City Chiefs victory. Fresh off a bye to rest up but still nursing some injuries, KC hosted the Los Angeles Chargers and didn't have much trouble en route to a 22-6 victory in front of a raucous crowd at Arrowhead Stadium.
With the win came plenty of positive contributions from young players. Others, however, are raising questions of whether they've plateaued for the time being. Week 7's showdown with the Seattle Seahawks on the road should help us learn plenty about the true colors of Kansas City's youngsters.
Following Week 6, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott isn't included due to him currently being on the physically unable to perform list .
This list contains plenty of usual suspects, headlined by the cornerback duo of Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane. The former had a brilliant Sunday, making multiple pass breakups and also flashing his ability as a tackler. The latter did have one terrible rep on a deep pass, although it served as one of the few low points in his debut campaign to date.
Along the defensive line, second-round edge rusher R Mason Thomas continues to win quickly. The sack numbers may not be there yet, but there's no denying his raw talent that simply must always be accounted for. First-round tackle Peter Woods is quiet in the box score for the most part but did earn the first half-sack of his career in Week 6.
Moving up a tier this week are a rookie and a sophomore. At the left tackle spot, Kansas City continues to game plan around having undrafted man Kahlil Benson in the lineup, but he shored up his play a bit coming out of the bye. He still has the occasional lapse — head coach Andy Reid alluded to one on Monday — but he's faring better than expected. Even if he isn't a clear-cut starter, he deserves props.
On the other side of the ball, defensive end Ashton Gillotte appears to be putting his plantar fascia injury behind him at least a little bit. He got a sack on Los Angeles quarterback Justin Herbert on Sunday and, per Pro Football Focus , has three pressures in consecutive games.
It brings me no joy bumping fifth-round rookie halfback Emmett Johnson down here, but his last few games haven't been very productive at all. In Weeks 4-6, he's toted the ball nine times and managed just 23 yards. That's despite combining to play 48 offensive snaps. Johnson's time should still be coming — this feels like a temporary demotion.
2025 fourth-round receiver Jalen Royals got targeted four times in the passing game with Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) out, recording a pair of receptions for 24 yards. He also played 45 snaps, marking the second game in a row his share has increased. Elsewhere as far as pass catchers are concerned, Jake Briningstool's elevation stems solely from workload (his snaps have increased by two in Weeks 4 and 6) and rookie wideout Cyrus Allen recorded his first two NFL catches over the weekend.
UDFA defensive tackle Bryson Eason isn't a primary special-teamer (he hasn't played there at all) but he also isn't seeing the field much on defense. He's somewhere in the middle, albeit not in his own tier.
There still isn't anything to see here. Simmons is making progress as he works his way back from a bulging disc , and Reid was noncommittal about his playing status on Monday. If the 2025 first-round pick isn't back this Sunday, look for Week 8 as a potential season debut spot.
Safety Nwankpa feels like he might be on the verge of increased playing time, although it might require an injury before he's unleashed on the defensive end. Running back Brashard Smith makes sense as a candidate to take special teams opportunities from wideout Nikko Remigio, who struggled once again against Los Angeles.
Jeffrey Bassa is turning himself into a trusted core player for coordinator Dave Toub on teams. Similar to Nwankpa, though, he's buried on the depth chart on defense.
Since playing 47 special teams snaps in the first three weeks of the season, fourth-round rookie cornerback Jadon Canady hasn't been active for a game. He's got to come down a tier.
Elsewhere, the trio of quarterback Garrett Nussmeier, tackle Diego Pounds and defensive end Jack Pyburn can be classified as organizational depth for now.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Is the Chiefs' Offensive Line Set for a Disappointment in Seattle?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 5-0 and alone atop the AFC as the only undefeated team in the conference, but they still have plenty of questions to answer ahead of their primetime Sunday night showdown against the Seattle Seahawks this weekend.
Every week here in the Chiefs On SI mailbag , we take your questions from @chiefs_kcsn on Twitter/X and @jbbrisco.com on Bluesky , navigating the biggest unknowns the Chiefs have as the season rolls on. Let's get to it!
Does the dam eventually break on the O-line without Josh Simmons? - @oscarbobo.bsky.social
It's sure looking like Sunday night's game in Seattle will be the O-line's most difficult test yet. With left tackle Josh Simmons still appearing to be in "ramp-up" territory this week, I'm assuming that undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson will get his sixth start at left tackle, while right tackle Jaylon Moore's status is questionable after leaving the Chiefs' win over the Los Angeles Chargers due to a concussion. With the inherent unknowns of concussions and the NFL's concussion protocol, Joshua Ezeudu could be getting the start at right tackle.
According to ESPN , the Seahawks have the No. 1 pass rush win rate in the league through Week 6. That has resulted in 16 sacks and the league's highest quarterback knockdown percentage and second-highest pressure percentage , so this isn't a great time to have a banged-up line.
Still, the Chiefs' interior of Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith can still be trusted, and they've managed without Simmons so far. I'd be surprised if the KC O-line was entirely overwhelmed in a game-altering way in Seattle, but I'd also be surprised if they pitched a shutout against the Seahawks.
Do all roads lead to another Chiefs vs. 49ers Super Bowl? - @toptrevor.bsky.social
It sure feels that way, doesn't it? I've been enormously impressed by how the 49ers have managed yet another injury-ravaged season, and I think their ability to stay afloat (and undefeated) despite health woes has earned them a reasonable claim to the No. 1 spot in some power rankings . However, those losses can stack up and cause more significant damage later in the year, so I fear for the Niners' long-term health.
While the Chiefs still have flaws, just like every other team in the NFL, I'm hugely excited by the possibility of them regaining Simmons and potentially ending the year healthier than they started it.
KCSN’s NFL Power Rankings heading into Week 6 📊 These rankings reflect the average of our hosts’ votes — who’s too high and who’s too low? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/dGx1EC3wdL
Good, bad, or both, what has surprised you the most about the Chiefs so far this season? - @MrEd315
The biggest positive surprise has to be the absolute dominance from Kenneth Walker III . I'm not surprised that he's been good—that was to be expected—but I'm amazed by how good, how consistent, and how diversely superb he's been, while totally transforming the KC offense.
The bad surprises come from the Chiefs' special teams. Many assumed that Harrison Butker's recent issues had been largely due to lingering injury issues, giving him a chance to return to his previous level after another offseason to settle back in, but he's still missing enough kicks to cause some fair concern .
Adding in issues with special teams penalties , Nikko Remigio's fumbled punt against the Chargers and the lack of a role for Brashard Smith amidst a generally underwhelming return game, the Chiefs' third phase still has a lot of work to do.
Considering the Broncos' upcoming schedule, is the AFC West still a live fight? - @oscarbobo.bsky.social
It absolutely is! The Broncos are coming off of a gross, uninspiring win over the Seahawks, but they're still 4-2 ahead of a relatively soft stretch in their upcoming schedule. If the Broncos beat the Chiefs in Denver on November 1, the divisional race will immediately be back on after KC's early lead. If the Chiefs win at Mile High Stadium in two weeks, it would make it extremely difficult for Denver to come roaring back.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Who Helped and Hurt Their Case in Week 6 Win vs. Chargers?
full_text:
Five games into the 2026-27 season, the Kansas City Chiefs have helped themselves in a major way by already picking up three wins against divisional opponents. Sunday's Week 6 triumph over the Los Angeles Chargers wasn't the prettiest of victories, but Andy Reid's team thoroughly outplayed its rival by a multitude of measurements nonetheless.
In the 22-6 outcome in favor of the hosts, several critical players managed to make an impact on their respective side of the ball. Others struggled to execute what was asked of them, although there's still plenty of time to turn things around.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 6's Chiefs victory against Los Angeles and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 7 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons over the weekend, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
The Chiefs' defense is performing at a very respectable level this season, and its new-look secondary is a significant reason why. A returning player from a year ago, 2025 third-round pick Nohl Williams, has starred to this point in the campaign and may have turned in his best outing yet on Sunday.
After making a big-time downhill tackle on the Chargers' opening drive, the Cal product was banged up but stayed in the game and continued to get noticed. A pair of pass breakups — one on a second-and-9 on the next possession and a third-and-goal stop in the second half — showcased his instincts and timing. Finally, Williams prevented wideout KeAndre Lambert-Smith from converting on a fourth down in the final frame.
The sophomore stopper is disruptive, tough and thorough in the defensive backfield, which is precisely what Kansas City needs.
What a turnaround it's been over the last month for one Xavier Worthy. Through three outings, he'd averaged five targets a game but managed only 6.3 yards per reception and looked more and more like an afterthought in the offense. In his last two weeks of play, he's gone for seven targets each time and racked up 143 yards in the process, good for 13 yards per catch. Sunday was his most complete showing to date.
Worthy had a 33-yarder wiped out by an illegal block by tight end Travis Kelce right out of the gate, then followed it up with a gain of 15 on the very next play. He notched 70 yards on five receptions in the first half alone and made a nice diving snag in the second half. With the KC wideout room severely banged up at the moment , Worthy's ability to step up and rise to the occasion is a pleasant surprise for the Chiefs as the season approaches its midpoint.
Speaking of players who made the most of their opportunities in Week 6, Noah Gray matched the receiving output of Kelce by mustering 53 yards in the home win. Gray hauled in each of the three targets thrown his way and displayed some rare post-catch chops on a 31-yard rumble to boot. Kelce's ankle injury limited his effectiveness and availability a bit, so Gray being the one to help insulate the pass catchers was a nice development.
There's only room for three here, but defensive end George Karlaftis deserves considerable praise for his recent play. He's undoubtedly turning into quite the productive player for Kansas City and has been a driving force in multiple victories.
This group of three didn't live up to the hype in Week 6. It isn't necessarily time to panic, but it's certainly time to be on watch.
Back to the aforementioned receiver injuries. Given that Tyquan Thornton is on injured reserve due to a dislocated ankle and Rashee Rice needed (at least) another week to rehab a hamstring issue , this was a massive chance for a lesser-discussed wideout like Nikko Remigio to take a role and run with it on Sunday. He did nothing of the sort on the offensive end, receiving all of two offensive snaps. He also had a special teams fumble.
Coordinator Dave Toub has preached patience with his group getting out to a slow start, but mistakes persist in multiple areas of special teams. Remigio, whose role seems defined, isn't doing anything to justify being a long-term solution as a returner.
It's now been several years in a row of Harrison Butker not matching the leaguewide perception of him being one of the best in the business. It's this writer's take that those days are clearly over now , even if the team won't admit it, especially given another missed extra point and some waning effectiveness on long-range boots.
Butker's trump card is his ability to make pressure-packed kicks, which is one heck of a positive to bring to the table, but everything else is questionable right now. Week 6 only underscored that.
Had he not gotten ejected for throwing a punch, defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace wouldn't have even been considered for a spot here. He made multiple solid plays elsewhere, including a big tackle for loss and a tipped interception that got nullified by a penalty. At the end of the day, though, you simply can't put your team in a compromising position like that.

title: Kenneth Walker is Rushing Past Reasonable Expectations, Straight Into Chiefs History
full_text:
It keeps getting more and more difficult to write about Kenneth Walker III.
Not because I'm bored of talking about Walker's unbelievable dominance—quite the opposite, in fact. Walker has been so outstanding that even a measured evaluation of his 2026 season sounds like the ravings of a madman.
The remarkable stats help tell the story, but even those feel insufficient. Still, they're worth knowing: Walker's 133 rushing yards per game are the most for any running back through six weeks since at least 2016 . He has a 40% forced missed tackle rate , the best in the NFL by more than 10%. He's the first player since 2002 to have 750+ scrimmage yards and 8+ touchdowns through the first five games of the year. The player who did that in '02? Chiefs Hall of Honor member Priest Holmes.
Many excellent running backs have starred throughout Chiefs history, as good-but-not-great teams often relied on dominant runners to carry their respective squads.
Christian Okoye—"the Nigerian Nightmare"—thundered into Chiefs history in the late '80s and early '90s. Marcus Allen left the rival Raiders to finish his career in Kansas City, taking the baton from Okoye. Holmes was the running back of my childhood—a workhorse that thrived behind a remarkable offensive line, instilling a love of smashmouth football in so many young Chiefs fans. Larry Johnson followed as a quintessential bellcow back, the engine of Chiefs offenses that relied on him to take on a superhuman workload.
Then came Jamaal Charles, my favorite running back of all time. Charles was a gamebreaker. He moved unlike anyone I've ever seen on a football field, skating past defenders with a smoothness typically reserved for athletes on ice.
In recent years, the Chiefs briefly had a true No. 1 back with Kareem Hunt, found excellent role players like Damien Williams and Jerick McKinnon, invested a premium pick in Clyde Edwards-Helaire, got two productive years from Isiah Pacheco, and patched up the weaker seasons with relative success until the wheels fell off the running back room in 2025.
But with all that history, all those legacies, and all of those yards... Through five games, Walker has been in a league of his own.
Walker's second touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday might have been the most on-brand run of his still-young Chiefs tenure. Look at this snapshot of Walker's situation moments before scoring a touchdown.
This was a touchdown. pic.twitter.com/uYSK1YJkof
By any NFL standard, that play is dead. The body is cold. The Chargers had the beat on the play. All they had to do was, y'know, tackle Walker. But that's been a problem for every team the Chiefs have faced through five games.
My favorite nugget from the Chiefs' win over the Chargers comes from Next Gen Stats .
"Walker gained 53 yards and 2 TDs on 6 carries against stacked boxes (8+ defenders). He leads the NFL in yards (183) and TDs (6) on those runs."
Kenneth Walker III forced 7 missed tackles against the Chargers, bringing his NFL-leading total to 52. Walker gained 53 yards and 2 TDs on 6 carries against stacked boxes (8+ defenders). He leads the NFL in yards (183) and TDs (6) on those runs. @LACvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/fsnBre5Mn5
One of the surefire selling points of Walker's contract with the Chiefs was that he would be able to take advantage of light boxes while opposing defenses respected Patrick Mahomes and the KC passing game, allowing Walker's life to get easier while the rushing attack got more productive. Instead, Walker is just slicing through heavy boxes, too. It's remarkable.
Can Walker keep up this outrageous standard of performance through 17 regular season games and a playoff push? Who knows. But at some point, we should probably stop asking “Can he keep doing this?” and start asking, “What if this is just who he is?”
I'm still struggling to flip that particular switch myself. Even if he does this for 15 more games, can he do it in 2027? 2028? Is his legacy evolving from “very good running back who won Super Bowl MVP on a team with a questionable quarterback” to a future Hall of Famer who truly evolved into a superstar once he joined the Chiefs? Will the rest of his prime be spent as a perennial Offensive Player of the Year finalist? Is he the most impactful non-quarterback in the league?
This is why it feels so difficult to properly talk about Walker through five games. The truth sounds like hyperbole, and hyperbole still isn’t strong enough to explain what Walker has done throughout the start of this season.

title: Chiefs WR Xavier Worthy Finally Stepped Up When Kansas City Needed Him the Most
full_text:
Amid the ongoing injuries to the Chiefs' receiving corps, there were concerns about how the wideouts would fare against the Chargers. Kansas City was without Tyquan Thornton whose fractured ankle will force him to miss most of the season, and Rashee Rice was also sidelined with a hamstring injury.
Third-year speedster Xavier Worthy had caught a lot of flak in recent weeks due to his mediocre start to the season. Through the first three weeks of the campaign, Worthy ranked in the bottom three in the NFL in yards per catch and was primarily used in the short game. The Chiefs weren't necessarily playing to his strengths , which include his ability to stretch the field as a long-ball threat. Worthy finally silenced those concerns in the game where KC needed him the most. He finished the 22-6 victory over the Chargers with a season-high seven receptions for 73 yards, hauling in all of his targets from quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Going into the contest, Worthy knew he'd have to take on an extended workload to help make up for the team's injuries. He couldn't have asked for a better opportunity to show that he was ready for it.
"They told me all week that [WR1] was going to be me," Worthy said in the locker room after the win. "I got to step up for the receiving room guys who went down, so I did my job."
It has been a long road for Worthy, whose progress during his 638-yard, nine-touchdown rookie season was derailed by a subpar sophomore year. He dislocated his shoulder in the 2025 season opener, and although he returned to action a few weeks later, he never had the same explosiveness or burst moving forward.
Regardless, head coach Andy Reid maintains that Worthy has always been capable of this kind of production and should be able to reach his full potential now that he's fully healthy and being given a more featured role in the aerial attack. "We had some injuries, and all of a sudden, he becomes the primary guy," Reid stated in his media appearance this afternoon. "But he's always had this ability and can do all of this. He's a good football player. It's just a matter of there's only so many plays, and so many times to spread the ball around."
All of the questions about whether Worthy's speed had diminished since his first year in the red and gold were put to bed in Week 6. His highlight of the night came on a blazing 19-yard catch that helped Kansas City tack on another three points before halftime.
Xavier Worthy hit 21.07 MPH on this play per @NextGenStats the 2nd fastest ball carrier of the week. https://t.co/XOmGcJ36nR
The length of Rice's absence remains to be seen, but Worthy should have plenty of confidence after finally getting a chance to show what he can do. If this version of Worthy sticks around, Kansas City's receiver room may not be as dire as it once appeared.

title: The Chiefs Have a Harrison Butker Problem, Whether They Care to Admit It or Not
full_text:
It's hard to go directly to nitpicking after a win, especially for a team that returned from the bye and improved to a perfect 5-0 . If there's one thing the Kansas City Chiefs have shown through five games, however, it's that multiple areas of the team are imperfect as the season's midpoint draws near.
For every instance in which the Chiefs' dominance of old has flashed, there's been a reminder or two that this is a new era. There's no greater example of that than the roller coaster ride that is the play of kicker Harrison Butker.
I will repeat again, Harrison Butker came into this game as one of the bottom 10 Kickers in the NFL to start 2026 and this performance in Kansas City is going to send him tumbling down the list.... Chiefs must look for replacements. pic.twitter.com/v0YSLh6u48
With data mounting that this is a new era for Butker as well, should that come with new expectations? It's clear that he isn't the same player right now, yet special teams coordinator Dave Toub preaches patience and sample-size variance for the entire special teams unit. Following Sunday's victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, head coach Andy Reid also danced around any Butker-related concerns.
"Butker, he's as consistent as anybody," Reid said. "He had a couple of misses in there, and that's not normally him, so he'll continue to work on that."
It'd be one thing if Kansas City admitted Butker isn't meeting the bar that's been set. A plan to establish more consistency — actual consistency, not the perceived press-conference backing provided by the team — would be a nice first step.
Instead, the club is paying Butker more on a per-year basis ( $6.4 million ) than all but three kickers in NFL history to provide negative value. Doing so while denying that is even worse.
The three-time Super Bowl champion is now several years removed from his last legitimately good effort. In 2023, he drilled 94.3% of field goals and didn't miss an extra point. In 35 regular-season outings since then, though, those respective accuracy marks are 84.2% and 91.4%. Last year saw the former seventh-round pick finish just 1.2% above the league average on field goals and 7.3% worse on PATs.
Following the Chargers game, Butker's missed one extra point in 2026 and is sporting an ugly 76.9% conversion clip on field goals. According to Pro Football Focus , his average starting field position on kickoffs (30.2 yards) is 18th out of 33 kickers with five or more tries. Last year, his 30.3 figure sat 26th among 44 players with double-digit kicks. That does, in fairness, have something to do with coverage.
There's also the question of long-range kicking. Something that was once a calling card for Butker has turned into another high-variance component, evidenced by him going 5-for-8 in 2025 and being off to a 1-for-4 start in 2026. The 31-year-old can still be relied upon to have a clutch gene, which is a damn good plus to have in the toolbox, but the positive traits are dwindling .
He was erratic on other kicks this preseason, too, which was followed by Reid saying he'll "learn from it and move on" and "make an adjustment."
Butker has been through a similar stretch before, connecting on 76.9% of field goals and 84.6% of point-afters entering Week 6 of 2025 and finishing the year strong. That doesn't mean it didn't impact him, as he admitted in June :
"I think when you start the season off with misses, your back's kind of against the wall [and] mentally, it kind of takes a toll on you," Butker said. "It's just not great. I climbed out of it; I finished the season, I think I was above middle-of-the-pack. Obviously, you don't even want to be there, but you don't want to start out the season missing as much."
Butker is held in too high of regard and making too much money to be an up-and-down player at best and a diminished version of himself at worst. An in-season change is mostly unrealistic, although the Chiefs coming to terms with their current reality and future salary cap flexibility shouldn't be. The glory days of not having to question whether KC had an elite kicker are over.
Now, both the team and those watching it should be questioning whether Butker's even good anymore.

title: Chargers' Justin Herbert Getting Some Tua Tagovailoa-Level Heat for Struggles
full_text:
There’s plenty of blame to go around for the Los Angeles Chargers .
Joe Hortiz deserves most of it for a bad streak of roster-building that has left coaches and coordinators with a lacking roster.
That won’t stop calls for Jim Harbaugh’s job , though, nor will it take the pressure off offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel for authoring perhaps the worst stretch of Justin Herbert’s career.
But make no mistake, Herbert himself is under the microscope, too. At some point, the blame has to go his way, whether onlookers like it or not.
What some won’t like hearing, though, is NFL coaches and others making odd-seeming Brock Purdy comparisons for Herbert in the wake of his recent struggles.
Anyone with a passing familiarity of the Chargers knows how much the organization has failed him over the years.
The Chargers constantly throwing new coordinators at him, not giving him quality non-Keenan Allen weapons and the refusal to admit that interior offensive line is important and worth a premium are just some of the factors at work here.
But Herbert’s been so poor, even compared to last year, that some are questioning whether he can even run McDaniel’s scheme.
Some NFL coaches told The Athletic’s Mike Sando that McDaniel’s scheme is overly complex and it just might not be a fit.
"There are a lot of formations and motions that he's gonna present to you," one NFL coach told Sando. "I don't know if that's easy to operate for those guys or not.”
Now, things are looping back to Tua Tagovailoa comparisons and even bringing up a name like Brock Purdy.
"In Miami, when they were rolling, it was because of the explosive skill they had, and a phenomenal system," another coach told Sando. "San Francisco rolls because of Brock Purdy. I just don't know if Herbert can handle that system. That is my take, and then couple that with their line being the worst we've seen."
It’s easy to scoff at these things. But one doesn't have to look far to find chatter around the Chargers about "simplifying" things over the bye. And it was at least worth a raise of the eyebrow over the summer when McDaniel started tweaking Herbert’s footwork and stuff.
The fact the Chargers aren’t firing McDaniel or announcing any changes at all during the bye hints that they believe this is a long-term fix that will be worth it.
We’ll see if that’s true, but the last thing anyone expected was Herbert getting thrown back into Tagovailoa comparisons.

title: Chargers Scouts Get Eyes on Top Prospects at Key College Matchups
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers college scouting department has been active so far this year. The current state of the Chargers roster displays several holes some of which were predictable, others brought upon by units being decimated by injuries.
The Chargers scouts are active on the scouting trail across the country. Part of a scouts role is to build as deep of a profile and understanding of college prospects from as early on as possible. We may have limited access to games they have attended but during the week scouts are stopping at campuses to catch practice and to talk to coaches.
The process never stops and extends throughout the offseason training programs and spring practices as well. By the time a prospect declares for the draft, unless they are extremely under the radar or late bloomers, most have years of information gathered on them.
Games  and game performances are a piece of the puzzle. Scouts getting an up close look at prospects in high profile moments and getting an in-person feel for the competitive environment gives scouts invaluable context to how players rise or crumble in key moments.
Los Angeles' scouts were publicly noted at three games this past weekend, two of which were massive games for standing or rivalries. Let's dive into the three and some key prospects that the Chargers likely have their eyes on.
The biggest match of the week pitted the second ranked Notre Dame Fighting Irish against the eighth ranked BYU Cougars. BYU took the victory but not without controversy on the final play in the endzone.
The Irish are stacked with NFL talent and the majority of their defense in on the NFL's radar. Notre Dame quarterback CJ Carr is performing well this season and has climbed his was into first round consideration as he continues to play well.
Cornerback Leonard Moore is the highest-ranked player on their team and very well could be the first defender off of the board on draft night. To go along with Moore, other top prospects include linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa, guard Anthonie Knapp, edge rusher Boubacar Traore are just the beginning of the long list of prospects playing for Notre Dame.
BYU has several prospects but their top prospect, running back LJ Martin, missed the game due to injury. One of BYU's other top prospects, linebacker Cade Uluave, is in his first year with the Cougars and he has been on my radar since his freshman season at Cal.
Uluave is a rangy, tough linebacker who popped on film next to current Ravens linebacker Teddye Buchanan. The Chargers were frequently in attendance at Cal's games over the past few seasons and undoubtedly have been keeping close tabs on Uluave.
The game between Florida State and Miami was a good old fashioned double overtime rivalry slugfest. The Chargers have recent history with Miami after taking edge rusher Akheem Mesidor in the first round in the most recent draft.
The Hurricanes are well stocked with NFL draft prospects including quarterback Darian Mensah, defensive tackles Ahmad Moten Sr. and Justin Scott, running back Mark Fletcher, offensive lineman Samsun Okunlola, linebacker Damon Wilson II and cornerback OJ Federique are just the start of their talented roster.
Florida State is much thinner in terms of prospects this season but 6'6 wide receiver Duce Robinson is undoubtedly on the Chargers' radar. Robinson is a enormous outside downfield threat and playmaker. He had two touchdowns and 113 yards in this game against Miami.
DUCE ROBINSON AGAIN FLORIDA STATE OMG pic.twitter.com/6J7OssUTYZ
This matchup has a handful of potential draft propects but neither team has prospect near the top of the class. The marquee player in this matchup is true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree.
Legree will not be draft eligible until 2029 but he is firmly in the heisman running at this point as he takes the country by storm. He is currently leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns through seven weeks. Going back to the conversation of how long scouts have their eyes on players, in two years, notes taken now will be compared to how Legree looks and performs as he gears up for his presumed final season of college football.

title: Which Teams Would Give Up Most Capital in a Justin Herbert Trade?
full_text:
Trading Justin Herbert is not something most Chargers fans want to think about. To be fair, this idea probably will never happen. Quarterbacks with his combination of arm strength, athletic ability and experience are difficult to find, and replacing one would be an enormous challenge.
A quarterback of his caliber would not simply attract a few phone calls, it would be much more.  However the most important part is what they would be willing to give up in return.
CBS Sports highlighted players they would like to see with a different scenery, and Herbert was one of thier picks.
Three teams stand out as the best potential buyers in that unlikely scenario, and I believe they would throw tons of capital the Chargers' way for a quarterback like Herbert.
Indianapolis might have the most interesting connection to Herbert, thanks to head coach Shane Steichen. Before becoming the Colts head coach, Steichen worked with Herbert in Los Angeles serving as the Chargers’ offensive coordinator in 2020.
That history is important. Steichen has already seen Herbert operate at the NFL level and understands what makes him such a difficult quarterback to defend. Rather than spending months evaluating whether Herbert fits his system, the Colts’ head coach would have firsthand experience to draw from.
Also their need for a quarterback in the last few weeks has been a topic of concern.
Any serious pursuit would likely require several premium draft assets, potentially including multiple first-round picks. The Colts would also need to account for Herbert’s contract while continuing to surround him with enough talent to compete.
Still, if Steichen believed Herbert could take the offense to another level, Indianapolis would have a compelling reason to explore the opportunity. The existing relationship makes this more interesting than a typical quarterback trade rumor.
Minnesota would be another team worth watching if a quarterback of Herbert’s ability suddenly entered the trade market. The Vikings have reason to think about their long-term future at the position, and landing an established quarterback could eliminate a major question for the organization.
They have a killer defense, which might be the best in the NFL. Also having elite receiver Justin Jefferson, and adding Herbert would mean championship hopes suddenly appear. Their problem is clearly finding a reliable guy under center.
If the Vikings believed their roster was ready to make a serious championship push, pursuing Herbert could become a conversation worth having. Finding a quarterback who can anchor a team for years is difficult, and opportunities like this rarely come along.
Miami could become one of the more intriguing teams in the conversation if Herbert ever became available. If the organization decided it needed a different direction at quarterback, pursuing an established talent would be an entirely different approach than starting over through the draft. A type of trade for this highly touted player would change their team around immediately.
Herbert would give the team a quarterback with the arm strength to attack every part of the field. He has shown he can make difficult throws and produce without everything around him being perfect, which would be especially valuable for a team trying to turn its offensive potential into consistent results.
There is no guarantee they would be willing or financially positioned to make that kind of move. But if Herbert unexpectedly entered the trade market, the Dolphins would have a reason to at least explore the possibility.

title: Chargers All-Star Offensive Lineman Returns to Practice, Quieting Season-Ending Rumors
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have started the 2026 NFL season at 0-6, marking them as officially the worst team in the NFL. They have dealt with injuries, poor play from multiple units and extremely poor coaching from coaches who seemingly have never had a track record of being bad.
While it has been an odd season filled with surprises, one thing has been unsurprising: injuries piling up for players in the Powder Blue uniform. Injuries always seem to happen for the Chargers, an unfortunate certainty fans can count on year in and year out.
One of the biggest injuries suffered thus far in the 2026 NFL season has been Pro Bowl offensive tackle, former Top 5 selection, Joe Alt. Alt suffered a neck injury against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 4 due to a freak helicopter-esque kick from Seahawks defender Nick Emmanwori.
The play where Joe Alt is injured by Seahawks DB Nick Emmanwori pic.twitter.com/2P0KMGTzAl
Cannot exactly say I have seen anything like that happen in an NFL game, but also I cannot say I thought the Chargers were going to be 0-6 to start this NFL season either.
Moving on, Alt has missed two games: the Chargers' losses to the Denver Broncos and the Kansas City Chiefs. Anytime you are dealing with a neck injury, it is important to prioritize safety over rushing back, allowing Alt to spend time with a specialist and get clearance to begin practicing on Oct. 18.
Alt has officially returned to practice today, Oct. 21, the Chargers' first practice since losing to the Chiefs. Along with his return, the Chargers' starting left guard, Kayode Awosika , has also returned to practice after missing time with his fibula injury. He missed a total of four games.
RT Joe Alt (neck) and LG Kayode Awosika (fibula) were participating during the portion of today’s Chargers practice open to the media.
Now that the Chargers are back with two more of their offensive linemen, the offensive line will once again be shuffled to ensure the "best 5" are out in front of Justin Herbert. With rookies Travis Burke, Logan Taylor and Alex Harkey all being starters over the last two weeks, who will be the rookies to be replaced first?
LT: Travis Burke LG: Kayode Awosika C: Jake Slaughter RG: Cole Strange RT: Joe Alt
This lineup sees Harkey and Taylor being replaced by Alt and Awosika, returning from their respective injuries. Burke continues in his role as the third tackle, continuing what has been a pretty impressive season for the fourth-round rookie.
The only step left for the Bolts is to see Rashawn Slater return from injured reserve and get this offensive line back to health. Who knows if that will be enough to turn the team around, but seeing Herbert have healthy linemen in front of him will hopefully bring more morale.
