title: Grading Rams Signing of Brandon McManus: The Latest Chapter in a Never-Ending Nightmare
full_text:
When the Los Angeles Rams put kicker Blake Grupe on injured reserve on Monday, it was reported that they worked out veteran kickers Brandon McManus and Matt Prater. After holding a competition, the Rams have opted to sign McManus according to NFL Media’s Ian Rapoport.
The #Rams are signing veteran kicker Brandon McManus, per me and @MikeGarafolo , the latest in Los Angeles’ kicker saga. He worked out today, along with FA K Matt Prater. McManus most recently kicked for the #Packers and #Broncos . pic.twitter.com/eyzO9QmQjt
Speaking to the media on Monday, head coach Sean McVay said that they were in the process of replacing Grupe. The group of Assistant GM John McKay, Special Teams Coordinator Bubba Ventrone, and General Manager Les Snead worked on different options and eventually opted with McManus.
McManus made just 80 percent of his field goals last year in the regular season with the Green Bay Packers, going 24-for-30. In the playoffs against the Chicago Bears, McManus went 0-for-2 on field goals, missing from 55 and 44 yards. He also missed an extra point in what was a 31-27 loss. T he Packers cut McManus in May.
Brandon McManus had only missed one playoff kick in his career going into tonight (11/12 on field goals, 4/4 on extra points). He's missed THREE kicks against the Bears: Two field goals and an extra point. #Packers #Bears #NFLPlayoffs pic.twitter.com/IdnJrdd6dQ
The Rams will hope that McManus can provide some immediate stability at the kicker position. At 35 years old, he’s at least a veteran presence and a known commodity. Even if he isn’t the kicker that he was in his prime, he still made a kick from 56 yards last year and is one season removed from making 95.2 percent of his field goals in 2024.
At this point in the season, there aren’t a plethora of great kicking options available.. This remains something that the Rams should have done in July rather than having to do it now in October. It’s a similar approach to the one the Rams took in 2023 when they signed Brett Maher.
No matter who the Rams signed at kicker, it would be an ‘is what it is’ situation. Matt Prater went 18-for-20 on field goals last year and 5-for-5 in the playoffs. Both options are simply putting a Band-Aid over a bullet wound, and neither provides a long-term solution. It still seems odd that the Rams won’t sign a player like Tanner Brown to their practice squad just to give them a younger option to develop.
The Rams’ handling of their special teams and field goal unit has been a disaster . Even if they had confidence in Harrison Mevis, he didn’t perform well enough to not have any competition this offseason. Grupe finally gave them some upside if he had worked out but got injured on his first kickoff because the coverage unit didn’t do its job.
Even with McManus, the Rams will likely be searching for another kicker during the offseason. Given how they handled Joshua Karty and the lack of development with Mevis, it’s fair to question whether this coaching staff and front office can identify and then develop a kicker that finally resolves the issues.
Sign up to our free newsletter and follow us on Facebook , X , and Instagram for the latest news.
Blaine Grisak is the Lead Publisher for Rams on SI covering the Los Angeles Rams. Prior to joining On Sports Illustrated, he covered the Rams for TurfShow Times. He's been credentialed for events such as the NFL in Australia, NFL Draft, NFL Combine, and Senior Bowl. A graduate of Northeastern University, Blaine grew up in Montana.

title: Bad News Emerges on Raiders' Latest Injury Report
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are no strangers to injuries, as the past few seasons have brought devastating injuries to the Silver and Black. This offseason and early regular season have seen the Raiders sustain various levels of injuries and physical ailments among some of their best players.
Las Vegas has done the best it can to move through the season with those injuries, as every team deals with injuries once the season starts. Week 7 is shaping up to be another Sunday of the Raiders facing a team with just as many, if not more, injuries than they do.
In total, Las Vegas had 11 different players on the injury report through Thursday, but it appears to be getting healthier overall. Friday will be the true test for the team's overall health.
Brock Bowers, Spencer Burford, Folorunso Fatukasi, Kolton Miller, Segun Olubi, Carter Runyon, Dont'e Thornton, and Trey Zuhn all fully participated in Thursday's practice. Tonka Hemingway and Quay Walker participated in practice on a limited basis on Thursday.
When asked if running back Mike Washington earned more reps, Kubiak stated, "Yes," he had. Washington was listed on the injury report as a limited participant on Wednesday and did not practice on Thursday afternoon. This could be bad news for the Raiders.
Or it could be precautionary, since Bowers missed Friday's practice before his first start of the season, and Jeanty did not practice late in Week 5 before Las Vegas faced the New England Patriots, but he still played that Sunday . Washington averaged about five carries per game before last Sunday.
It is unclear how much Washington's injury will affect the Raiders' game plan, since Jeanty isn't listed on the injury report and is presumably nearly as healthy as he has been this season. This is only the second time this season that Jeanty has not been listed on the injury report.
Heading into Week 6, Jeanty averaged nearly 18 carries per game before that number was cut in half last Sunday, as Washington carried the ball double his season average per game. If Washington is out on Sunday against the Rams , Jeanty's health and durability will be tested.
Las Vegas' injury list is filled with primarily offensive players. The unit's long list of injuries only add to the deficiencies the unit has when healthy. Luckily, the list is long, but most of the players on it practiced on Thursday and should be good to go on Sunday.
The Raiders' coaching staff must maximize the talent that is on the field this Sunday. It will not matter how well Las Vegas' defense plays if their offense waits until the fourth quarter to take and execute shots downfield. Raiders' offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko shed light on the staff's mindset.
“You’re always looking for different ways to create explosives , and each game, each series is different. So, if there’s a way to exploit something with the defense in a certain manner, we try to get that and just try to put our players in the best position to make plays at any time in the game, asking them to use their specific skills, run game, pass game,” Janocko said before Thursday’s practice.
“And then that allows our coaches to develop those guys, and I think our coaches do a great job, whether it’s in the receivers room with Zach [Azzanni], Steck [Luke Steckel] in the tight ends room, Omar [Young] developing Mike [Washington Jr.] as he goes along."
"But those guys just being able to maximize their players’ talents, and Klint [Kubiak] and I being able to put the guys in the best position possible.”
The Raiders face a talented Los Angeles Rams team on Sunday, but LA will be without several of its best players. However, the Patriots were missing even more players than the Rams are and thoroughly outplayed the Raiders. Las Vegas has no room for error on Sunday.
The Raiders can end one streak and start another by beating the Rams on Sunday, with a winnable game against their old quarterback, Geno Smith, and the New York Jets on the road in Week 8. First, Las Vegas must take care of home after dropping their last two games at Allegiant Stadium.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Weekly Musings: Rams Run Into Raiders’ Buzzsaw
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.--The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are playing host to the preseason Super Bowl favorites from the NFC, the Los Angeles Rams (2-4), on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium.
Rumors are swirling around the NFL trade deadline, but the team is totally focused on getting back on track and getting the big win.
Here are my weekly thoughts surrounding this team, and I can attest that these are not the same old Raiders.
In the past, when the team started to lose, I never saw them quit. An admirable trait for sure, but there was a sense of doom, and the proverbial “Here we go again.”
That isn’t the case with this team and their three-game losing skid. The Raiders are angry at themselves, and every player and coach has been quick to take the blame.
The Rams are incredibly talented, but they are walking into a buzzsaw on Sunday. Will the Raiders be able to get over the top? I think so, but we shall see.
I asked Klint Kubiak about the impressive attitude of the locker room.
“Yeah, as professionals, that's part of the price of admission for being here. At least that's what we talk about, and they have to go do it. So you stress things and you look for team-oriented guys and you promote team-oriented guys, and you celebrate those things. And so, I do like where we're headed in that regard."
"But I think a lot of that comes from mom and dad, who those who those people are, and how they were raised, and our scouting department identifying those traits when drafting or signing guys.”
It is no secret to anyone who watched Fernando Mendoza, the young man NFL executives anointed as the best QB prospect in the last four NFL Drafts, marching towards a Heisman Trophy that he has terrific skills with the ball in his hands.
Because of that talent, I asked Klint Kubiak about using him in short-yardage situations, not because of a QB controversy- there isn’t one- but to utilize his skill set.
"Yeah, that's a great point. I think there's something too coming off the field cold on the most important down of the drive. It's probably maybe why that doesn't happen more, but I know it's definitely a valid point."
Mendoza’s progress is being seen internally, while the NFL world waits optimistically to see what he can do. Kubiak addresses his progress.
“Yeah, I'm very pleased with where he's at, and none of us really know until he goes and plays. But he's doing everything that we're asking him to do. Really, he's doing more than asked, and that's just his character.”
Kubiak went into more detail about what “More than asked” means, and it shed some light on the burgeoning young star.
“Yeah, I think it's as simple as me just walking down the hall here to go get in the steam room when everybody's gone and he’s out here on the field by himself. So, he's not the only guy that's doing that, but he's putting in the extra time.”
It is no secret that the third quarter has been a nemesis for the Silver and Black this year. Kubiak brought it up himself. He talked about how you coach the team through it, and it opened a fascinating window for fans to understand his mindset.
"Yeah, I think it's a lot of energy, too. So, as a coaching staff we've got to make sure our guys have more energy coming out of that of that second half. There's a lot of things that we've discussed. It's point of emphasis. Obviously, starting the game is really important, and starting the game in the third quarter. So, it's an area of our team that we have to improve."
Credit players like RG Jackson Powers-Johnson (JPJ) and CB Darien Porter, who, at times in their young careers, have been up and down, starting and sitting on the bench. Neither has shown any quit, and while Porter seems to have taken a slight edge in his battle at CB, JPJ remains in a battle. Kubiak credits them for not quitting and keeping up the fight.
"Yeah, obviously guys are disappointed, but you look no further than guys like DP [Darien Porter]. You keep competing. You're going to get a chance again and make sure you're ready when you are. You're a professional, you've got to do that."
The Raiders under DC Robbie Leonard are getting plenty or pressure on the QB, but getting home has been an issue. Kubiak sees it, and thinks there are good reasons for it.
"Yeah, I think when you get further into the season, obviously, teams know what you do. The more reps that you get, they have more time to see your scheme, so it's an evolving scheme. It's getting the players home, and then when we do get home, making sure we get the ball out. So, that's the cat and mouse game of the NFL."
In year 15 as an NFL QB, Kirk Cousins leads the NFL in touchdown passes (14), ranks sixth in yards (just under 1,600), and continues to lead and shine in many other categories. What makes the stellar vet seemingly get better with age? For Kubiak, the identifying quality is easy to see.
"Yeah, I think you go back to April with any player I think that's playing well right now, you look at what their April looked like. They had a good April; they had a good training camp. You just keep stacking days, and whether it's the quarterback position, any position, safety, guard. I think when you just can stack days, it builds confidence."
Cousins showed an amazing arm that is often foolishly criticized the entire time he has been in Vegas. But in the second half of the loss to the Bills, he had a 50-yard bomb to WR Tre Tucker that was nothing short of impressive.
With the team stacking the box and the Cousins-to-Tucker chemistry on fire, Kubiak talked about using that to stretch the field and open up the running game.
“I do. Obviously, any time you can make that part of your offense, it's going to make the whole team successful. But I really love his decision making, and it's not something you just go throw it up in the air and hope something good happens. You got to get the right look with the right guy running the route. But for us to be successful, I think that's part of a formula that we can use. But you got to read the defense, that's the most important thing.”
Even with Mendoza on the bench, the Raiders rookie class is having a great season. From the 53-man roster to the IR (Injured Reserve) to the practice squad, all ten 2026 NFL Draft picks are still here, along with seven additional UDFAs.
Recently, NFL Draft expert Justin Melo ranked the Raiders rookie class as the third-best in the NFL, and I asked Kubiak to address their success.
"Yes, a lot of key contributors and guys that we're still counting on. I think that's a big part of being successful in the NFL is getting your young guys to play early, and credit to John Spytek for the young men that he's brought in, not only as good players, but guys that are team-oriented individuals that are about the Raider Way."
"So, they just have to keep developing. And young guys, they have setbacks too. You have a good game, okay, you get beat, and now you just keep competing. That's the league. It's the most competitive business that I know, and that's what makes it the most rewarding."
McVay is the Rams' highly talented coach and is considered an offensive savant. He is using an inordinate number of 13-personnel sets this year (One RB, three TE), and Kubiak talked about this new Rams wrinkle.
"Yes, they do. They're probably the best offense in the NFL. Very well-coached. Utilize their tight ends, they are a very impressive group. So, it's going to be a really important week of preparation for us. They're a very good offense, very good operation. We have a lot of respect for them."
Kubiak’s father, Klint, was an NFL QB for nine seasons and a Super Bowl-winning coach. No stranger being praised as an offensive mind like his son, Kubiak talked about using his father as a resource in his scheming and in developing an offensive game plan.
"Yeah, every day, every day. Very, very grateful for my dad, for my mom. That's such a unique relationship that I get to have him as a resource, and just so grateful for him and his tough love more than anything,…

title: Raiders Hit With Concerning Injury News Ahead of Rams Game
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.--  The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are playing host to the Los Angeles Rams (2-4) on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium.
To say the Raider Nation is excited about this football game would be an enormous understatement.
But ahead of the big renewal of the rivalry, the Raiders got some concerning news in their latest injury report.
Rookie RB Mike Washington Jr. is a key part of the heralded 2026 Silver and Black rookie class , and the fan base has been clamoring for more of him with each successful performance.
Earlier this week, I asked Kubiak, who constantly preaches to his team about earning more reps, if Washington Jr. had earned more; he said yes.  The Raider Nation was elated, as they stand united about needing to get the run game going.
Kubiak explained what the Arkansas Razorback had done to earn those reps.
“He's putting the work in, and you see the practice come to life in the game. ”
Late Thursday, Mike Washington Jr. showed up on the injury report and was listed as not participating.
On Wednesday, he was listed with a foot/back injury and was limited, but he did not participate on Thursday.  That change is very significant.
Klint Kubiak likes to give players opportunities in games after successful practices.  While it is not impossible, Kubiak’s track record makes it seem improbable that if Washington Jr. doesn’t practice on Friday, he would play on Sunday.  That is purely speculative and not from the team; it is simply an inference from Kubiak’s previous statements and implications.
Since day one, Washington Jr. has been Ashton Jeanty's backup.  But he continues to expand his team's trust in him with each successful play.
I asked QB Kirk Cousins on Wednesday about his maturation and growth into what, at the time, looked like a significant contributor on Sunday.  His answer was telling.
“When you see the 30-plus-yard run for a touchdown against the Saints, you see the ability to break away. In practice, it’s hard because you’re not being brought to the ground often. So, until you get to the real thing, it’s difficult to evaluate. I think he’s run hard, and he’s continuing to get comfortable in the offense. I think every week as a rookie, no matter what position you're playing, you’re gaining confidence and earning trust. It’s a building process, and coming up on Week 7, the sample size is getting large enough to build that up.”
I asked OC Andrew Janocko about the rookie’s growth, and his praise was both glowing and telling.
“I think it’s just started by proving it in the practice field, taking it from the meeting rooms to the practice field, taking it from the practice field, and then doing specific things well in a game. When you do that, that’s how a young player earns more reps. He takes it step by step and then applies it onto the field.”
We will learn more late Friday morning when I speak to Kubiak and ask him for an update.  The 'Raiders' run game has struggled this season, and Mike Washington Jr. was a big reason for optimism that it would take off.
If Washington Jr. can't go, look for Dylan Laube to get more carries, and possibly for the first time all season, UDFA RB Roman Hemby getting called up for his first regular-season action of the season from the practice squad.

title: Overachieving Raiders: Top Trade Deadline Rumors Ranked by Insiders
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) host the Los Angeles Rams (2-4) this weekend in what has been an overachieving 2026 season, and the intrigue could have a long-lasting impact.
Sunday’s impact goes beyond one game on the schedule. With an upset victory, the Raiders would plant themselves in the NFL Playoff hunt; with a loss, they'd be reminded this is a Raiders rebuilding year, with all eyes on the future.
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is approaching on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 4 PM ET/1 PM PT, and the sooner the Raiders have clarity on the franchise's direction, the sooner some angles on how they approach it will come into focus—emphasis on some.
Raiders GM John Spytek has done a masterful job since the team decided to move on from Pete Carroll and build the franchise the right way by developing and following his scheme and plan. He hasn't wavered or faltered once.
Regardless of whether this season was a rebuild or an all-out push towards the playoffs, the Raiders are always, every year, every day, and every season going to be buyers. If Spytek can upgrade his roster talent, he'll always be willing to buy.
Similarly, just as the Raiders will always be buyers when they can upgrade, the playoff scenario has no bearing on trading players who don't fit the long-term plan, young or old. But any player, young or old, who is determined not to be part of the long-term plan can and would be shipped out.
But where the angles change is if the Raiders are in playoff contention.
When Spytek selected No. 1 overall the QB that NFL executives raved over and called the best QB prospect in the last four NFL Drafts, Fernando Mendoza, he found his long-term franchise QB.
The plan never was, and never will be, for Kirk Cousins to be the long-term answer. The 15-year veteran is a masterful short-term leader and mentor, but not the guy who will lead the Raiders in 2036. Ideally, that would be Mendoza.
But with the Raiders overachieving in 2026, trading Cousins to a contender is no longer a given if the playoffs are still on the table.
If an older player isn’t a long-term answer, such as QB Kirk Cousins, but is vital to the current playoff push, he's likely to stay.
The Raiders have needs in several areas. RG is still wide open, and LG Spencer Burford is on a one-year deal. The Raiders also need help on the defensive line. While the Raiders have young talent, they also need help in the defensive backfield and at other positions.
We all know the Raiders have no clear WR1, but having one available at the trade deadline doesn’t seem to fit the NFL ethos this year. A blockbuster trade of that magnitude would likely happen in the offseason.
According to people across the NFL, here are some names that the Raiders could potentially target.
These aren't the only players, but many in the NFL see them as the most viable. If the Raiders move players currently on their roster, this list could change dramatically.
This is not the NBA, MLB, or even the NHL, but the NFL world is changing, and each year, as of late, the trade deadline, often overlooked in the NFL in the past, isn’t anymore.
Here are some potential players currently on rosters who have interest around the NFL, or who could have niche interest.
QB Aidan O'Connell is a very interesting player. The conventional wisdom around him in the NFL is fascinating. As one GM said, “He hasn’t shown enough to eliminate him as a potential QB1, but he has shown enough to know he isn’t a lock. He intrigues a lot of us as a great backup.”
Many believe the Raiders made the rare move of keeping three QBs on the 53-man roster because of his value and the likelihood of trading Cousins. That was before the NFL playoff chances were legitimate.
Klint Kubiak’s father backed up John Elway for 11 years in Denver. I know factually the Raiders love him, trust him, and believe in him. Would the Raiders be willing to pay him handsomely as an insurance policy for Fernando Mendoza, or does O’Connell want to move on, spread his wings, and get a legitimate shot at QB1? That isn’t happening in Vegas.
If Cousins isn’t moved and O’Connell wants to test free agency, his comp pick value isn’t high, so while unlikely, he is a potential candidate to be moved.
Tre Tucker has a contract that ends at the end of this season, and he is going to get paid. It seems highly unlikely that the Raiders would want to lose him. With that in mind, with no WR1 and his production on the rise, his cost is going up nearly every week.
If the Raiders don’t see him as a long-term guy, or if a deal can’t get done to their liking, and they're out of the NFL playoff hunt, he'll be a name that comes up. A market exists for the young man at the deadline.
Jeremy Chinn is only 28 and has performed well for the Silver and Black. The Raiders will have to determine his value in a long-term deal and whether both parties are on the same page. An NFL executive brought his name up to me, but Chinn has earned another deal and is young enough to fit the long-term vision. If his cost is prohibitive in Spytek’s mind, then that is a real possibility, but it's hard to imagine him being shipped out with them in the hunt, given his play and his youth.
Adam Butler is under a great contract for any team, is playing at a high level, but also isn’t young. Next year will be his 10th in the NFL, and there's definitely a market for him. Would the Raiders want to extend him for two, or even three, more years, or could Spytek make a significant offer the Raiders couldn’t say no to? That is a real possibility for the man playing like a beast, consistently.
Maxx Crosby is playing some of his best football. The Raiders are not shopping him, but they did trade him once this year. He isn’t asking for a trade either, but Crosby craves championships and isn’t getting any younger. Could a legitimate contender come calling with an offer the Raiders couldn’t say no to? Teams want Crosby, but the deal would have to make sense for the team calling, the Raiders, and Crosby. Far-fetched? Not at all. Probable? Maybe.

title: Why Next Three Games Will Determine Raiders’ 2026 Season
full_text:
It was a blistering start to the season for the Las Vegas Raiders, who jumped out to a 3-0 record, with wins over the Dolphins, Chargers, and Saints.
Since then, the Raiders have lost three consecutive games against the Chiefs, Patriots, and Bills. Las Vegas' three wins come against teams with a combined 2-15 record. Meanwhile, its losses are against teams with a combined 14-3 record. Was the Raiders' fast start a mirage? We'll find out over the next few weeks. We'll also learn where Las Vegas' season is trending during this stretch. Here's why.
With the trade deadline on Nov. 10, these next three weeks are when teams teetering on the line will have to identify themselves as buyers or sellers. Las Vegas' final game before the deadline is against the San Francisco 49ers on Nov. 8. The Raiders also face the Rams and Jets during this span.
If the Raiders are still within striking distance of the playoff picture, we could see general manager John Spytek make some calls to improve the team. However, if Las Vegas' woes continue and it's 3-6 or 4-5, the front office could turn the page to the future and look to move pass rusher Maxx Crosby. Even at 4-5, the Raiders would be in a spot to challenge for a playoff spot, but with several contenders needing edge rushers, the organization could look to sell at maximum value.
Kirk Cousins has been a pleasant surprise, considering the last two years in Atlanta indicated the 38-year-old quarterback was on his last legs. In head coach Klint Kubiak's system, Cousins has looked like a completely different player, compiling 1,582 yards, 14 touchdowns, and five interceptions, while completing 63.4 percent of his passes. However, as the losses mount, so will the pressure on the coaching staff to turn the keys to the rookie quarterback.
Switching to Mendoza wouldn't necessarily mean the Raiders would be sellers at the deadline, but it would signal that the coaching staff believes Cousins is no longer the best option. That said, making the switch from the veteran to the future franchise quarterback would mean the team is trending in the wrong direction. What transpires from now until the first week in November will paint a clearer picture for the rest of the Raiders' 2026 season.
Losing will expedite the Raiders' turn to the future, and who knows, Cousins could be a trade candidate in this scenario.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Raiders' Biggest Offensive Fix Becoming Impossible To Ignore
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' offseason was the first of many that will see several players come and go, as the Raiders' front office continues to rebuild. Over the past two offseasons, Las Vegas' front office has invested cap space and premium draft picks in revamping its roster.
Las Vegas' 3-3 start to the season shows where they are in that process. They have shown they are no longer the worst collection of talent that was worthy of the top pick in this year's NFL Draft. However, they are just getting started and still have a long way to go.
The season's first three games confirmed what the Raiders can be when they play well on both sides of the ball. Their loss to the New England Patriots offered a glimpse of what they are when everything goes wrong. Then, there are the other two games Las Vegas has lost this season.
Against both the Kansas City Chiefs and the Buffalo Bills, Las Vegas lost close games. In both games, Las Vegas' offense fell flat at critical moments, then battled back after it was too late to beat either team. Both factors matter when analyzing where they stand.
Against the Chiefs, the Raiders scored 13 points through three quarters, including zero in the third quarter. They scored 14 points in the fourth quarter, more than the first three quarters combined. A similar trend has continued during their three losses.
Against the Bills , Las Vegas scored 13 points through three quarters, including zero in the third quarter. They scored 17 points in the fourth quarter. The trend essentially held even against the Patriots, when the Raiders scored 10 points through three quarters and seven in the fourth.
During their three-game losing streak, the Raiders trailed by double digits in each of those fourth quarters. Then, the unit exploded for more points, or nearly as many points as they had in the first three quarters combined. That is not an accident.
All three teams tried to stop the Raiders from scoring, yet Las Vegas kept pushing the ball downfield in ways they had barely tried in the first three quarters, even as they fell behind by double digits. Kubiak was encouraged by the success the unit had in moving the ball late against the Bills.
“I do. Obviously, any time you can make that part of your offense, it's going to make the whole team successful. But I really love his decision-making, and it's not something you just go throw it up in the air and hope something good happens,” Kubiak said before Wednesday’s practice.
“You got to get the right look with the right guy running the route. But for us to be successful, I think that's part of a formula that we can use. But you got to read the defense, that's the most important thing.”
A loss is a loss, and the Raiders have lost three straight. There are no moral victories, but the Raiders can take something from all three losses, especially the two close ones. Both the Chiefs and the Bills are likely to make deep playoff runs, and either could go to the Super Bowl.
Yet the rebuilding Raiders just went toe-to-toe with both, while missing several starters. This should make it easy for Kubiak and his coaching staff to keep the team locked in through a tough losing streak. Frustration naturally comes with a streak like that, but it can be productive.
Specifically, the Raiders' losses to two of the league's top teams confirmed the need for more pieces, but they largely have the tools to beat those teams eventually. The Raiders have the building blocks for the future. They just need to get those pieces.
Realistically, those pieces won't arrive until the offseason. The Raiders can compete and win right now, but their offense has to play the entire game as it does in the fourth quarter. As shown during their three-game winning streak, doing so would help their defense with some issues they have had.
The Raiders need more pieces to compete consistently and beat the elite teams in the future. However, if they clean up a few things on their end, they could be there sooner than many may think.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Key Areas Raiders Must Improve Ahead of Rams Matchup
full_text:
Three weeks ago, many wondered what could come next for the surprising Las Vegas Raiders, unbeaten after three games and looking to turn things around on a dime one year after winning three games in the entire 2025 season. Three weeks later, Las Vegas is reeling with a trio of losses.
The No. 3 seems to be an important component for the Raiders this season. Three wins to start, three losses after, and a pattern of madness have led head coach Klint Kubiak to look for answers to Las Vegas' struggles.
Some of these issues may not be resolved this season, and next offseason will play a pivotal role. With that in mind, here are three areas the Raiders must improve as they approach this weekend's important matchup against the lackluster superteam Los Angeles Rams.
I feel this is a trend for most teams in the thick of a rebuild, as the third quarter seems to be the most treacherous part of the season for the Raiders. Kubiak must do a better job of getting points on the board quickly in the second half once his offense has the ball, as momentum seems to stall after halftime.
Las Vegas has the worst third-quarter point differential in the NFL at -26. For the Raiders, they can't win the games by skipping the third quarter, and they must outscore their opponents or at least match them after the half.
It feels like we're witnessing deja vu with the run game from last year, only with a better offensive line and an intriguing rookie backing up the starter. It's clear Ashton Jeanty is not healthy, and the Raiders need to sit him down and allow him to be at full strength. Some of the issues are on him, too, but Las Vegas (specifically Kubiak) must do better with establishing the run.
The best way to do that is to run more gap concepts and let rookie Mike Washington Jr. follow pulling guards, using his speed to burst into the secondary. The big-play ability is there, and it could happen against the Rams' battered defensive front if Kubiak can establish the ground game.
Interestingly, according to Next Gen Stats, the Raiders rank 13th in team sack rate (6.8%) and 17th in pressure rate (36.4%). Yet their average time to pressure is fourth-worst in the NFL (2.82), and their average get-off time is seventh-worst (0.86). This tells me they are struggling to generate quick pressures because of the lack of impact, quick-winning defenders up front opposite Maxx Crosby.
Defensive coordinator Rob Leonard must try something, anything, to improve those latter numbers. His defense has shown excellent flashes of being a high-level unit, something they might be a year away from. If the Raiders are to be more successful on defense, getting fast wins in their pass rush must be a priority.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: 4 Storylines I'm Watching Most in Raiders' Week 7 Matchup
full_text:
Klint Kubiak and the Las Vegas Raiders are in the middle of a losing streak that has quickly made clear where they stand compared to the league's best. As they turn their focus to the Los Angeles Rams in Week 7, they are still very much a work in progress.
Below are the four storylines I am watching the most on Sunday.
Both teams are on losing streaks: the Rams have lost two straight, and the Raiders have lost three. Which team will win and snap its losing streak will be determined well before the final whistle blows. For the Raiders, it starts in the third quarter.
Two teams on losing streaks could force one or both to play poorly down the stretch if it's another close game. This could work in the Raiders' favor, as they have been in close games in almost every game this year.
On Sunday against the Buffalo Bills, Las Vegas started Caleb Rogers at right guard instead of Jackson Powers-Johnson. One of the biggest storylines I will watch in Week 7 will be who starts along the line and how the starting unit performs.
Las Vegas' line needs help and more time together to gel comfortably. Yet they still face several formidable defensive lines over the next few weeks and throughout the season. The rest of the season will likely clarify which positions in the unit they address most aggressively this offseason.
Las Vegas' offense has made significant progress from last season. Yet the past three weeks have clarified where the unit needs additional help. Roster-wise, their weaknesses were well known; however, they've now shown up on the field.
Specifically, Las Vegas has struggled to close out multiple games they could have won. A significant reason they suffered those close losses was the offense's inability to generate enough points when the chances presented themselves.
“I think when you get further into the season, obviously, teams know what you do. The more reps that you get, they have more time to see your scheme, so it's an evolving scheme. It's getting the players home, and then when we do get home, making sure we get the ball out. So, that's the cat-and-mouse game of the NFL,” Kubiak said before Wednesday’s practice.
Along with veteran additions Las Vegas made over the past two offseasons that have bolstered the roster , another part of the Raiders' rebuild has been their reliance on young players thrust into critical roles early in their careers. Young talent played a significant role in all three wins.
The Raiders' success in 2026 and beyond will largely depend on the coaching staff's ability to get the most out of those young players. Las Vegas has lost three straight games, but against the Bills, most of the young players Las Vegas will lean on had productive outings.
“A lot of key contributors and guys that we're still counting on. I think that's a big part of being successful in the NFL is getting your young guys to play early, and credit to John Spytek for the young men that he's brought in, not only as good players, but guys that are team-oriented individuals that are about the Raider Way,” Kubiak said.
“So, they just have to keep developing. And young guys, they have setbacks too. You have a good game, okay, you get beat, and now you just keep competing. That's the league. It's the most competitive business that I know, and that's what makes it the most rewarding."
As the Raiders face the Rams in Week 7, one of the biggest storylines I will watch is whether Las Vegas' young players can build on last week. Las Vegas has assembled a solid mix of young players and veterans who work well together when they are clicking on all cylinders.
It will be interesting to see whether they can build on the productive things they have done during their losing streak , make the necessary corrections, and make enough progress between Weeks 6 and 7 to beat a talented but beatable Rams team.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders HC Klint Kubiak Knows What 'Winning Mindset' Looks Like
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are entering their Week 7 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams on a three-game losing streak. Still, no heads are hanging in Las Vegas' locker room. The team has responded nearly the same way after three losses as it did after three wins.
Las Vegas' offseason moves were about more than progress on the field. John Spytek and the Raiders' front office wanted to change the culture. Fully turning around the roster and the culture within the locker room takes time. It also takes a team handling both wins and losses well.
That is where Klint Kubiak's Raiders find themselves after six games . After playing three of the league's best teams, the Raiders now face a reeling Rams team. Yet both teams are on a losing streak, with the Rams losing in a row and three of their last four.
On paper, the Rams have the better roster, but they are far from unbeatable. Los Angeles has sustained injuries to several of their best players, who may either be out for Sunday's game or not at full strength. Still, as their loss to the New England Patriots proved, none of that really matters.
During their three-game losing streak, the Raiders have confirmed that if they play their best football, they can compete with the league's best teams. When they do not play their best football, games like Week 5 happen. It really is that simple for this Raiders team.
Right now, the Raiders' success depends not only on what they do, but also on what they do not do. In two of the three games they lost, the Raiders did not play bad football or fail to do many things, but the things they failed at were significant.
Notably, Las Vegas has failed to capitalize on moments in the game that could put them in better positions down the stretch. Against the Kansas City Chiefs and the Buffalo Bills, the Raiders had chances to take a lead in the second half, but failed to do so.
Repeated three-and-outs at critical moments are easy to overlook until a team loses by three points twice in three weeks against two of the league's best teams. The Raiders would not need gargantuan fourth-quarter comeback bids if they took care of business in the third quarter.
Yes, Las Vegas has struggled to finish games, but finishing strong starts with strong second-half starts. Not halfway through the fourth quarter, when down by double digits to Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen. Finishing games will be a focus of Kubiak's staff moving forward.
“It's such a competitive game and if you're just hoping to keep it close in the fourth quarter, that's not a winning mindset. So, just having the mindset when you have an opportunity to make a play, when you're playing complementary football on one side of the ball, special teams gives you good field position, you got to go score on that drive,” Kubiak said before Wednesday’s practice.
“[Our] Defense gets a turnover; you got to go score on that drive. If there's a sudden change defensively, then we got to get a stop. So, just having the ultimate competitor's mindset of not being okay with having the game be close in the fourth quarter. That's not what we're here to do.”
The Raiders are ahead of schedule, and losing close games as they did in Weeks 4 and 6 is undoubtedly better than what happened in Week 5.
The Raiders are only six games into a rebuild that will take multiple offseasons' worth of roster additions. They are further along than nearly anyone expected after six games. It will naturally take them more time to grow together.
In this league, growth and rebuild often coincide with losing winnable games against elite teams. The Raiders have shown they belong. However, with them already ahead of schedule, it is not unfair to believe that with more time together and overall growth, they can actually beat those teams.
Kubiak's Raiders are close. The growth and need for growth they have shown through six games are consistent with a .500 team. There is no making a three-game losing streak better, but last year's Raiders would have loved to be as good as this year's.
Yet there is another level for Las Vegas can get to, and they can get to that level this season.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Inside Story: Why Raiders Passed on Marvin Harrison Jr.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) have overachieved this season as the Los Angeles Rams (2-4) limp into Allegiant Stadium.
The rebuilding Raiders didn’t get the memo about the rebuild, as they have a chance to upset the unanimous pre-season Super Bowl favorite without fighting for their post-season life.
Since the Raiders decided to move on from Pete Carroll last December, after a complete collapse of the 2025 season , GM John Spytek's plan has been thorough and disciplined. Spytek is blameless in the 2025 collapse, but has been charged with the recovery.
2026 was a rebuilding year; 2027 is the season to make sure all is right, and the expectation is that the Silver and Black get into the NFL Playoffs in 2028 and never look back.
The 2026 team didn’t get the memo.
The team knew coming into the season that they didn’t have a true WR1. They also knew that they don’t grow on trees. With the way the impressive NFL Draft fell, the Raiders had no chance to get one via free agency or trading up, but that was OK.
The disciplined leader of the Silver and Black, John Spytek, wasn’t going to mortgage the future on one player; that didn’t match the cost. The Raiders would love to make a move for a true WR1, but they'd only do so if it matched the value.
So many people think that putting a WR1 on the field is easy. Stunningly, someone suggested recently on one of my podcasts that the Raiders “Trade Kirk Cousins” for Justin Jefferson, or that Spytek should be on the chopping block for not picking one in the NFL Draft.
Clearly, delusional suggestions like that don't come from bad people, but from people who don’t understand the game.
An NFL executive who saw my podcast and the suggestion of Cousins for Jefferson reached out to chuckle about it.
I told him that for this article, I was going to explain what a true WR1 is, and he sent me this to show how his franchise defines that position. It just isn’t putting anyone out there, and it isn’t a short receiver like the Raiders' Tre Tucker (5’8”), who is an excellent player, but a WR2.
Here is how my friend’s franchise defines the position of WR1:
We reported repeatedly that the Raiders didn’t have a WR1, but there was no panic. The disciplined Spytek and Kubiak, for that matter, were not willing to take the process off the rails to chase a player or overpay.
When the Raiders came storming out of the gate with a 3-0 start, it was a clear overachievement, and when they almost beat the Kansas City Chiefs, the expectations of a malnourished fan base were set on fire.
With each win in the first three weeks of the season, the glaring hole became obvious, and fans' aspirations shifted from a disciplined rebuild to a full emotional push for the playoffs.
Marvin Harrison Jr. was the No. 4 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft by the Arizona Cardinals. Coming into that year's NFL Draft, there was immense excitement about him joining the league.
One GM, who is highly successful in the league’s annual player selection process, evaluated Harrison Jr. like this:
“If you take off his jersey so you don’t see his dad’s name, and that he plays with Ohio State who has more talents than some NFL teams, in my opinion he might be the third best wide receiver in this league.”
He added, “He played with exceptional talent, but each week in college isn’t like each week in the NFL. I am not buying the hype.”
Harrison Jr. entered the league and nearly instantly had off-field business issues. On top of that, he had multiple QBs and coaches over his less than two and a half years in the NFL, with low production, questionable effort, and football issues. In fairness to the young man, none of the issues around him were off-field or character issues.
With the Raiders season heating up, and Harrison’s production going south when it quietly became known around the NFL that the Cardinals were willing to trade him, the Raiders did their due diligence.
When the Raiders realized what the Cardinals were asking, the Silver and Black were not interested at all. In fact, a source close to the situation told me, “If the cost doesn’t match, no way you make that move.”
I reported that immediately. The story, was that there was no story.
As soon as the national media reported Harrison’s availability, they mentioned the Raiders had a need.
The problem was that he isn’t a WR1, and his track record of essentially unimpressive production with multiple coaches and quarterbacks took the Raiders out of the discussion; that never went anywhere.
No one questions that Harrison Jr. can play WR in the NFL, but he clearly isn’t a WR1 and didn’t hold the value the Cardinals were trying to get. More on that in a moment.
Raider Nation, however, got played as social media " took off.” Rumors flew, despite my repeatedly shooting them down, because of the outlandish cost and the reality of production. The Raiders are looking for answers, not drama, question marks, and other people’s problems.
Some on social media had a field day stoking the fires of a hungry fan base with baseless rumors that got clicks but had no substance, like the Raiders being in it.
Prompting one member of the Raiders organization to say, “Who believes this (excrement)."
Essentially, the Houston Texans overpaid, bidding against themselves for a player the vast majority of NFL teams saw the same way the Raiders did. They gave up a second-round pick to reunite Harrison Jr. with his college QB, CJ Stroud.
One NFL executive for this article said, “The days of the Raiders being that team are long-gone. That isn’t how Spy (John Spytek) does business. He will talk, listen, and even jump in the fray for anyone, but it has to make sense. He isn’t cheap, he just ain’t buying a Vega, for the cost of a Corvette.”
He added, “The way he and Tom (Brady) think, look at (Tyler) Linderbaum and (Klint) Kubiak, they would rather buy the Corvette, they aren’t cheap, but they aren’t stupid. Houston got fleeced.”
Did the Raiders check in? Yes. Were they ever legitimate players? Not after the initial look. A lot of people played Raider Nation, but the ones who didn’t, and deserve a ton of credit, are the Raiders.
They understand they will put maximum effort into getting a WR1 next year.
They also understand it will happen when they decide to, not out of panic. The Raiders weren’t a true WR1 away from a Super Bowl; even if they were, Marvin Harrison Jr. isn’t one.
They have a long way to go, but you can already see how much closer they are today than last year. Why?
Because John Spytek is one of the smartest GMs in the NFL, and the Raiders are finally disciplined.
Or, as the executive said, “It’s gotta be nice for the fans (Raider Nation) to be able to talk about their team using terms like discipline, smart, and steady. Been a long time. Good for them.”
The Raiders may very well trade their second-round pick next season (the ultimate cost the Houston Texans paid), or perhaps they use it.
However they spend it, remember it could have been spent on a player who had only proven he isn’t a WR1 in the NFL.
When that happens, remember to silently say, “Thanks, John,” and start listening to those who know what is going on.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Would the Dolphins Really Consider Trading Jordyn Brooks?
full_text:
It seems everybody, or just about everybody is fair game when it comes to the NFL trade deadline and the Miami Dolphins.
It was expected that we would see the names of Zach Sieler and Austin Jackson mentioned among trade candidates given their contract status and age, plus the obvious situation in which the franchise finds itself.
That one, we have to say, surprised us when we saw him included in a list of top 50 trade candidates put together by The Athletic.
Yet there was Brooks at number 21, between Jets edge defender Will McDonald IV and Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley.
"The Dolphins are executing their tank effectively," writer Daniel Popper began. "They have remained moderately competitive while still losing five straight games to begin the season. Their rookie class looks promising. The next step would be accruing some more draft capital for 2027. One issue, though, is they do not have many tradable players. Brooks, a reliable veteran off-ball linebacker, is one of the few. He signed a three-year extension in July and has close to $13 million in guaranteed salary in 2027, so any acquiring team would be making a multiyear commitment. The Dolphins would take on $15.6 million in dead money in 2027 if they traded Brooks. This regime, with coach Jeff Hafley and GM Jon-Eric Sullivan, has not been afraid of dead money thus far."
Brooks' name came in trade speculation in the offseason, with the Dallas Cowboys and Cincinnati Bengals mentioned as logical suitors, and Popper mentioned the Cowboys, Bills and Steelers are potential trade partners now.
But the big question here is simple: Why would the Dolphins trade Brooks only a few months after giving him a contract extension that included a $20 million signing bonus?
If they were to trade Brooks, the Dolphins would be on the hook for Brooks' bonus when it comes to the cap space on top of already having signed that check.
After the Dolphins signed Brooks to his extension after doing the same with De'Von Achane and Aaron Brewer, GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley both spoke of making sure to hang on to franchise "pillars," good players who do things the way the Dolphins want them done.
Hafley also talked about showing players that the franchise will reward those who produce and do things the right way.
What kind of message would it send to sign Brooks to an extension and then trade him in the middle of a season that's gone not too far from where the organization figured it would or could go after they dumped high-profile veterans and saddled themselves with $180 million of dead space to clear the books for future years.
Sure, Sullivan has shown a willingness to take dead cap money if it accomplishes a goal, but what goal would be accomplished by dumping Brooks if the Dolphins can't get a premium pick in return.
And that's what it boils down, as always, because there's no player for whom the Dolphins shouldn't entertain an offer too good to be true.
But what could the Dolphins realistically expect to get for Brooks?
In terms of his appeal and market value, he probably was more valuable in the offseason coming off his All-Pro season than he is right now after dealing with an injury in training camp and then leaving the Week 5 game against the Cincinnati Bengals with a foot injury.
Would a third- or fourth-round pick in 2027 be more valuable to the Dolphins than having Brooks next season and the one after, both in terms of talent but also in terms of intangibles — Brooks' leadership plus keeping the player you just extended?
The bottom line is stranger things have happened, which is why we'll never say never, but a Brooks trade seemed a lot more likely then than it does now because making a deal months after giving a player an extension and giving him $20 million in signing bonus just doesn't compute.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Examining the Pending Dolphins UFAs Who Could Be Playing Their Way to an Extension
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins roster has a lot of new faces this year, and it figures to be the same thing next season as they continue the rebuilding project that began with the regime change.
The Dolphins have 22 players currently on their roster who are scheduled to become free agents in 2026 and the questions is how many of them will be back for another go-around.
The breakdown of free agents includes 12 UFAs free to sign with any other team barring the Dolphins using the franchise tag, which we already can tell you is highly unlikely given the financial commitment to a single player; five RFAs, who require a qualifying tender for the right to match an offer they might receive from another team; and and five ERFAs, who the Dolphins basically will keep if they want because any qualifying tender gives them exclusive rights to those players.
The 13 pending UFAs are T Austin Jackson, TE Greg Dulcich, CB JuJu Brents, P Bradley Pinion, CB Darrell Baker Jr., WR Jalen Tolbert, EDGE Joshua Uche, LB Willie Gay Jr., S Zayne Anderson, LB Ronnie Harrison Jr., EDGE Malik Herring and EDGE Robert Beal Jr.
The five pending RFAs are OL Jarrett Kingston, LB Shaka Heyward, TE Cole Turner (who's on IR), WR Jared Wayne and C Andrew Meyer.
The five pending ERFAs are LS Tucker Addington, LB Jackson Woodard, T Chukwuebuka Godrick, CB Reese Taylor and QB Kyle McCord.
As we evaluate the outlook for those players and their status with the team, we should not it's entirely possible — if not downright probable — that some of them will be gone before the end of this season.
But, for now, here are our best projections as to which players will be back in 2027, understanding that for UFAs it's a two-way street that requires both the team and the player to want to continue working together.
CB JuJu Brents — This is a player the Dolphins should prioritize because he still continues to perform at a high level and plays a premium position. The ability to stay healthy has been the issue so far in Brents' career, but he hasn't missed a game yet (knock on wood) so far in 2026.
TE Greg Dulcich — The Dolphins showed they valued him by giving him considerably more than most of their other free agents when they re-signed him in the offseason, though they did make it a one-year deal. But he's still pretty young, has good upside, and it's not like the Dolphins are swimming in high-end tight ends.
EDGE Joshua Uche — While he's been around a bit, Uche still is only 29 years old and he's been easily the second-best edge defender on the team, if not the best. The biggest question with him is whether the Dolphins will resist the temptation to move him before the trade deadline if a team offers a draft pick in a trade.
P Bradley Pinion — Yes, this might sound weird, particularly since Pinion is 33, but the fact is he's punted well all season — we can forgive him that blip when he dropped the ball proceeding to get into his punting motion — he's not expensive and punters can work in the NFL into their late 30s with no issues.
T Austin Jackson — Despite his poor Pro Football Focus standing (he's dead last among all NFL tackles), Jackson is a solid veteran tackle who's simply off to a bad start. The issue with Jackson is how it would cost to bring him back in what probably wouldn't be a starting role and whether he even would be interested in that idea after being asked to take a pay cut this year.
WR Jalen Tolbert — It's hard to imagine the veteran wide receiver wanting to come back to Miami after he found himself behind not only Malik Washington but the team's three draft picks at the position — Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr.
S Zayne Anderson — The special teams specialist got his big chance when he was in the starting lineup at safety in the opener, but he's now gone back to his previous role of working mostly in the kicking game. He's also 30 years old, which won't make him a priority to bring back.
LB Ronnie Harrison Jr. — Harrison was one of the latest free agent acquisitions in the offseason and he made the 53-man roster after a strong training camp showing. But he's been out since Week 1 because of a hamstring injury and he's also 30 years old.
The lowest qualifying tender for restricted free agents in 2026, which simply gave teams to right to match an outside offer with no compensation if declined, was $3.5 million. None of the pending RFAs signed for more than $1.1 million this year, so it's highly unlikely — if not an outright foregone conclusion — the Dolphins will not be extending any qualifying offers.
That means the Dolphins then would have to decide which to try to bring back, and we've got three we've got pegged as most likely to return.
OL Jarrett Kingston — Kingston, claimed off waivers from the Houston Texans, had a solid outing in relief of Jonah Savaiinaea in the Week 5 game against Cincinnati.
OL Andrew Meyer — The Dolphins have been developing Meyer for three years now and offensive linemen always are a valuable commodity.
TE Cole Turner — That the Dolphins placed Turner on injured reserve in training camp and didn't simply waive him injury suggests they think he's got potential worth investigating.

title: Examining the Mestemaker-to-Miami Draft Opinion Surge
full_text:
There's a lot of time until the 2026 season is over for the Miami Dolphins, but a good chunk of the fan base has already has moved on to next season's NFL Draft, which can shape the future of the franchise depending on who they select.
Any position on the team can receive an upgrade with what will likely be a very high draft pick, if not the first overall. But if the Dolphins were to pull the trigger at quarterback, t hey have a few options to choose from, but one name is standing out as of late.
And, no, it's not Arch Manning, the son of Cooper Manning and nephew to both Peyton and Eli Manning. After a pair of unsuccessful outings for him as of late, the focus has shifted to a redshirt sophomore in the Big 12 Conference.
Drew Mestemaker didn't even begin his football journey as a quarterback. He was a dual-threat option at both punter and safety in high school before making the change to QB when he walked on at North Texas. With the Mean Green, he had one of the best seasons at the position in 2025, recording 4,379 passing yards, 34 touchdowns, and nine interceptions.
When UNT head coach Eric Morris took the job at Oklahoma State ahead of 2026, Mestemaker followed suit, and he hasn't lost a beat despite the tougher competition in the Big 12. Their loss to Tulsa to begin the season has only become more confusing, since they proceeded to take down Oregon the week after, who was ranked ninth in the nation.
The Cowboys then rattled off three more wins before a tough loss on the road to 20th-ranked Houston. Through it all, Mestemaker has had an excellent season with 1,940 yards and 16 touchdowns, but six interceptions through six games, three picks away from his 2025 total, with at least six more games to go.
Regardless, the national consensus has been overwhelmingly positive on Mestemaker and believes he has what it takes to be the first QB picked in the 2027 draft. The following outlets believe the Miami Dolphins will select him with their pick, which is expected to be somewhere in the top three.
CBS (Josh Edwards) - #1 Overall
ESPN (Field Yates) - #2 Overall
SI (Gilbert Manzano) - #2 Overall
Athlon Sports (Luke Easterling) - #3 Overall
Bleacher Report (Brent Sobleski) - #3 Overall
All of these mock drafts have been done within the past seven days, with Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith ending up on either Tennessee or the Los Angeles Chargers. It's worth noting that the biggest outlet that doesn't think Miami is selecting Mestemaker is USA Today, with Michael Middlehurst-Schwartz predicting the Dolphins will select Smith with the first overall pick.
Mestemaker feels like a jack-of-all-trades quarterback, being able to achieve whatever North Texas and Oklahoma State have asked of him. He has a powerful, accurate arm that coincides with smart decision-making for someone who's only 20 years old. On top of that, he's surprisingly mobile, having rushed for 142 yards and two touchdowns this season.
As mentioned earlier, he has thrown a considerable number of interceptions. It feels like the bad decisions he makes come from trying to do too much, spearheaded by the Cowboys' defense, which gives up 358.2 yards and 23.7 points per game, both on the lower end of the Big 12.
The other big knock on Mestemaker is that there isn't much film to go off of. He didn't play QB at all in high school and has clocked one and a half seasons at the position in college. Granted, what we've been able to witness is a lot of good, but the experience isn't quite there.
With that said, any team that drafts Mestemaker might be better off sitting him for a season, learning from NFL quarterbacks about what to do and what not to do. Look towards Fernando Mendoza, learning from Kirk Cousins and taking the occasional snap during blowouts. Yes, if he's drafted by Miami, that likely means one more season of Malik Willis.
In reality, Mestemaker having a quality season isn't the only reason he's emerged as a top QB in the draft. The other big reason is how Arch Manning has regressed in his senior season. Both he and Texas looked promising, with a 24-23 win over Ohio State, taking the top spot in the nation from the Buckeyes.
After losing to Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry, then to Florida at home the week after, Texas is currently 19th in the nation. Manning has had a pedestrian season with 1,295 yards, 11 touchdowns, and five interceptions. Granted, he's faced extreme, maybe unfair expectations because of his last name, but this isn't the best time to have a mediocre season with the draft around the corner.
The falloff of Manning has painted a picture of how volatile the position is at college. The outlook on a draft hopeful at any position can drastically change with one bad performance, especially at quarterback. Right now, Mestemaker is the front-runner, but there's no guarantee he'll stay that way after a few weeks, at the end of the regular season, or when a champion is crowned in the CFP.
In the event he isn't, there are a handful of other quarterbacks who could make their case to be a top pick. That includes Miami's Darien Mensah, a Heisman front-runner who's led the top-ranked Hurricanes to an undefeated season up to this point, but he's coming off his worst performance against Florida State. The Canes will hope that this is a one-time occurrence before their premier matchup against Notre Dame on November 7.
Not far behind Mensah is Trinidad Chambliss, who began his college career at Division II Ferris State before leading the Rebels all the way to the Fiesta Bowl last season. Unlike Mestemaker, Chambliss has film for days as a sixth-year senior, but there might be too much, as he's already 24 years old. Only four quarterbacks aged 24 or older have ever been drafted in the first round: Phil Simms, Jim Druckenmiller, Brandon Weeden, and Bo Nix.
One final first-round hopeful (Assuming that Manning continues to struggle) is C.J. Carr. Notre Dame's QB is as smart on the field as he is in the classroom, but he only has 17 starts to his name in college. He'll need a quality performance against a top-rated opponent to become a true top candidate, which could come against the aforementioned Hurricanes in early November.

title: Why the Dolphins Should Keep an Eye on Their Former Head Coaches
full_text:
It's starting to look like it could be only a matter of time before former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel becomes former Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator, and it's a situation the team he led for four seasons (and their fans) should monitor.
McDaniel's offense turned in yet another poor performance during a Week 6 loss at Kansas City that dropped the Chargers to 0-6 on the season, leaving them as one of only two teams this season without a win.
The other, of course, is the Dolphins, who will take an 0-5 record into MetLife Stadium coming off their bye next Sunday.
The Chargers scored a season-low six points against the Chiefs on Sunday, the fifth time in six games they failed to score more than 17 and it doesn't take long watching them to see how disjointed and dysfunctional the whole offensive operation looks, from a badly regressing Justin Herbert at quarterback to an offensive line that's again among the worst in the NFL and dealing again with injuries to their quality starting tackles, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt.
Things haven't improved one bit since a shocking loss against Arizona in the opener and it might be that Jim Harbaugh will have no choice but to fire McDaniel to, if nothing else, inject some life into an offense that has shown little while the defense keeps battling.
Harbaugh's comments after the loss at Kansas City and heading into the Chargers' bye didn't sound great for McDaniel when he said he would have to evaluate things when asked whether McDaniel would continue calling plays.
And, of course, where it gets fun for Dolphins fans is that the logical replacement for McDaniel based on play-calling experience is the man who preceded McDaniel's predecessor, Adam Gase.
Gase had been out of the NFL since he was fired by the New York Jets after the 2020 season when the Chargers hired him as a pass game specialist, and the question is what kind of changes he might make to the offensive scheme if he were to take over.
This is important because McDaniel's complex scheme clearly isn't a fit with Herbert and the rest of the offense with its complicated verbiage, shifts and motions, and timing-based offense. That scheme worked for a while in Miami, and it's fair to ask how much of that was the presence and skill set of Tua Tagovailoa at quarterback and how much was prime Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle overwhelming defenses with their speed.
The reality is that if the Chargers don't make a change, it's difficult to envision them winning many games navigating a schedule that's about as tough as that of the Dolphins.
It does seem at the moment as though a major revamping is needed for the Chargers to have offensive success and win some games.
As it stands Monday morning, the Chargers hold the first position in the 2027 draft order and it could be that it comes down to them or the Dolphins for that No. 1 spot.
And it very well might be that the status quo would benefit the Dolphins in this instance, and that status quo is the Chargers keeping McDaniel.
Meanwhile, McDaniel's three coordinators from last season all are enjoying some team success this season.
Former offensive coordinator Frank Smith now is an assistant head coach with the Minnesota Vikings, who at 5-0 stand as one of the three undefeated teams in the NFL — though it should be pointed out that team's success has a lot more to do with the defense coordinator by Brian Flores.
Former defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver is handling the same role with the Baltimore Ravens, who are in a three-way tie atop the AFC North, although the team just squandered a 13-3 fourth-quarter lead in a last-second loss against divisional foe Cleveland on Sunday.
Lastly, special teams coordinator Danny Crossman now works for the team tied for first at 4-2 in the AFC North, the Pittsburgh Steelers.

title: 10 Stats That Help Explain the Dolphins' Tough Start (And What Can Be Done About Them)
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sat out the Week 6 action of the 2026 NFL regular season before getting back to work Monday looking to bounce back after an 0-5 start.
While stats often can be deceiving stats, we've come up with 10 numbers that help explain the winless start along with some analysis as to how to move those numbers in the right direction.
29.5 — That's the gap in completion percentage for Malik Willis from his 2025 season with the Green Bay Packers (85.7) and his first five games with the Dolphins (56.2)
Nobody should expect a full-time quarterback to come close to an 85 percent completion rate, but 56 percent isn't good enough and Willis can help himself by simply being willing to accept and take the safe, short completions.
10.1 — That's Willis intended air yards per pass attempt, according to Pro Football Reference. That figure leads the NFL, with Lamar Jackson second at 9.8.
This goes right to our first point. The Dolphins maybe need to stop taking shots down the field with a less-than-stellar wide receiver group.
3.2 — That's the average yards of separation for Malik Washington, which is the highest figure of any Dolphins player. That figure is tied for 35th-best in the NFL. The next-best Dolphins player in that category is tight end Greg Dulcich at 2.6, all the way down to tied for 79th in the NFL.
And this number illustrates, only in part, the issues with the wide receiver group.
3:09 — That's the Dolphins' rushing average on first-and-10 rushing attempts, tied with the Philadelphia Eagles for second-worst in the NFL, with only the Green Bay Packers doing worse.
Ollie Gordon II is coming off two productive games in relief of De'Von Achane, so maybe this number will improve organically after the bye without having to make any kind of schematic adjustments.
3:09 — That's Ollie Gordon II's NextGen Stats efficiency number, which measures the yards ran per yard gained, with the lower the number the most North-South the runner is. Gordon's figure is second-best in the NFL behind only the 3.01 of the Chicago Bears' Kyle Monangai.
This is what we're talking about with Gordon ... maybe the Dolphins need to give him more first-down carries.
76.0 — That's the completion percentage allowed by the Dolphins, which is on track to set a dubious NFL record. The record currently belongs to the 2016 Detroit Lions at 72.7 percent, according to StatMuse.
We get that part of Jeff Hafley's defensive scheme involves a willingness to give up short completions, but at some point the coverage needs to tighten up, particularly if the pass rush doesn't start getting to the quarterback.
4 — That's the number of sacks for the Dolphins through five games, their lowest total at this stage since at least 1981. They had five sacks in the first five games of 2019.
And that brings us to this, though it's never all about sack numbers but also affecting the quarterback. And the Dolphins have come up short on both ends. This might require more blitzing, which will leave the secondary more vulnerable to big plays, but getting nickel-and-dimed to death as they were against Cincinnati last week might not be much better.
41.27 — That's the Dolphins offense's third-down conversion rate, 12th-best in the NFL through Week 5. The only time since 2010 the Dolphins have finished a season with a higher conversion rate was in 2023 (the 11-6 season) when they were at 42.08.
Imagine how much better it could be if the Dolphins did better with their first-and-10 rushes. This also is one positive for Willis in the midst of all the criticism (some of it warranted) thrown in his direction.
34.1 — That's the kickoff return average allowed by the Dolphins, which puts Miami dead last in the NFL. It's on pace for the Dolphins' worst showing since 2023 when they finished 32nd by allowing 30.5 yards per kickoff return.
The Dolphins have used 53 different players on special teams, and the only way this gets better is continuing to churn the roster to find answers because we're thinking (at this point) it's not a schematic issue.
0 — That's the number of leads the Dolphins have held this season, one short of the NFL record of six games to start a season without a lead, a mark that belongs to the 2005 Houston Texans.
And we close with maybe the most painful stat of all, and will repeat our suggestion from last week that the Dolphins should elect to receive if they win the coin toss. Yes, it's usually preferable to defer to be able to potentially get the back-to-back possessions, but desperate times call for desperate measures. And there are times when playing with a lead or a deficit changes game strategy. And it would be nice for the Dolphins not to be chasing the game all the time, like they did against Cincinnati when they won the toss, deferred, gave up an 81-yard kickoff return and were down 7-0 before a minute of game action had expired.
