title: 4 Big-Time Storylines That Could Define Patriots' TNF Battle with Bears
full_text:
CHICAGO — Before the season started, I had the New England Patriots at 4-2 heading into a primetime matchup with the Chicago Bears. Now that we're in Week 7 and the Patriots are set to face these Bears tonight, I'm going to pat myself on the back (although I did have them beating the Jaguars and losing to the Bills).
I think this game will be a real litmus test for the Patriots , who are entering the game on a three-game winning streak. Impressive wins over the Bills and Raiders gave some hope, but last week's victory over the Jets left head coach Mike Vrabel feeling "lucky" with the result. This game, and opponent, doesn't offer that same level of grace.
"There's a lot of volume. They do a lot of things well, and you'll have to be prepared for some unscouted looks," Vrabel said Wednesday on the Bears offense. "But (head coach Ben Johnson) stays aggressive. He has a lot of faith in those guys on fourth down. He marries up formations and motions."
Here are four things to watch when both sides take the field Thursday night, including one of the league's best quarterback matchups of the entire season.
It was not an ideal home opener for Brown, who returned to the field after a high-ankle sprain and a four-week stint on injured reserve. Brown caught just three passes for 27 yards , and was targeted a team-high 10 times. He also dropped three more passes and flubbed an onside kick recovery opportunity.
"It's A.J. Brown. Last week is what it is," Drake Maye said Tuesday. "I wish I had some throws back and attempts I targeted his way, and I think it's part of this league. You want to make a play so bad, you want to have plays back, and there are plays that I want back every week, and that's part of it."
That one game won't define Brown's first season with the Patriots, but he's yet to truly make his mark on the field yet. If he can catch fire on a short week as the team's best offensive weapon, he could help this Patriots offense shine under the lights.
Back in 2024, the Patriots and Bears faced off from Soldier Field. At the time, both sides had rookie quarterbacks and head coaches no longer on the sideline. Two years removed, and Maye and Chicago's Caleb Williams have blossomed into some of the NFL's top gunslingers .
Maye has rebounded from a shaky start to round into form, and Williams — who missed several games with a hamstring injury — is back in full force. Both quarterbacks offer their teams the capabilities to win the game with their arm strength and mobility. They're often compared to each other because of their rookie class, but their play has also earned plenty of praise.
"Him in the pocket, I don't know if I could do some of the things he can do," Maye said. "He's special in the way he can move and kind of escape and evade pressure, and throwing on the run is pretty cool to watch. So, I don't know if I'm that shifty in the pocket. He can do some cool things, and he's got crazy arm talent, and it's fun to watch."
A lot of talk is centered around the Bears' potent offense. But their defense is equally as strong. Getting Kyler Gordon back last week added an extra layer to the secondary, and that unit has a whole has been stout all season.
"It's excellent. It's very good," Vrabel said. "So, I think we have to stay balanced, but also find ways to run the football. They just haven't had a lot of plays against them. When you play with the lead, then you don't see a lot of runs. So that's the challenge."
Heading into Week 7, the Bears rank sixth in scoring defense (19.8 points allowed per game) and eighth in rushing defense (90.5 yards allowed per game). They're about middle of the pack when it comes to passing defense, and that's how the Patriots can put up some points.
Both Vrabel and Johnson have turned their teams around fast, and were both finalists for last year's Coach of the Year award — an award Vrabel would end up winning. But Johnson interviewed for the Patriots' gig back before the 2025 season and there are still some fans around New England who talk about wanting Johnson's extensive offensive playbook.
These are two of the NFL's top head coaches and it should be a fun one to watch from Soldier Field.

title: 5 Players to Watch in Patriots' Primetime Battle Against Bears
full_text:
The New England Patriots' matchup against the Chicago Bears on Thursday night will be among the team's biggest tests of the season.
New England has been hot in recent weeks, riding a three-game winning streak. In that same span, quarterback Drake Maye has scored 11 total touchdowns and thrown just one interception.
But can the Patriots continue that momentum into Thursday night? Here are five of the most important players to watch who could dictate whether or not New England will pull off the win.
The Patriots' run defense has its work cut out on Sunday. Chicago averages the most rushing yards per game in the NFL, with north of 160. However, New England has succeeded in the same department this season. Its 91.8 yards allowed on the ground per game is the ninth-best mark in the NFL.
So, how can the Patriots slow down the Bears' run attack? Enter Williams . After a relatively slow start to the season, New England's star interior defensive lineman has plugged the middle of the field in recent weeks.
"I appreciate what Milt does -- his leadership, his efforts and his impact," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said Monday. "I know that every player wants great stats, but to be able to be disruptive, to play hard and do some of those things that he does and has continued to do in the last three weeks have really helped us defensively."
In his first game back from injured reserve l ast weekend, Brown disappointed. The 29-year-old dropped a career-worst three passes on Sunday. Although he was finding himself open on a consistent basis, the former Philadelphia Eagle simply had a case of the drops.
But now, with fellow receivers Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs on injured reserve, New England may need a high-level performance from Brown on Thursday.
"I think he could've probably made a few more plays, come down with a few more plays," Vrabel told reporters Sunday. "He's been out for a while. I know that he wanted to do well for his football team, and unfortunately it wasn't his best effort. I know that he knows that, and we have all the confidence in the world in A.J. just to be able to finish those plays."
After struggling toward the end of his 2025 campaign, Campbell has shined for the Patriots in his second year. The 22-year-old allowed just one pressure last weekend against the New York Jets, per PFF. Plus, he has allowed just one sack all season. The Bears' defense has tallied tallied the fifth-most sacks in the NFL with 17. With a difficult opponent across the line, another shutdown performance from Maye's blindside protector would be invaluable.
"Just doing everything I can to try to get my body in the best space possible, which I would do anyway," Campbell said on Tuesday. "Just excited. I like these types of weeks. It's fun. A primetime game against a really good team. It's gonna be awesome."
This season, Ponder has been one of the NFL's best edge rushers. The 2025 undrafted free agent sits top-three in the league in sacks (5.5) and tackles for a loss (8). On Thursday, he may be the biggest deciding-factor in whether or not the Patriots can win.
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams was a lethal 24-for-24 from clean pockets last week, per Next Gen Stats. If New England struggles to get pressure on Chicago's third-year signal caller, the game could get out of reach quickly.
The Patriots have dealt with a plethora of interior offensive line injuries this season. Starting right guard Mike Onwenu landed on injured reserve, while left-side starter Alijah Vera-Tucker suffered a hamstring injury on Thursday and has since been ruled out against the Bears. Plus, backup Ben Brown has also been ruled out with a knee injury.
That leaves reserves Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor as New England's two starters on Thursday. In 27 combined pass blocking snaps last week, neither allowed a pressure. While it's a large ask for them to replicate that performance again, a high-level performance from the interior offensive line could play a major role in boosting the Patriots to a win.
"It was fun to watch those guys take advantage of the opportunity," Vrabel said on  Tuesday when asked about Rouse and Pryor. "They helped us. There was a huge drive at the end of the game, to go down there and be able to take time off of the clock."

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.

The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .

title: Saints' Moore Speaks From Paris: Giants Win, Injuries and Steelers Preview
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have arrived in Paris, France, with much-needed momentum after Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants .
Fresh off ending a three-game skid, the Saints face the Pittsburgh Steelers in an international matchup that requires adjusting to a seven-hour time zone difference.
Head coach Kellen Moore noted Monday that arriving early gives players time to acclimate before Wednesday's practices and offers a team-bonding opportunity following their game in New Jersey.
Reflecting on the win over New York, Moore praised the rushing attack, takeaways, and mid-game execution, but stressed the need to finish better after nearly losing a 34-10 fourth-quarter lead.
He also addressed rookie Jeremiah Wright's performance, injuries, and his history with Steelers coach Mike McCarthy from their time in Dallas.
Here is what Moore had to say about the Saints' arrival in Paris, Sunday's victory and preparations for Pittsburgh.
We just got here. Good travel, all that. Our guys were able to get out on the field and walk around and get a light lift in at the hotel.
Obviously, there's a little bit of an acclimation process, but I think it's a great setup. It's an awesome opportunity for our football team to spend some time together while focusing on a really good opportunity to play out here in a great atmosphere. It's been a really fun week.
I think there's a few elements. The acclimation thing is important. For our guys to get here, have a couple days to get acclimated, and then it allows us to have a normal workflow.
Wednesday through Sunday is going to be as normal as possible. I think that's going to be a great opportunity for our guys.
There's always an added bonus of guys having an opportunity to spend a little bit more time together. The bonding element of a team atmosphere, I think it'll be great for our guys.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly: Saints Finally Win, but Major Problems Remain
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally have a reason to celebrate. Their 34-27 victory over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Sunday was far from seamless, but it brought a much-needed end to a troublesome stretch.
Riding a three-game losing streak and facing mounting questions about the franchise's direction, New Orleans desperately needed a win. The Saints delivered by overcoming an early 10-0 deficit, though they nearly squandered a commanding 24-point lead late in the second half.
Quarterback Tyler Shough completed 16 of 30 passes for 144 yards and three touchdowns, guiding an offense that showed encouraging progress on the ground. Meanwhile, the defense created three interceptions despite struggling to contain New York's passing game.
The win gives head coach Kellen Moore 's squad welcome breathing room, after the team entered the week under heavy scrutiny following critical remarks from franchise icon Drew Brees and owner Gayle Benson .
Still, the team's inability to comfortably close out the game after building a 34-10 advantage underscores ongoing concerns about their consistency and ability to finish strong.
Here is a look at the good, bad and ugly from the Saints' victory over the Giants.
Following weeks of criticism regarding a stagnant ground attack, the Saints may have uncovered a workable formula.
New Orleans ran for a season-high 175 yards, offering vital balance to an offense that had relied far too heavily on Tyler Shough to make plays.
Kendre Miller paced the backfield with 70 yards on 20 carries, while C.J. Donaldson added 39 yards on six attempts. Alvin Kamara chipped in 34 yards on seven carries, and Shough contributed 32 yards along with a rushing touchdown.
This collective output was an encouraging sign for a unit that had failed to establish any momentum during its three-game slide.
However, the Saints still have considerable work ahead.
Even so, efficiency remains an issue; Miller averaged just 3.5 yards per carry, reflecting the play-to-play inconsistency that still lingers.
Lineman Jeremiah Wright provided a notable spark after replacing the injured Cesar Ruiz at right guard. His presence was felt in the second half, as the Saints repeatedly—and successfully—ran behind the right side of the line.
To sustain this progress, the offensive line must open cleaner lanes up front rather than depending on backfield effort to gain positive yardage.
While far from dominant, Sunday's performance marked a meaningful step toward a more balanced attack.
Despite forcing three interceptions, the Saints' defensive backfield repeatedly yielded big plays during New York's late comeback bid.
Receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely caused major problems throughout the contest.
Nabers hauled in 12 receptions for 165 yards, while Likely added six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing starter Jameis Winston , backup J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, orchestrating three straight touchdown drives to cut a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
New Orleans did deliver key playmaking moments: Martin Emerson Jr. picked off two passes, Julian Blackmon intercepted another, and the pass rush brought down Winston four times.
However, surrendering 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights persistent pass-coverage issues that defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must resolve.
For three quarters, the Saints looked poised for their most convincing win of the year—a strong statement following three straight home defeats.
Instead, they nearly suffered a catastrophic fourth-quarter collapse.
After trailing 10-0 early, New Orleans reeled off 34 unanswered points using balanced rushing, opportunistic turnovers, and efficient red-zone execution.
Shough's 18-yard touchdown strike to Chris Olave early in the fourth quarter pushed the lead to 34-10, prompting the Saints to begin rotating in reserves.
However, the momentum quickly shifted.
With McCarthy at quarterback, New York scored 17 unanswered points over the final 11 minutes, exploiting defensive breakdowns and stalling offensive possessions.
An offense that had scored on four straight drives suddenly went cold, finishing an alarming 4-for-15 on third down.
Meanwhile, the defense surrendered multiple scoring drives as New York steadily chipped away at the deficit.
The Giants eventually cut the lead to 34-27 and drove deep into New Orleans territory. The Saints survived only when McCarthy's fourth-down pass to Likely fell incomplete near the end zone.
For a Saints team already facing criticism over its lack of consistency, nearly blowing a 24-point advantage raises legitimate questions about its ability to finish games.
Moore and his staff deserve credit for halting the losing streak, but nearly letting a 24-point lead slip away shows that New Orleans still has significant work ahead to compete with top-tier opponents.

title: 4 Takeaways From Saints' 34-27 Week 6 Victory Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally have something to celebrate, although Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium was far from convincing.
After three consecutive losses, mounting criticism, and growing questions about the franchise's direction, New Orleans desperately needed a win. The Saints delivered one, overcoming a sluggish start before nearly squandering a commanding 34-10 lead in the second half.
Quarterback Tyler Shough , who completed 16 of 30 passes for 144 yards and three touchdowns, and the offense showed encouraging signs, particularly with an improved rushing attack, while the defense produced three interceptions despite struggling to contain former Saints quarterback Jameis Winston and JJ McCarthy .
The victory also provided some much-needed relief for head coach Kellen Moore , whose team entered the matchup facing increased scrutiny following public criticism from franchise legend Drew Brees and owner Gayle Benson .
However, the Saints' inability to put away the Giants after building a 24-point advantage demonstrated why significant questions remain about their consistency and ability to finish games.
Here are four instant reactions from New Orleans' much-needed victory.
The Saints always have at least one special teamer that becomes a star whether it’s Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis or Steve Gleason .
This time, it has been linebacker Isaiah Stalbird , who has been valuable on special teams all year, and he made the biggest play of the game.
Trailing 10-3 with less than a minute remaining in the first half, New Orleans looked set to enter halftime with another double-digit deficit. However, Stalbird delivered arguably the biggest play of the afternoon on special teams.
The rookie safety forced a fumble on Charlie Jones 's kickoff return, allowing tight end Oscar Delp to recover the football and give New Orleans possession deep in Giants territory.
Shough capitalized on the turnover, connecting with rookie Bryce Lance for a touchdown that tied the game at 10 with one second remaining before halftime.
The sequence completely changed the momentum.
After struggling offensively throughout much of the first half, the Saints suddenly found themselves in position to take control. New Orleans carried that momentum into the third quarter, scoring 24 additional unanswered points to build a commanding advantage.
Although Stalbird's contribution won't receive the same attention as Shough's four-touchdown performance or Martin Emerson Jr. 's two interceptions, his forced fumble was arguably the game's most important play.
After weeks of heavy criticism in regard to its horrendous rushing attack, the Saints may have figured out the formula.
New Orleans finished with a season-high 175 rushing yards, providing much-needed balance to an offense that has frequently relied on too much on Shough to generate production.
Kendre Miller led the charge with 70 yards on 20 carries, while C.J. Donaldson contributed 39 yards on six attempts. Alvin Kamara added 34 yards on seven carries, and Shough chipped in another 32 yards and a touchdown run.
The production was particularly encouraging considering New Orleans had struggled to establish a reliable ground game during its three-game losing streak.
However, the Saints still have considerable work ahead.
Miller averaged just 3.5 yards a carry, highlighting the inconsistency that continues to plague the rushing attack despite the improved overall numbers.
Another player worth monitoring is offensive lineman Jeremiah Wright , who came in for the injured Cesar Ruiz at right guard. His impact became noticeable as it was a trend that the Saints ran the ball to the right a solid amount in the second half and with success.
The Saints need their offensive front, including Wright when he is involved, to create more consistent running lanes rather than relying on individual efforts to generate positive yardage.
Sunday's performance was hardly a dominant rushing effort, but it represented a meaningful step forward for an offense desperately searching for balance.
Despite grabbing three interceptions, the Saints' secondary once struggled once again against a solid receiving corps in coverage during New York's fourth-quarter comeback.
Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely torched New Orleans’ secondary all game.
Nabers recorded 12 catches for 165 yards, while Likely had six catches for 99 yards and a touchdown.
After replacing Jameis Winston, J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards in just over 11 minutes, sparking three straight touchdown drives to trim a 34-10 deficit to seven points.
Still, the defense created crucial takeaways: Martin Emerson Jr. had two interceptions (one off McCarthy), Julian Blackmon picked off Winston, and the pass rush logged four sacks on Winston.
Yet, allowing 461 total yards (377 passing) highlights the already serious concerns on whether or not the secondary can slow so. Defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must fix these coverage breakdowns to prevent future collapses.
Few teams entered Week 6 under more pressure than the Saints.
Following three consecutive losses, including a disappointing 23-13 defeat against the Minnesota Vikings , New Orleans found itself under intense scrutiny from fans, former players and ownership.
Former Saints quarterback Drew Brees, who called the game for Fox and was inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime during the loss to the Vikings, criticized the team's offense and Moore's play-calling .
A few days later, Saints owner Gayle Benson publicly expressed her frustration with the team's 1-4 start during a speaking engagement at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club, making it clear that recent performances were unacceptable.
Benson specifically challenged the team's leadership, including Moore and general manager Mickey Loomis , to address the mistakes that had contributed to the disappointing start.
Those comments placed additional pressure on Moore, whose second season as head coach has been defined by inconsistent performances and questions about the team's direction.
Sunday's victory provided a much-needed response.
The Saints showed resilience after falling behind 10-0, capitalized on turnovers and demonstrated the offensive explosiveness that had been largely absent during their losing streak.
More importantly, they found a way to win.
Yet blowing nearly all of a 24-point fourth-quarter lead highlighted the issues behind Benson's criticism. With execution and closing troubles nearly turning a blowout into a loss, the 2-4 Saints face major questions before playing the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris. Snapping the streak offers short-term relief, but New Orleans must show real growth to make this a true turning point.

title: Saints vs. Giants: Can New Orleans Snap Its Losing Streak? Our Staff Predicts
full_text:
The pressure continues to mount on the New Orleans Saints as they head to the Meadowlands for Sunday's Week 6 showdown against the New York Giants , desperately searching for answers amid a disappointing start to the season.
Following a frustrating 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , the Saints (1-4) have dropped three consecutive games, raising questions about the team's direction under second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
The struggles have even drawn the attention of team owner Gayle Benson , who recently expressed frustration with the organization's performance and made it clear that continued losing would not be tolerated without consequences.
With expectations rising and patience wearing thin, New Orleans faces another difficult challenge against a surprising Giants team that has emerged as an early contender in the NFC East.
Here are our predictions for Sunday's game.
This is the Saints' first road game since Week 2, and it’s a strategic one at that, as the Saints will immediately fly out of New York for their game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris next week. However, this is a critical game for coach Kellen Moore , and maybe even longtime general manager Mickey Loomis .
I don’t think Tyler Shough will have many games like he did last week in the loss to the Vikings, but he will have another matchup against a top-10 defense as the Giants are ninth in total defense. The strength of the defense is its ability to defend the pass, allowing only 199.7 yards per contest, which is good for seventh in the NFL, and have forced six interceptions, which is good for fourth.
While I think Shough will do much better, the Giants have the players needed to at least limit Shough, and New Orleans’ rushing attack is one of the NFL’s worst and will be ineffective. While the Giants have struggled to stop the run, they will have no trouble stopping the Saints.
Defensively, I think the Saints will do enough to keep the game close but not enough to win. The Giants aren’t the greatest offense in the world, but Cam Skattebo is a decent running back, while the receiving threats of Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely are going to give the Saints’ defense a heap of trouble.
I predict a one-score game in the Meadowlands with the Giants pulling it out.
Which Saints club will show in the Meadowlands today? Will it be the one from the first three weeks of the season, or the one from the last three?
We know this: those leading this organization have been put on notice by the woman that holds the checkbook. For the first time as owner of the Saints, Gayle Benson is faced with a situation that will require resolve and a possible move that will force her to make decisions that will be uncomfortable. She has put her trust and belief in those in charge. After seeing where her club has gone in the last few weeks, and the fan reaction to that direction, Mrs. Benson is having to rethink that trust.
Meanwhile, a two-week road trip followed by the Saints open/bye week may be just what the doctor ordered for Moore and his troops: a chance to regroup and rethink where things are.
Being a "glass-half-full" kinda guy, I'm getting this feeling this may be the first step to Moore, his coaches, and his players turning things around. However, don't bet the house on who I choose to win today. I've only been right once in five prognostications this year.

title: Saints vs. Giants: Three Things New Orleans Must Do to Win at the Meadowlands
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter Sunday's Week 6 matchup with a trip to the Meadowlands against the New York Giants looking to avoid their fourth consecutive loss, but a familiar face stands in their way and remains a fan favorite in New Orleans.
Former Saints quarterback Jameis Winston will lead the Giants against his former team as New Orleans attempts to rebound from a disappointing 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings .
The Saints (1-4) have struggled to find consistency on both sides of the football, particularly offensively, where turnovers and an ineffective rushing attack have contributed to their disappointing start.
Meanwhile, the Giants (3-1-1) have emerged as one of the NFC's early surprises under first-year coach John Harbaugh , overcoming injuries and inconsistent quarterback play to remain atop the NFC East.
Beyond Winston's reunion with New Orleans, the Saints must contend with two dangerous receiving threats in Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely while finding a way to exploit New York's ball-security problems.
A persistent issue for New Orleans throughout Kellen Moore ’s tenure has been their inability to build early momentum.
Across 22 games with Moore at the helm, the Saints have managed a mere 35 points in the first quarter. During this stretch, they have logged 29 three-and-outs—the highest tally in the league—and have yet to top seven points in any opening period.
These early-game woes have persisted into the current season. Atlanta built a 14-0 first-quarter cushion against New Orleans in a 45-24 Saints loss. The following week, Minnesota held New Orleans scoreless in the opening frame as the Saints were limited to 142 total yards.
Finding an offensive rhythm from the opening kickoff must be a top focus for Moore.
Achieving this requires steering clear of costly penalties, executing on third down, and keeping quarterback Tyler Shough in manageable down-and-distance scenarios.
With a playmaking Giants offense on the horizon, another slow start risks burying New Orleans in a hole too deep to climb out of.
Containing wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely—quarterback Jameis Winston's primary targets—presents the New Orleans defense's most formidable task, even as Winston draws significant focus.
Together, Nabers (29 receptions, 329 yards, two TDs) and Likely (33 receptions, 284 yards, four TDs) account for most of the team's targeted passes and 58% of its overall offensive yardage.
Nabers, the former LSU standout, has successfully recovered from a season-ending knee injury. His recent performances include a six-catch, 112-yard game with a touchdown against Arizona in Week 4, followed by an 11-reception, 121-yard, one-touchdown outing on 20 targets versus Washington.
Over-focusing on Nabers creates chances for Likely, the former Baltimore Raven who has emerged as Winston's top redzone option. Against Washington, Likely caught 11 passes for 94 yards and two scores, becoming the first tight end in Giants franchise history to record at least nine catches and two touchdowns in a single game.
Standing 6-foot-4, Likely poses significant coverage challenges due to his size and athleticism. Following recent difficulties against Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers , limiting Likely will be a critical test for the Saints' defensive scheme.
New Orleans must balance its coverage duties to avoid exposing defensive backs to disadvantageous single-coverage looks against either receiver.
Despite their contrasting records, both the Saints and Giants have struggled with ball security this season.
New York has committed seven turnovers through five games, including three interceptions and four lost fumbles. Meanwhile, New Orleans enters Sunday's matchup with a minus-six turnover differential.
However, the Giants have compensated for their mistakes by intercepting six passes, tied for third-most in the NFL, while the Saints have recorded just one interception.
That discrepancy could prove decisive, particularly with quarterback Tyler Shough coming off a disappointing performance against Minnesota.
Shough completed 16 of 25 passes for just 96 yards and two interceptions, finishing with a 38.1 passer rating. Through five games, he has thrown for 1,299 yards, nine touchdowns and five interceptions.
For the Saints, protecting the football, forcing Winston into difficult throws and capitalizing on New York's mistakes could determine whether they snap their three-game losing streak.

title: Giants Injury Report: O-line Looking Better, but Two Key Defenders Still Sidelined
full_text:
The New York Giants injury picture appears to be improving, at least on one side of the ball.
Offensive tackles Andrew Thomas (groin), Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), and Marcus Mbow (knee) were all limited participants on Thursday after sitting out Wednesday’s session.
Thomas looks likely to play after the team last week held him out even after he passed the concussion evaluation and despite the offense’s attempt to mount a comeback, even though he had been evaluated for a concussion and passed the tests. But the veteran left tackle has been laboring through his groin injury, raising the question of how much longer he can keep going.
Eluemunor missed last week’s game against the Saints because he couldn’t establish an anchor given his injured leg. His return would be huge as the Giants face a Houston Texans pass rush that features league sack leader Will Anderson Jr., along with Danielle Hunter and Jadeveon Clowney.
Mbow, the swing tackle, is also a key player, as he’d be the first off the bench if Thomas or Eluemunor couldn’t go the distance.
On the other side of the ball, the Giants remain without two key pieces on defense. Inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds (shoulder) and cornerback Greg Newsome II (concussion) missed their second straight day of practice, and their statuses for Sunday’s game remain uncertain.
Edmunds wears the radio in his helmet, but if he can’t play, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said the Giants have options.
“We have options. Micah (McFadden) — he can call a defense. Arvell (Reese) can call a defense. Jack Kelly can call a defense. Zaire (Barnes), we’ve done this in preseason. We’ve done it throughout training camp. All the guys have had the opportunity to call a defense, and we’ll see how it shakes out come Sunday,” he said.
Tight end Chris Manhertz (calf) was added to the injury report after missing practice on Thursday. Cornerback Colton Hood (concussion), punter Jordan Stout (right knee), and outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux (illness) were all upgraded to full participation.

title: “Unacceptable”: Dennard Wilson Vows to Fix Giants’ Defense After Poor Showing Against Saints
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ change at quarterback has dominated the headlines this week as Big Blue is set to launch the J.J. McCarthy era, with the hope that the more mobile McCarthy will change how opposing defenses approach the Giants’ offense, particularly the stagnant running game.
But another area of concern has been flying under the radar for the team: run defense, which remains an issue despite the resources pumped into the unit’s improvement.
The Giants’ run defense has surrendered the fourth-most rushing yards (813) through six weeks, and its 5.0 yards allowed per carry is the second-worst mark in the league, trailing only Carolina’s 5.1.
The Giants’ run defense has also allowed opponents a 63.7% success rate on their runs (10th in the league) and a 73.3% conversion rate on third-down rushing attempts, the second-worst rate in the league.
It goes without saying that the run defense has not been good enough, especially given the investment in the defensive front.
Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has taken notice.
“We put some stuff on tape that was not characteristic of a New York Giants defense, and it’s unacceptable, and it will be changed,” Wilson said.
Wilson said those things included players not running to the ball and sloppy tackling technique.
“I look at guys that don’t run to the ball, and I call them traitors because they’re traitors to the defense. At the end of the day, when you have a traitor to the defense, you either have to make adjustments to get them off the field, you have to get somebody else on the field, or they have to correct their behaviors,” he said.
The Giants have been trying to beef up their run defense ever since Wilson was hired by head coach John Harbaugh to run the unit, and it seems like they have been trying to get it right for years.
While each year might have its own story, the recurring theme seems to be discipline.
“I think sometimes just a little bit of the fits on just some of the stuff — cleaning up that type of thing,” said defensive lineman D.J. Reader. “We’ve let some quarterback runs beat us in some places.
“I think it is just a discipline of play in and play out. Teams are going to keep trying to attack you with different runs. The plunge play was a play that we fit well sometimes, and we didn’t fit as well sometimes. So, it was just about seeing more looks and getting those fits figured out.”
The Giants’ run defense, which also ranks second worst in the league for the most big-play runs of 20+ yards allowed (4.5%), has especially struggled against pre-snap motion, which has put defenders in gaps they haven’t adjusted to or that leave them at a disadvantage.
“Sometimes a motion here or something like that might put you in a different gap. And you’ve just got to revert to knowing your basics and be confident in the rest of your brothers to make sure they’re going to be where they’re at, so you need to be where you’re at,” Reader said.
Besides the pre-snap motion giving the run defense some fits, the Giants’ tackling in their Week 6 loss to the Saints also left a lot to be desired.
Per PFF, the Giants had 13 missed tackles , seven of them against the run . In an even more alarming stat, the Giants had 16 run plays last week in which a defender made contact with a ball carrier but failed to get him to the ground on first contact, which ranked 11th in the league in Week 6, per PFF data.
“Last week was one of our worst tackling games for whatever reason,” Wilson admitted.
“It’s really going back to the basics. We have to go near hip, near half. We have to attack the ball carriers in the center mass, and we’ve got to run our feet on contact. A few plays got out, especially in the pass game, because of missed tackles. Then last week, we weren’t happy, and I wasn’t happy with our effort running to the ball.”
Wilson believes the poor tackling stemmed from not enough people running to the ball and, more importantly, poor technique.
“A couple of plays that we had last week, instead of going near hip, near half and trying to run through a ball carrier, we stuttered our feet,” he said.
“When you stutter your feet, you give them a two-way go. So, we have to be like heat-seeking missiles. When we break in coverage, when we break on the ball coming out of the stack, we need to attack the near hip and near half, and we need to run through ball carriers instead of catching them.”
Wilson is determined to get the team playing up to the level he believes it’s capable of as a collective, especially against the run. He said it all starts with everyone communicating and doing their assigned jobs.
“It takes all 11. That’s a huge emphasis for us,” he said. “For us, it’s about getting lined up, getting set, and then with the motions, the pre-snap and post-snap movement, we have to communicate a lot better.
“That’s been a big point of emphasis, not only from the start, but even picking up even more right now. Once we get our feet in the ground and they start moving, we have to communicate. … Then we’ve got to come downhill, and we’ve got to tackle.”

title: Jameis Winston Takes Demotion in Stride as J.J. McCarthy Steps In for Giants
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston is no stranger to shifting job status during his 12-year NFL career.
Four games after the Giants named him their starter following a season-ending knee injury to Jaxson Dart, Big Blue is pulling Winston from the starting lineup. Head coach John Harbaugh announced on Wednesday that the team would switch to former No. 10 overall pick J.J. McCarthy for the Week 7 matchup with the Houston Texans.
The move, which Harbaugh wouldn’t call a permanent one, came after Winston’s mistake-filled performance against the New Orleans Saints last Sunday, in which he completed 14 of his 26 pass attempts for 152 yards and threw two interceptions that helped the visitors pour on 34 unanswered points to open up a rout in the second half.
McCarthy replaced Winston in the final 11 minutes of the fourth quarter and set league history by throwing for 243 yards, leading New York into the red zone three times and falling one touchdown short of carrying them back from a grueling defeat.
The effort was enough to convince the Giants’ coaching staff to move forward with the newly acquired McCarthy. For Winston, the demotion to backup is purely a change in role, not a change in the mindset he has held since day one with the organization.
“Just focusing on one day at a time is the biggest thing,” Winston said about the quarterback change following the team’s practice on Wednesday.
“I’m extremely grateful that I still get to do what I love, and that’s play football at a high level for the New York Football Giants. And being able to accept roles and understand what your significant role is, and how you can be the best at your role with this team, is one of the things that you have to adjust to in this league.”
For most of his professional career, Winston has made himself into a player who could go on stretches where he impresses a team and its fanbase with his volatile arm, the same one that made him the No. 1 overall pick in the 2015 draft and produced three seasons with over 4,000 passing yards and at least 22 touchdowns in his first five years.
At the same time, the typically charismatic Winston has repeatedly struggled to hold on to the starting job with the four franchises he’s played for because he tends to force the ball into tight windows, leading to a whopping 118 interceptions in 113 career games.
Despite the ugly side to his résumé, the Giants brought Winston back in 2026. They offered him a two-year extension, believing he was still among the best options to step into the fold if anything took Dart off the field for an extended period.
That insurance policy became necessary less than two games into the year. It paid off, as Winston put forth what Harbaugh called “a tremendous job,” throwing for 806 yards, six touchdowns, and just two interceptions to lift the Giants to a 2-0-1 stretch and put them in first place in the NFC East for the first time in well over a decade.
One hideous outing against the Saints quickly shifted the narrative. With a more prepared McCarthy waiting in the wings, both sides realized New York’s best chance of staying in the playoff race would be handing the reins to the 23-year-old quarterback.
“I believe that last game, it wasn’t what it was capable of being,” Winston said of the team's performance against the New Orleans Saints last week. “I think every single week, as a football team, you’re defined by the last time you stepped foot on the field.
“So, I believe that based on the last game, my job is to lead the New York Football Giants to a win, and that didn’t happen. So that being said, I understand where I’m at now.”
With one week left before their bye, Winston finds himself back in the role the Giants originally signed him for: backing up a younger quarterback.
Still, instead of a promising second-year player in Dart, he gets to mentor a fellow former first-round pick in McCarthy, who missed all of his rookie year with a torn meniscus in his right knee and barely got a fair shake in 10 starts with the Vikings in 2025.
It’s never an easy transition for a veteran who knows he’s on the back nine of an NFL career and has had to prove multiple times that he can overcome his faults to earn a team’s trust again.
If anyone is suited to be McCarthy’s tutor in this situation, it is Winston, given the experience he’s gained in creating new chances at the highest level. He knows he must show that level of selflessness to help his new teammate revive his talents and carry the Giants to additional wins down the stretch.
So, while he won’t impact what happens on the field this coming Sunday in Houston, he’ll certainly be in McCarthy’s corner in practice and along the sidelines, cheering him on while looking for lessons he can take toward improvement and remaining grateful that he can still play a role in the Giants’ success.
“By being my very best,” Winston said.
“That’s how you support a young man: by coming to work, being the same person every single day, by showing respect and gratitude for the opportunity that he’s presented with and the opportunity that I had, and understanding that gratitude is the key to abundance in all of this.
“When you come to work and you approach it from a grateful mindset, it leads out to the entire building, and nothing really changed but the role itself.
“Every day is going to continue to be focused on getting one percent better in terms of preparation, in terms of who I am to my teammates, in terms of being ready when opportunity presents itself when I’m on the field again.”

title: Why J.J. McCarthy Feels Better Prepared for Giants' Starting Opportunity
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is no stranger to starting at quarterback in the NFL.
Before Big Blue acquired him on Sept. 28, the 10th overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft started 10 games for the Minnesota Vikings in 2025, posting a 6-4 record as the club’s QB1.
Unfortunately, inconsistencies and clashes with Minnesota’s coaching staff led to his demotion and eventual exit from the Land of 1,000 Lakes.
Yet less than a week after leading New York’s offense on three fourth-quarter scoring drives in its 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints in Week 6, McCarthy has been named the Giants’ new starter , replacing 12-year veteran Jameis Winston .
Armed with the experience of one failed experiment, McCarthy is determined to make the most of his new opportunity in East Rutherford.
“It has been a whirlwind,” McCarthy said. “But just being here and getting this opportunity, I am just so blessed. And I thank God every single day; I thank the Mara family and this organization for allowing me this opportunity.”
McCarthy’s ascension to New York’s starting role came as little surprise, given his performance against the Saints.
Despite being used only in select packages in the Giants’ 27-27 tie with the Washington Commanders in Week 5, McCarthy entered the game with 11 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, taking the offensive reins after Winston’s second interception of the day.
Though his first drive ended in an interception of his own, the best was yet to come for the 6-foot-3, 219-pound quarterback.
He finished the game having completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards and one touchdown.
McCarthy had the most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any player this season, and the second-most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any quarterback who didn’t start over the last 25 seasons.
For McCarthy, it was an opportunity not only to showcase his potential, but also to demonstrate that he has learned from his past struggles with the Vikings.
“Yes, sir. I believe just experience does wonders,” McCarthy said. “Being able to be in that same situation where you might have made a mistake the last time, this time you’re just going to react better and make a more well-rounded response decision in that situation.
“Just being around great talent and great coaches is great,” he continued. “I absolutely love everyone on the offensive side of the ball, and the defensive side of the ball does a tremendous job of just giving us opportunities and always making sure we stay in the game and fight to the last seconds of each game.”
While McCarthy’s tenure in Minnesota can hardly be described as disastrous, his statistical output did little to impress. The 23-year-old struggled with accuracy and decision-making.
He ultimately completed 140 of 243 pass attempts for 1,623 yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. He also ran 37 times for 181 yards and four touchdowns.
Still, McCarthy knows more is expected of him as a New York Giant. Big Blue is currently in first place in the NFC East with a 3-2-1 record.
As their Week 7 road matchup with the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium approaches, McCarthy will be called upon to lead his team in practice and serve as a central figure in the locker room.
In that regard, the former Michigan Wolverine is ready to accept the responsibility that comes with his newfound power.
Simply put, McCarthy is ready to seize the opportunity head coach John Harbaugh has given him. In the spirit of his head coach, he will take each moment in stride.
“Every time you step on the field, it’s an opportunity,” McCarthy said.
“Whether you’re the starting guy, whether you’re not, you have a chance to prove yourself, prove it to your peers, and prove it to everyone around you. And at the end of the day, I approach it the same way. How can I attack that next rep? How can I win this day and go from there?”

title: Giants QB Switch Q&A: Why McCarthy, Why Now?
full_text:
From the very moment the New York Giants acquired quarterback J.J. McCarthy in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings, it became just a matter of time before the team would flip the switch to McCarthy over Jameis Winston, the backup to Jaxson Dart, who, before the start of the 2026 season, signed a two-year extension to continue as the team’s quarterback understudy.
But when Dart went down with a season-ending knee injury seven snaps into their Week 2 game, concerns began to arise because the Giants’ offense, as constructed, wasn’t set up to favor Winston’s more classic dropback style of play.
That became evident right off the bat when, seven snaps into Week 2, Dart had to exit the game, leaving Winston, the “next man up” who coaches will tell you has to be ready at any given time, to struggle his way through an offensive game plan that didn’t suit his strengths.
So here we are: McCarthy is the starter, and Winston has been demoted to backup. Let’s break down the big move.
Two reasons. They apparently feel comfortable enough with McCarthy’s knowledge of the playbook and, just as important, his ability to protect himself if they should have to deviate.
The second reason is that, despite Winston leading the team to a 2-1-1 record, that record came with a struggle. The run game suffered because Winston isn’t an ideal fit for the RPO/designed-run part of the playbook.
And with the NFC East there for the taking, the decision was made to make the move now rather than put off what was widely regarded as inevitable.
Like the pro he is. Winston, a team captain, said, “I’m extremely grateful that I still get to do what I love, and that’s play football at a high level for the New York Football Giants. And being able to accept roles and understand what your significant role is, and how I can be the best at my role with this team, is one of the things that you have to adjust to in this league.”
As he did in a support role with Dart, Winston intends to support McCarthy and the rest of the team in whatever capacity he’s asked.
The best way to describe his public reaction is humility. McCarthy said he views this opportunity with the Giants as a chance for a fresh start, and he’s focused on getting up to speed on the offense and repaying the team’s confidence in him.
“I’m focused on that next thing, what’s next? No matter what, there’s going to be factors that are outside of my control that are going to steer me in certain directions,” he said.
“I’m going to continue to focus on the things that I can control, and go from there, and yeah, that’s kind of how it went.”
For the same reason you saw play out. Winston can go in there for part of a game or even for a handful of games and keep you in the mix, which is what he did for the Giants.
But his days of carrying a team for an entire season are long gone. The Giants, in realizing that they have an opportunity to win the division, made the switch and will have Winston, who has been a model locker room citizen and a big-time help to the younger quarterbacks in their meeting room, serve as a support system, which is what his original role was intended to be.
To be honest, we’d have concerns about that pass rush even if they could play. But McCarthy is mobile.
He can use his legs to move the pocket as need be. Winston? Not so much.
That doesn’t mean the Giants have nullified the Texans’ pass rush with this move, but there is hope it won’t be as productive as it might have been with Winston.
A little. He’s been here less than a month, so it’s fair to wonder about his chemistry with his receivers, especially since Winston is thought to have gotten the bulk of the reps with them in practice.
But to his credit, McCarthy often stayed after practice to work on various routes with receivers to get up to speed on verbal and nonverbal communication.
Simple. McCarthy’s ability to execute the RPO/designed runs now gives the defense another runner they have to account for, which means they might think twice about crowding the box.
The Giants have faced the sixth-most crowded boxes this season, and much of that is because opposing defenses know Winston really isn’t a threat to run.
McCarthy is, so the hope is that his presence will discourage so many stacked boxes, which in turn should help the sagging running game get back on track.
First, let’s hope he doesn’t struggle, because that would mean the season is heading in the wrong direction. But if McCarthy struggles this week against the Texans, it’s highly unlikely he’ll get a quick hook. In fact, because his skill set is a better fit for the offense and how it’s been designed, barring injury, it’s hard to envision McCarthy not finishing out the season as the starter.
Nothing. Dart is going to be the starter. If McCarthy does well, the Giants will have the option to trade him or Winston to a quarterback-needy team next offseason, a move that would undoubtedly bring in draft picks.
If McCarthy does well, the Giants will almost certainly pick up the option year in his rookie deal, a decision they have to make after this year. So that is something else to keep in mind.

title: Giants Open as 10.5-Point Underdogs at Texans
full_text:
With just one game left before their bye week and uncertainty at quarterback, oddsmakers have reached their lowest point in backing the New York Giants .
After their disappointing performance against the New Orleans Saints last Sunday, Vegas appears to expect a worse outcome for Big Blue in Week 7. FanDuel Sportsbook has made the Giants a 10.5-point road underdog as they make a trip down south to face the Houston Texans.
The opening line marks the largest underdog number the Giants have faced this season and extends their streak to three straight games as the doubted franchise. FanDuel also set the total at 43.5 points.
The Texans got off to a rocky 0-4 start to the 2026 season, but have since won two straight games in which their offense has looked much sharper and their defense, led by the pass rush, has been heating up and causing real problems for opposing offensive lines.
On offense, Houston has ratcheted up scoring to 26 points or more in the last two weeks, a trend built on the rising confidence of quarterback C.J. Stroud, who has completed 71.6% of his pass attempts in that span and has a 6-1 touchdown-to-interception ratio.
Their coverage game is certainly nothing to write home about when they’ve been attacked through the air.
Still, the Texans make up for that weakness with the strength of their pass-rushing duo of veterans Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter, who have already combined for 14 sacks and 60 total pressures with more than half a season left.
Having those two top-five defenders coming at the Giants’ banged-up offensive line off the edges could pose a huge threat to either quarterback’s hopes of creating the offensive efficiency they need to keep up with the Texans’ fiery offense.
The Giants were without both of their starting offensive tackles for part of the game against the Saints, with Jermaine Eluemunor missing the contest with a calf injury and Andrew Thomas leaving the game due to his groin injury.
As soon as both men were removed from the starting front and replaced by rookie J.C. Davis and Marcus Mbow, the offense began to deal with more pressure from the Saints defense, which made it hard for Winston or McCarthy to have the most time to make their reads and attack the best options through the air.
Looking back at both teams’ recent history, it makes sense that Vegas is leaning heavily toward the hosting Texans, who are coming off an electric divisional win against the Jaguars in London last Sunday.
For the Giants, the start of the week has brought nothing but questions at the most important position on the field and a few roster changes.
Even for a resilient group like the Giants, all the negative press is bound to affect how the rest of the football world sees their chances as the more difficult portion of their schedule arrives.

title: Giants Have Bigger Problems Than the QB Decision
full_text:
The eagerness to see how head coach John Harbaugh will manage his quarterback situation Sunday against the Houston Texans may have overshadowed a few other issues the team still needs to figure out this week.
The New York Giants have yet to establish a consistent ground attack. The offensive line has not blocked as well as expected, and the stable of running backs that opened the season hasn't performed to its potential. Suffice it to say that both of those units must share the blame - and at least one of these units needs to step up its production in a hurry.
"I thought we'd be running the ball better at this point in terms of outcome and result, and we haven't been able to do it," Harbaugh said this week.
"We're not blocking well enough. We're not running well enough. We're not putting up enough yards. We're not putting up enough consistency. We're not efficient in our run game."
The Giants rank 19th in the NFL with 104.8 rushing yards per game and 22nd with 3.8 yards per attempt. On the flip side, the Texans' defense stands third in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game (83.0) and in rushing yards per attempt (3.4).
The Giants face the same issue on defense, ranking 29th in stopping the run (135.5) and 31st in rushing yards per carry (5.0). It almost doesn't matter how weak an opponents' ground game is when you haven't shown the ability to slow things down. So, Houston is apt to try running the ball with Woody Marks despite the league's 25th-rated run game (84.8) that has gained just 3.6 yards per try (29th)
"I think it is just a discipline of play in and play out," said nose tackle D.J. Reader. "The teams are going to keep trying to attack you in different runs. ... And you’ve just got to revert to knowing your basics and be confident in the rest of your brothers to make sure they're going to be where they're at, so you need to be where you're at."
The slide on special teams over the past two weeks has been the most surprising development, considering this unit was among the NFL's elite after the first four games of the season. Penalties, porous kick/punt coverage, mistakes in the kicking/punting game - and the "turning point" kickoff return turnover against New Orleans - have contributed to the Giants' bumpy road to 3-2-1.

title: Harbaugh Explains Switch to J.J. McCarthy at QB: “This Is Going to Be Our Direction”
full_text:
Every decision New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh makes is meant to serve the franchise’s best interests, and that’s no different for his big switch at quarterback from Jameis Winston to J.J. McCarthy.
“What gives us the best chance to be our best? Gives us the best chance to play the best offense we can?” Harbaugh said after making the news official on Wednesday.
“I thought Jameis has done a tremendous job. Won us games, played well. But as we go forward here, this is going to be our direction, and we think it gives us some good options on offense.”
By switching to McCarthy, the Giants get a quarterback with a skill set much closer to what they lost when starter Jaxson Dart went down in Week 2. At that point, New York had to abandon its designed runs and RPO packages, which weren’t a fit for Winston’s skill set.
Still, with a modified game plan for Winston each week, the 12-year veteran quarterback helped the team reach a 2-1-1 record.
Although Harbaugh wouldn’t say the move was permanent for the rest of the season, he admitted that “J.J.’s got a skill set that we can take advantage of, and we’re excited to see what we can do with it.”
Harbaugh said the offense will be mostly the same for McCarthy as it was for Winston and Dart, but admitted some plays were better suited to each quarterback than to the others.
“The concepts are still there, the blocking schemes are the same. It’s not going to be a big adjustment for the rest of the guys,” he said.
“I’m not going to say it’s not a work in progress — everything is a work in progress. I’m not going to say it would be like having your starting quarterback from the beginning; it’s definitely different. But it can be done.”
He added that the goal is to win a very winnable NFC East.
“We’re trying to take it as far as we can and win as many games as we can,” Harbaugh said. “We’ve got goals, and we’re excited to go play this game (against Houston). But we’re up for it. Up for the challenge, and we can’t wait to get down there.”

title: Giants Injury Report: Giants O-line Thinned By Injuries
full_text:
The New York Giants will face one of the best defenses on Sunday when they travel to Houston to meet the Texans. So it was a bit alarming that on Wednesday, the team’s top three offensive tackles were not practicing.
Starters Andrew Thomas (groin), Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), and swing tackle Marcus Mbow (knee) were not participating in practice during the media viewing period.
Thomas, who has sat out Wednesday and Thursday over the past several weeks and returned to practice on a limited basis on Friday and Saturday before being cleared to play, is someone to watch this week.
Last week he came out of the game just before the big fourth-quarter comeback attempt against the Saints; the veteran left tackle was visibly laboring through his groin injury throughout the game.
Eluemunor missed last week’s game as well with his injury after saying he would test it to see if he could anchor; he is also someone to watch this week. And with MBow now nursing something, the Giants could be thin at offensive tackle if he can’t play.
The Texans have league sack leader Will Anderson, Jr. on one side of their formation and Danielle Hunter on the other. That would be quite the test for rookie J.C. Davis, who would presumably play left tackle; at right tackle, the Giants could potentially move Sisi Mauigoa from right guard to tackle, the position he played in college.
Inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds (shoulder) and cornerback Greg Newsome II (concussion) were not spotted at practice during the media viewing portion.
If Edmunds can’t go, Micah McFadden would get the start. The question then becomes who would wear the radio in his helmet: rookie Arvell Reese, the most likely candidate, or someone else.
Starting safety Jevon Holland was spotted at practice, off to the side with a trainer. Newsome and Holland have been the Giants defensive secondary’s best players so far this season, so hopefully their absences aren’t serious enough to keep them out of Sunday’s game.
Rookie Colton Hood (concussion), receiver Darnell Mooney (neck), safety Tyler Nubin (neck), and tight end Theo Johnson (neck) were spotted at practice during the media viewing portion.
Cornerback Paulson Adebo’s 21-day practice window is now open. If he clears, he could fill the roster vacancy left after Tuesday’s release of running back Najee Harris and defensive lineman Jihad Ward.
Adebo has been on IR since Week 2 with a knee injury and would serve as depth if Newsome doesn’t clear the protocol in time.
Speaking of the cornerback position, Newsome did not practice, but rookie Colton Hood (concussion) did.
With their top three offensive tackles — Andrew Thomas, Jermaine Eluemunor, and Marcus Mbow — all injured, the New York Giants signed offensive lineman Josh Sills from the Colts practice squad to their 53-man roster.
Sills, 6-foot-6 and 325 pounds, was originally an undrafted free agent out of Oklahoma State whom the Eagles signed in 2022. That season, Sills, who has played guard in his short NFL career, was one of three undrafted free agents to make the Eagles roster but only appeared in one game for Philadelphia.
After the 2022 season, Sills was . He then joined the Colts in 2023, for whom he appeared in 20 games with no starts.
Sill has played  in his NFL career, most of them at guard. Before the NFL, he played college ball at West Virginia and Oklahoma State,  on the offensive line.
The Giants had two open roster spots this week. They filled the first with outside linebacker Trace Ford, whom they signed off their practice squad after cutting defensive lineman Jihad Ward. Sills takes the spot that opened after running back Najee Harris was cut on Tuesday.

title: Giants Will Start J.J. McCarthy Over Jameis Winston Against Texans
full_text:
The New York Giants have decided on their starting quarterback, and Big Blue will hand the keys to the offense to J.J. McCarthy this weekend against the Houston Texans, head coach John Harbaugh confirmed.
“All things considered, what gives us the best chance to play the best offense we can,” Harbaugh said after announcing the move. “I though Jameis has done a tremendous job — he won us games, played well. But as we go forward this is gonna be our direction and we think it gives us some good options on offense.”
Winston, a team leader and captain, predictably took the news of his emotion with the utmost professionalism.
“I'm extremely grateful that I still get to do what I love and play football at a high level for the New York Football Giants, and being able to accept roles and understand, ‘What is your significant role? How can I be the best at my role with this team?’ That’s one of the things that you have to adjust to in this league.”
The decision between McCarthy, whom the Giants acquired in a trade less than a month ago , and Jameis Winston, who has driven the offense since starter Jaxson Dart went down with a season-ending knee injury seven snaps into the team’s Week 2 game against the Los Angeles Rams, doesn’t really come as much of a surprise.
McCarthy is more of a mobile quarterback who, unlike Winston, can run the RPO game and hence give the Giants’ sagging rushing offense, which has averaged just 3.8 yards per carry, another player for whom the defense now must account.
Last week, Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy praised McCarthy as being “A+” in his grasp of the Giants offense. The former Vikings draft pick showed some moxie for the Giants when he entered the game with a little more than 11 minutes remaining.
McCarthy led the Giants back from a 34-10 deficit to within one score of tying the Big Blue’s Week 6 game against the New Orleans Saints. He finished 11 of 21 for 243 yards, one touchdown and one interception, and led the Giants’ rushing attack with 26 yards on two carries.
McCarthy, who failed to grab the starting job with the Vikings, said he thinks this time around he’s better prepared to make the most of the opportunity he’s been given.
“I believe just experience does wonders. You know, being able to be in that same situation where you might have made a mistake the last time, this time, you're just gonna react better and make a more well-rounded decision in that situation.
“Just being around great talent and great coaches — absolutely love everyone on the offensive side of the ball and the defensive side of the ball does a tremendous job of giving us opportunities and always making sure we stay in the game and fight till the last seconds of each game.”

title: Confidence Meter: How Close I Feel the Jets Are to Firing Aaron Glenn in Week 7
full_text:
The Jets were historically bad in 2025, finishing 3-14 and becoming the first team in NFL history to finish a season without recording a single interception. Despite this, New York opted to give head coach Aaron Glenn another year.
New York didn’t let him off the hook easily. By replacing 12 of his 22 assistants from last year’s staff and making roster additions across the board, it’s evident that the Jets’ brass wants to see improvement under Glenn.
Improvement was Glenn’s goal entering his second season , and so far, New York has made some progress.
Through six weeks, Gang Green currently sits in third place in the AFC East with a 2-4 record. The Jets have been far more competitive than last season, with all but one of their losses having been tightly contested, and the defense has shown improvement.
However, some issues remain, with poor coaching decisions and trouble executing in the final two minutes of the first half among the most concerning.
Although the team doesn’t look as bad as it did last year, Glenn must fix these issues if he wants to remain the head coach. Here's how I'm feeling about the Jets head coach's outlook and whether a potential firing is on the horizon.
One of the biggest changes from last year is that Glenn has taken over defensive play-calling duties. So far, the decision has appeared to pay off.
Under Glenn’s aggressive approach, the defense has significantly improved at generating pressure, tying for fifth in sacks (17) and ranking 10th in pressure rating (24.3%). Additionally, the Jets have impressed against the pass, ranking fourth in passing yards allowed per game (185) and 11th in air yards allowed (662).
New additions David Bailey and Dane Belton have been key contributors to the unit’s success.
Bailey has been New York’s most consistent pass rusher, leading the team in pressures (23) and sacks (5). Meanwhile, Belton continues to make plays all over the field and has stood out against the run, earning an 89.7 run-defense grade , per Pro Football Focus, ranking third among 98 qualifying safeties.
Glenn’s defensive improvements have kept the Jets in games. Through six games, the defense ranks seventh in points allowed per game (20.7) and has given up more than 30 points only once. Last year, New York allowed 30 points or more three times in its first six games and eight times in the season.
The defense’s success has played a critical role in New York’s two victories, allowing just 10 points to the Titans and 12 to the Browns.
While the Jets still have plenty of issues to address, the defense’s progress is an encouraging sign for Glenn in his second season. Although they need to do a better job of creating turnovers and containing the run, the unit has taken a step forward.
If Glenn wants to remain in New York, he needs the defense to maintain a similar level of play moving forward.
For the most part, Glenn has done well on the defensive side. Still, he’s made several questionable decisions, which have arguably cost the Jets a win or two.
In last week’s game against the Patriots, Glenn opted to go for it on fourth down twice instead of kicking from 48 and 57 yards. It’s one thing to be aggressive later on when the game is getting out of hand and nothing is working, but passing up potential points in the second quarter while trailing by a touchdown is another story.
It didn’t help that offensive coordinator Frank Reich— who's also drawn criticism this year —dialed up a run in shotgun formation on fourth-and-one and a quarterback sneak.
Another questionable decision by Glenn in this game came on New England’s 42-yard touchdown pass to receiver Romeo Doubs (h/t NFL). On the play, Glenn rushed just three players and dropped David Bailey into coverage.
42-yard touchdown from Maye to Doubs! NYJvsNE on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tKpDzX136o
This gave Patriots quarterback Drake Maye seemingly all the time in the world to find the open Doubs, punishing Glenn for the terrible call.
Glenn’s game management hasn’t been much better either. The Jets’ inability to execute in the final two minutes of the first half has been one of the team’s biggest weaknesses since Glenn’s arrival.
Through six games this season, New York has been outscored 20-0 in this situation. The problem extends beyond this season, as this has been a recurring problem since Glenn joined. In his 23 games as head coach, the Jets have been outscored 100-6 in the first half's final two minutes (h/t ESPN 's Rich Cimini).
To break this down further, they’ve been outscored in the final two minutes of the first half, 100-6, over Glenn’s 23 games. Next closest team: Packers, -40 pt differential. https://t.co/GTMDrAvwAD
Whether it’s clock management, play-calling, or execution, the Jets struggle in moments where every possession matters. Finding ways to score in these situations has to be a priority moving forward, especially given how close their games have been.
The other major concern is that the offense hasn’t improved under Reich. New York brought in the former head coach of the Colts and Panthers, hoping that his experience would help turn things around on offense. However, he’s been extremely underwhelming.
The Jets have scored just 112 points this season, fewer than the 123 they scored through their first six games in 2025. Given all the additions and changes to the coaching staff and roster, their lack of progress on offense has been disappointing.
Reich has failed to use Garrett Wilson consistently , targeting him heavily in some games while turning away from him in others. Wilson has had more than seven targets in just two games and must find a way to get the ball to their star receiver more often, especially in the red zone.
Through six games, New York ranks last in red zone touchdown efficiency (37.5%).
While Reich deserves his share of the blame, Glenn deserves scrutiny for the offense’s continued struggles as well. As head coach, he is responsible for holding his coordinators accountable and ensuring the team improves in its weakest areas. Glenn’s continued public support of Reich raises questions about whether the coaching staff is doing enough to address the offense’s problems.
Despite the Jets’ struggles, I don’t believe Glenn is on the verge of being fired. Even if the numbers don’t back up the offense, the team has improved from a talent and execution standpoint and is significantly more competitive than last season.
However, I do believe Glenn’s seat is undoubtedly getting warmer. With the offense continuing to underperform, it’s held them back and cost them some games. Just look back at their Week 2 loss against the Packers.
After taking a 10-point lead, the Jets managed just one first down before punting. They later failed to convert on fourth-and-1 near midfield. After taking two sacks in overtime, they punted, allowing Green Bay to drive down the field for the game-winning field goal.
Even as the team continues to make mistakes, Glenn remains confident in the team’s direction, comparing the Jets’ competitive stamina to the 2022 Lions, who started 1-6 before finishing 9-8. While this comparison offers some optimism, New York must turn its competitiveness into wins.
That’s why this week’s upcoming matchup against the Dolphins could be an important test. It’s a game they should win against an inferior team, but a loss would add to the mounting pressure on Glenn and his coaching staff.
I don’t believe Jets owner Woody Johnson and the Jets’ brass would move on from Glenn mid-season. However, if the team doesn’t progress and poor coaching decisions continue, his long-term future in New York will become increasingly uncertain.
For now, Glenn’s seat is warm, but there’s still plenty of football left for him to turn things around—or make his situation worse.
